sessions.name: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI

questions.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
questions.stem: According to the AMA definition used in Session 1, marketing is the activity, institutions and processes for creating, communicating, delivering and exchanging offerings that have:
options: Value for customers, clients, partners and society
Competitive advantage over rivals
Awareness among target segments
Profit for shareholders
questions.explanation: The AMA definition ends with 'value for customers, clients, partners, and society at large'. Profit and competitive advantage are outcomes a firm hopes for, not the definition. Awareness is only the first funnel stage.
questions.trap: Profit sounds like the obvious goal of marketing; the definition is about value exchanged.

questions.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
questions.stem: Levitt's line 'People don't buy a quarter-inch drill, they buy a quarter-inch hole' is used in Session 1 to make which point?
options: Value comes from solving the consumer's problem, not from the product itself
Customers always prefer physical products to services
Advertising should describe product features in detail
Products must be cheaper than competitors' products
questions.explanation: Levitt's quote illustrates 'sell solutions': value creation means thinking about the consumer's problem and offering a solution. It is not about price or feature lists. The slide pairs it with 'I feel alone → love and belonging'.
questions.trap: Choosing a feature-focused answer when the point is the need behind the purchase.

questions.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
questions.stem: Session 1 explains value using Maslow's hierarchy of needs. Which statement about the hierarchy did the slides make?
options: The hierarchy applies to B2B markets only
Customers prioritise lower needs before higher ones
Higher needs are always more profitable to serve
Only self-actualisation needs create brand loyalty
questions.explanation: Slide 19 states that customers prioritise lower needs. Value is created by satisfying a need at any level, for example clothing sold as belonging or self-esteem. The other options are not claims made in the course.

questions.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
questions.stem: The STP framework is presented as the middle path between two extremes. Which pair correctly names those extremes?
options: Identity vs image
Treat all customers the same vs treat each customer differently
Mass production vs mass customisation
Market research vs marketing analytics
questions.explanation: Slide 25: the two extremes are treating all customers the same and treating each customer differently; STP (segmentation, targeting, positioning) sits between them. Identity vs image is the positioning distinction, not the two extremes.
questions.trap: Identity vs image belongs to positioning, a step inside STP.

questions.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
questions.stem: In the targeting step of STP, which set of criteria did Session 1 list for evaluating segments?
options: Size, growth, alignment, competition
People, products, periods, places
Reach, frequency, impact, cost
Awareness, interest, desire, action
questions.explanation: Slide 27 lists size, growth, alignment and competition, and says to target the segments with the highest ROI. AIDA is the purchase funnel; People-Products-Periods-Places are Kopalle's dynamic-pricing drivers from Session 6.
questions.trap: AIDA and Kopalle's 4 Ps are planted as familiar four-item lists.

questions.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
questions.stem: Positioning, as defined in Session 1, is about how the firm wants customers to perceive the brand. The slide warns that 'identity ≠ image'. What is the difference?
options: Identity is online; image is offline
Identity is the logo; image is the advertising
Identity is for products; image is for services
Identity is what the brand intends; image is what customers actually perceive
questions.explanation: Identity is the intended position the firm communicates; image is the perception that forms in customers' minds. They can diverge, which is why positioning must be checked with research. The other pairs are not the course distinction.

questions.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
questions.stem: Which list correctly names the 4Ps of the marketing mix as taught in Session 1?
options: Product, Positioning, Price, Persuasion
People, Products, Periods, Places
Product, Price, Place, Promotion
Planning, Pricing, Packaging, Publicity
questions.explanation: The marketing mix is Product, Price, Place and Promotion (often attributed to Borden, 1964). People-Products-Periods-Places is Kopalle's definition of dynamic pricing in Session 6, a deliberate near-miss.
questions.trap: Kopalle's dynamic-pricing 4 Ps versus the marketing-mix 4Ps.

questions.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
questions.stem: Which element below belongs to the Place P of the marketing mix rather than Promotion?
options: Advertising budget
Channel coverage and logistics
Public relations
Message and media choice
questions.explanation: Slide 33 lists channel members, channel coverage, locations, logistics and service levels under Place. Message, media, budget, PR and advertising all sit under Promotion.

questions.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
questions.stem: Session 1 says STP belongs to the strategic stage and the marketing mix to the tactical stage. Which activity is tactical?
options: Choosing how the brand should be perceived against competitors
Identifying groups of similar customers
Setting the product's price, packaging and sales channels
Deciding which customer segments give the highest ROI
questions.explanation: Slide 31 says that after STP 'we now reach the tactical stage' and decide price, packaging, advertising and channels, the marketing mix. Segmenting, targeting and positioning are strategic steps.
questions.trap: Targeting sounds operational but is part of strategy in the course map.

questions.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
questions.stem: The canonical purchase funnel introduced around 1898 by St. Elmo Lewis is known as:
options: AIDA
STP
RACE
4Ps
questions.explanation: AIDA (Attention, Interest, Desire, Action) is the canonical purchase funnel model from about 1898. STP and 4Ps are the strategy and tactics frameworks; RACE is not part of the course.

questions.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
questions.stem: How does the customer journey concept differ from the AIDA funnel in Session 1?
options: The journey is used only for B2B customers
There is no difference; the terms are interchangeable
The journey only covers post-purchase; AIDA covers pre-purchase
The journey maps physical and digital touchpoints on the way to purchase and beyond; AIDA is a staged mental sequence
questions.explanation: Slide 38 defines the customer journey as physical and digital touchpoints on the way to purchase and beyond, often paired with personas. AIDA describes stages in the consumer's mind from attention to action.

questions.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes market research from marketing analytics, as defined in Session 1?
options: Research is for new products; analytics is for pricing
Research is done by agencies; analytics is done in-house
Research uses qualitative data; analytics uses quantitative data only
Research is the systematic study of a specific marketing problem; analytics is constant measuring and monitoring of marketing performance
questions.explanation: Slide 42 defines market research as systematic design, collection and analysis of data relevant to a specific marketing problem; slide 44 defines marketing analytics as constant measuring, monitoring and analysing of marketing data and performance. Both can use qualitative and quantitative data.
questions.trap: Qualitative vs quantitative is a data type split inside research, not the research–analytics split.

questions.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
questions.stem: Data collected first-hand for a specific problem is called:
options: Primary data
Synthetic data
Panel data
Secondary data
questions.explanation: Primary data is collected first-hand; secondary data already exists. Synthetic data (Session 2) is generated by an LLM and is neither of the classic two.

questions.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
questions.stem: Which pairing of data type and description is correct according to Session 1?
options: Qualitative – words, meanings, experiences
Quantitative – words, meanings, experiences
Secondary – collected first-hand
Qualitative – numbers and statistics
questions.explanation: Qualitative data is words, meanings and experiences; quantitative data is numbers and statistics. Secondary data is existing data, not first-hand.

questions.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
questions.stem: Session 1 lists examples of what marketing analytics covers. Which option is NOT among them?
options: Focus-group moderation
Optimisation and machine learning
Forecasting
Marketing dashboards
questions.explanation: Slide 44 lists dashboards, forecasting, optimisation and machine learning under marketing analytics. Running focus groups is a data-collection method within market research.
questions.trap: Focus groups are research, not the constant monitoring of analytics.

questions.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
questions.stem: A fashion retailer says 'we sell a sense of belonging, not clothing'. In Session 1 terms, this is an example of:
options: Price discrimination
Channel coverage
Creating value by satisfying a need in Maslow's hierarchy
Secondary data analysis
questions.explanation: Slide 20 asks 'do we sell clothing or a sense of belonging or self-esteem?' to show that value is created by satisfying a need. It has nothing to do with pricing, channels or data.

questions.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
questions.stem: A manager says 'Our customers differ in age, personality, purchase history and location, so one message fits nobody.' Which Session 1 concept does this describe, and what does it justify?
options: The customer journey, justifying more touchpoints
Customer heterogeneity, justifying STP
Positioning, justifying higher prices
Secondary data, justifying desk research
questions.explanation: Slide 24 lists demographics, personality, life experience, purchase history and location as sources of customer heterogeneity, and slide 25 says this is why we apply STP instead of treating everyone the same.

questions.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
questions.stem: A brand has a clear intended position of 'premium craftsmanship' but surveys show customers see it as 'overpriced'. Which Session 1 distinction explains this gap?
options: Primary vs secondary data
Identity vs image
Strategy vs tactics
Segmentation vs targeting
questions.explanation: Identity is the intended perception; image is what customers actually perceive. The gap between 'premium craftsmanship' and 'overpriced' is exactly identity ≠ image. The other pairs describe different parts of the marketing process.

questions.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
questions.stem: Session 1 says managers base decisions on three things. Which trio is correct?
options: Research, analytics, AI
Awareness, interest, action
Experience, intuition, data
Budget, timing, competition
questions.explanation: Slide 41: managers base decisions on experience, intuition and data, with the line 'In God we trust, all others bring data'. Market research and marketing analytics are the two firm functions that supply data.

questions.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
questions.stem: Which assessment weights were set out for MKTG644 in Session 1?
options: Participation 25%, project 25%, exam 50%
Participation 20%, project 40%, exam 40%
Participation 25%, project 35%, exam 40%
Participation 30%, project 30%, exam 40%
questions.explanation: Slide 8: class participation 25%, group project 35%, final exam 40%. The slide adds that quality and relevance of contribution matters.

questions.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
questions.stem: In the Session 1 team exercise on whether AI is a marketing friend or foe, which structure was the class asked to use?
options: A ranking of AI tools by price
A forecast of marketing jobs lost by 2030
A SWOT of the top five AI vendors
Impact on marketing vs other functions, revenues vs costs, strategy/mix/MR/MA, and consumer behaviour
questions.explanation: Slide 49 asked teams to analyse AI's impact on marketing vs other functions, on revenues vs costs, on strategy, marketing mix, market research and analytics, and on consumer behaviour, then conclude friend or foe. The professor wants a structured analysis, not opinion.
questions.trap: A 'friend or foe' verdict without structure earns little; the frameworks are the point.

questions.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
questions.stem: Which reading cited in Session 1 reported that 65% of CMOs expect advances in AI to dramatically change their role within two years?
options: McKinsey – The State of AI in 2025
BCG – From Campaigns to Business Value
HBR – AI Is Upending Marketing on Two Fronts
Gartner CMO survey
questions.explanation: The Gartner survey is the source of the 65% CMO figure. BCG and McKinsey are the other two Session 1 readings; the HBR 'two fronts' article belongs to Session 3.
questions.trap: The HBR article is a Session 3 reading planted as a near-miss.

questions.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
questions.stem: The group project brief says a segment that is psychologically interesting but cannot be reached on an ad platform is unusable. Which Session 1 targeting criterion does this most directly extend?
options: Segment size
Alignment with the firm's capabilities and ability to reach the segment
Competition intensity
Growth
questions.explanation: Targeting evaluates size, growth, alignment and competition. Identifiability on Meta is a practical form of alignment: can the firm actually serve and reach this group? A large or growing segment that cannot be reached still yields no ROI.

questions.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
questions.stem: Across the course, which Session 1 idea is the root of personalised advertising (S4), personalised pricing (S6) and segment-specific creatives (group project)?
options: The Place P of the marketing mix
The AIDA funnel
Customer heterogeneity leading to STP
Secondary data
questions.explanation: Personalisation is STP taken to its limit: because customers differ, different messages, prices or creatives create more value. AIDA describes stages, not differences between people; data types and Place are unrelated.

questions.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
questions.stem: Segmentation, as defined in Session 1, means:
options: Mapping all touchpoints before purchase
Setting a different price for each customer
Choosing the one most profitable customer
Identifying a small set of groups of similar customers
questions.explanation: Slide 26: segmentation identifies a small set of groups of similar customers. Choosing which groups to serve is targeting; individual prices are dynamic pricing (S6); touchpoint mapping is the customer journey.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between a synthetic participant and a digital twin, as defined in Session 2?
options: A participant is used for quantitative research; a twin for qualitative
A twin is cheaper because it needs no human data
A participant is an LLM adopting a persona; a twin is calibrated on a specific real person's prior survey or interview answers
A twin is a more detailed persona prompt than a participant
questions.explanation: Slide 22 defines synthetic participants as LLMs prompted to adopt a persona. Slide 23 defines a digital twin as an AI model calibrated on a specific real person's actual prior answers, used to predict how that person would respond to new stimuli. A twin needs rich, recent human data, so it is not 'just a detailed persona'.
questions.trap: Treating the twin as merely a richer persona.

questions.stem: Which list gives the four cons of synthetic participants exactly as the Session 2 slides present them?
options: Bias, variance, noise, drift
Hallucination, overfitting, sampling error, non-response
Hallucination, bias amplification, regression to the mean, trained behaviour
Cost, latency, bias, privacy
questions.explanation: Slide 25 lists hallucination (also in interpreting the prompt), bias amplification (stereotypes), regression to the mean (average internet opinion) and trained behaviour (harmlessness and fairness tuning). The other lists mix statistics or ML terms not used on the slide.

questions.stem: A synthetic panel reports narrower, more 'average' opinions than real consumers. Which con is this?
options: Bias amplification
Regression to the mean
Hallucination
Trained behaviour
questions.explanation: Regression to the mean means the LLM reports the average internet opinion, so the spread of answers is narrower than real humans'. Bias amplification is the opposite failure, exaggerating stereotypes; trained behaviour is politeness from safety tuning.
questions.trap: Bias amplification and regression to the mean are opposite failures that students swap.

questions.stem: A persona prompt says 'above median income' and the LLM assumes the respondent prefers premium, higher-quality products. Which con is at work?
options: Regression to the mean
Trained behaviour
Sampling error
Hallucination in interpreting the prompt
questions.explanation: Slide 25 gives exactly this example under hallucination: 'also in interpretation of prompt, e.g., more expensive = higher quality?'. The model invents a link not stated in the prompt.

questions.stem: Synthetic respondents are suspiciously polite, agreeable and avoid negative views. The slides attribute this to:
options: Regression to the mean
Bias amplification
Few-shot prompting
Trained behaviour from harmlessness and fairness tuning
questions.explanation: Trained behaviour: harmlessness and fairness are part of LLM training, which makes answers polite and agreeable. Regression to the mean is about averaging opinions, not politeness.

questions.stem: Korst, Puntoni and Toubia (2025), cited in Session 2, describe four roles for AI in market research. Which option correctly pairs a role with its example?
options: Fill gaps – auto-transcribing interviews
Create new – coding open-ended answers
Support – digital twins
Replace – synthetic participants
questions.explanation: Slide 21: support = speed up existing methods (transcribing, coding open-ends); replace = synthetic participants instead of human data; fill gaps = insight where human data is unavailable (niche segments, sensitive topics); create new = digital twins.
questions.trap: Digital twins belong under 'create new', not 'support' or 'replace'.

questions.stem: Session 2 lists pros of synthetic participants. Which is NOT one of them?
options: New capabilities such as digital twins
Access to hard-to-reach groups and sensitive topics
Speed, scale and cost
Guaranteed representativeness of the population
questions.explanation: Slide 24 lists speed/scale/cost, access to hard-to-reach groups, and entirely new capabilities. Representativeness is a weakness, not a strength: the slides warn of regression to the mean and bias amplification.

questions.stem: The PNAS reading tested LLMs with the 11–20 money request game. What did the game measure, and what did the authors find?
options: Reasoning depth; LLMs showed lower reasoning levels and a different answer distribution from humans
Brand recall; LLMs recalled more brands
Risk appetite; LLMs were identical to humans
Price sensitivity; LLMs were more price-sensitive than humans
questions.explanation: The 11–20 game tests reasoning depth. Slide 27: LLMs showed a lower level of reasoning than humans, their distribution did not match the human one, and results varied across LLMs and task designs.

questions.stem: In the PNAS study, which technique made LLM responses human-like and not significantly different from human responses?
options: RAG with access to the original paper
Adding demographics to the prompt
Fine-tuning on many sample answers
Chain-of-thought zero-shot prompting
questions.explanation: Slide 31: RAG made results more human-like but still significantly different; fine-tuning (updating parameters on many sample answers) produced human-like results not significantly different. Zero-shot tricks and demographics did not help (slide 29).
questions.trap: RAG improved results but did not close the gap; only fine-tuning did.

questions.stem: Which statement about few-shot prompting matches Session 2?
options: It always makes results more stable than zero-shot
It provides sample answers; results are strongly driven by those samples and not necessarily more human-like
It gives the LLM access to external documents at inference time
It updates the model's parameters with new examples
questions.explanation: Slide 30: few-shot provides sample answers (common and less common), model parameters are not updated, and results are strongly driven by the provided samples. Parameter updates are fine-tuning; external documents are RAG.

questions.stem: Zero-shot tricks such as chain-of-thought, 'take a deep breath' or changing the input language and role were tested in the PNAS study. The slides report that:
options: They did not make responses more human-like and language/role changes made results highly unstable
They only worked when combined with RAG
They made responses reliably more human-like
They reduced hallucination to zero
questions.explanation: Slide 29: chain-of-thought and task breakdown did not make results more human-like; input language and role made results highly unstable; demographics did not help either.

questions.stem: The slides ask a pointed question after showing that fine-tuning on human answers makes LLMs human-like. What is it?
options: Why do LLMs refuse to answer money questions?
Why fine-tune when RAG is cheaper?
Why use synthetic participants if we already have the human data?
Why do humans reason less than LLMs?
questions.explanation: Slide 31 ends with 'Why would we use synthetic participants if we already have the data?'. If you need real human answers to calibrate the model, the cost advantage of synthetic data shrinks.

questions.stem: Slide 32 asked whether LLMs can explain their own behaviour. An LLM chose 19 'because of loss aversion' and still chose 19 when the payout was fixed regardless of the number. What does this show?
options: The stated explanation did not actually drive the choice; self-reports are unreliable
The LLM understood loss aversion perfectly
The game was badly designed
Fixed payouts make humans choose 19 too
questions.explanation: When the payout no longer depended on the number, loss aversion could not explain choosing 19, yet the LLM still did. Its explanation was a post-hoc story, so you cannot trust an LLM's account of its own reasoning.

questions.stem: Session 2 concludes the synthetic-research discussion with which stance?
options: Apply but remain cautious; severe validity concerns may fade as LLMs improve
Use only for quantitative surveys
Replace human research entirely; validity concerns are outdated
Never use synthetic participants
questions.explanation: Slide 33: huge benefits in speed, scale and cost; severe concerns about validity; concerns may fade as LLMs improve; 'apply but remain cautious'. Asking the right question to a synthetic participant may be an even greater challenge than to a human.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly lists the market research pipeline from Session 2?
options: Sampling → survey → dashboard → optimisation
Data collection → problem definition → reporting → analysis
Problem definition → research design → data collection → processing and analysis → reporting and strategy
Hypothesis → experiment → publication
questions.explanation: Slide 7 gives the five-step pipeline: problem definition, research design, data collection, data processing and analysis, reporting and strategy. Slide 17 adds: don't stop after analysis; translate into recommendations.

questions.stem: 'If we introduce a new white label design, will sales increase compared with current volume?' is an example of which research type?
options: Causal research
Descriptive research
Exploratory research
Secondary research
questions.explanation: Slide 9: causal research applies when the problem is clearly defined and asks whether a change causes an outcome ('Do we sell more if we use white labels?'). Exploratory handles ambiguous problems; descriptive profiles who buys.
questions.trap: Descriptive research vs the descriptive analytics question type in Session 8.

questions.stem: Research types sit on a scale of uncertainty. Which ordering from most to least uncertain is correct?
options: Descriptive → exploratory → causal
Exploratory → descriptive → causal
Causal → descriptive → exploratory
Causal → exploratory → descriptive
questions.explanation: Slide 9 shows increasing problem clarity: exploratory (ambiguous problem, 'is there a market for customised wine?'), descriptive (aware of problem, 'what kind of people buy our products?'), causal (clearly defined, 'will a new design raise sales?').

questions.stem: Which sampling technique is a probability technique according to the Session 2 taxonomy?
options: Convenience sampling
Stratified sampling
Quota sampling
Snowball sampling
questions.explanation: Slide 15: probability techniques are simple random, stratified and cluster sampling. Convenience, judgmental, quota and snowball are non-probability techniques.
questions.trap: Quota sampling sounds systematic but is non-probability.

questions.stem: In sampling terms, a single customer selected for research is called the:
options: Sample
Stratum
Population
Element
questions.explanation: Slide 14: population = all target customers, sample = customers selected for research, element = a single customer. A stratum is a subgroup used in stratified sampling.

questions.stem: Why is traditional market research expensive, according to Session 2?
options: Data storage is costly
Software licences dominate the budget
Participant recruiting, screening and compensation, instrument design, and analysis all cost money
Regulators charge fees for surveys
questions.explanation: Slide 19 lists participant costs (recruiting, screening, compensation), instrument design (survey, focus group, experiment) and analysis, plus the problems of finding participants and dealing with bots. This cost is what makes synthetic participants attractive.

questions.stem: The first Tesla Model Y example prompt led respondents to focus on EVs and hybrids. Slide 37 proposes adding instructions such as 'allow some respondents to prefer petrol cars'. What dilemma does the slide raise?
options: Whether to switch from Tesla to BYD
Whether such steering corrects bias or steers participants too much
Whether to use 50 instead of 100 respondents
Whether the prompt is too long for the model
questions.explanation: Slide 37 asks 'Or would this steer participants too much?'. Adding independence and variety instructions reduces one bias (EV focus) but risks imposing the researcher's assumptions. Honest reflection on this trade-off is what the exercise rewards.

questions.stem: The Session 2 exercise asked you to generate 100 synthetic responses on four things. Which option is NOT one of them?
options: Whether the product is in the consideration set
Willingness to recommend on a 0–10 scale
Perceived price point (too high / fair / too low)
Main competitors
questions.explanation: Slide 35 lists consideration set, main competitors, perceived price point, and strengths and weaknesses versus competitors. Net-promoter-style scores were not part of the brief.

questions.stem: The example prompt on slide 36 has two parts. What is the second part?
options: Ask the LLM to fine-tune itself
Ask the LLM to translate into Mandarin
Ask the LLM to generate ad images
Ask the LLM to act as an analyst and tally consideration, competitors, price fairness and top strengths/weaknesses
questions.explanation: The prompt first generates 100 consumers' answers, then says 'Now act as an analyst' to count how many would consider the Model Y, list competitors by mentions, summarise price fairness and rank strengths and weaknesses by frequency.

questions.stem: The Nespresso group project ran two independent analyst passes with an 88% agreement check and cross-checked counts against raw data. Which Session 2 concern does this most directly address?
options: Hallucination in the analysis step and the need to treat synthetic results as hypotheses
Regression to the mean in pricing
The uncanny valley
Participant compensation costs
questions.explanation: The LLM can hallucinate not only as a respondent but also as the analyst that counts answers. Independent analyst runs and raw-data checks test the reliability of the analysis, consistent with slide 33's 'apply but remain cautious'.
questions.source: S2 slides 25, 33; Group project prompt pack

questions.stem: RAG appears in Session 2 and again in Session 7. Which statement captures the difference in what each session asks of it?
options: S2 asks whether RAG makes LLM surrogates more human-like; S7 asks whether RAG makes chatbot answers correct and current
S2 says RAG updates parameters; S7 says it does not
There is no difference; both sessions treat RAG as fine-tuning
S2 uses RAG for images; S7 for text
questions.explanation: Same mechanism, different test. In S2, RAG gave the LLM the original 11–20 paper and made answers more human-like but still different. In S7, RAG grounds chatbot answers in company documents so they are current and citable. RAG never updates parameters; that is fine-tuning.
questions.trap: Same word, different purpose across sessions.

questions.stem: Which trio correctly names the three types of search goals and queries from Session 3?
options: Relevance, importance, authority
Informational, transactional, navigational
Organic, paid, generative
Awareness, consideration, purchase
questions.explanation: Slide 8 lists informational, transactional and navigational queries, which roughly align with stages of the customer journey. Organic/paid/generative are search-marketing approaches; relevance and importance are ranking pillars.

questions.stem: The query 'dbs contact number' is best classified as:
options: Transactional
Informational
Exploratory
Navigational
questions.explanation: Slide 9 lists 'dbs contact number', 'singapore airlines website' and a product manual as navigational queries: the user wants to reach a specific site or page. 'Best baby stroller' is informational; 'buy coffee machine online' is transactional.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly separates SEO, paid search and GEO as defined on slide 10?
options: SEO improves visibility in LLMs; GEO improves organic rank; paid search is obsolete
SEO pays for position; paid search improves organic rank; GEO improves visibility in LLMs
All three pay search engines for placement
SEO improves organic rank; paid search pays for an ad slot; GEO improves visibility in LLMs
questions.explanation: SEO improves organic search rank without paying the engine; paid search buys a position in an ad slot; GEO improves visibility in LLM answers. Slide 22 stresses 'we don't pay search engines' for SEO.

questions.stem: Search engines do not search the live web at query time. Instead they:
options: Search a massive database built by crawling and indexing
Query each website's server in real time
Rely on paid listings only
Ask an LLM to summarise the web
questions.explanation: Slide 12: a search engine searches a massive database of web content created by crawling (following links from seed sites) and indexing (storing and categorising content).

questions.stem: The two pillars search engines use to judge the quality of a match are:
options: Speed and freshness
Clicks and conversions
Keywords and images
Relevance and importance
questions.explanation: Slide 17: relevance is the extent to which page content matches the query; importance is the number of sites linking to the page and the importance of those sites. Click-through rate and loading time are secondary factors (slide 20).

questions.stem: Which statement about the 'importance' pillar is correct?
options: Importance is measured by page length
Importance is the number of keywords matching the query
Importance depends on the number and the quality of incoming links; a link from Forbes boosts it more than one from a small blog
Importance is the same as click-through rate
questions.explanation: Slide 19: importance is measured by incoming links, and not only their number but their quality. The World Bank beats 'Jason's blog' for similar content; a Forbes link gives a big boost. Keyword overlap is relevance, not importance.
questions.trap: Relevance (text match) vs importance (links).

questions.stem: When judging relevance, why do search engines 'control for length of text'?
options: Pages with more text are more likely to match more query words by chance, so raw overlap would favour long pages
Short pages load faster
Google penalises pages over 1,000 words
Long pages are always spam
questions.explanation: Slide 18: relevance is the overlap between query and page text, but pages with more text are more likely to match, so engines control for length and assign weights to words (some words matter more than others), and handle spelling, synonyms and word order.

questions.stem: Which factor was listed on slide 20 as likely to LOWER search rank?
options: Higher click-through rate
A suspiciously large increase in importance
A steady increase in importance
Fast loading time
questions.explanation: Slide 20: click-through rate (+), increase in importance (+), suspiciously large increase in importance (−), presence of malware (−), long loading time (−). A sudden link spike looks like manipulation.

questions.stem: In SEO, developing helpful content around researched keywords is called ______, while attracting links from other sites is called ______.
options: Paid search; organic search
Indexing; crawling
Off-page SEO; on-page SEO
On-page SEO; off-page SEO
questions.explanation: Slides 25–26: from keyword to content is on-page SEO (improves relevance); content promotion that attracts links is off-page SEO (boosts importance).

questions.stem: Puntoni (2026), cited on slide 28, names two key developments that force firms to move beyond SEO. They are:
options: Paid search inflation and ad blockers
Cookies disappearing and privacy law
Learning without websites and bots as customers
Mobile search and voice search
questions.explanation: Slide 28: 'learning without websites' (customers use LLMs and often never visit the source site) and 'bots as customers' (decisions outsourced to LLMs). Both require rethinking marketing strategy.

questions.stem: On slide 29, where do LLMs sit relative to social media and search engines in the consumer journey?
options: LLMs create need awareness; social media handles transactional search
All three play identical roles
Social media creates need awareness; LLMs are used for early information search; search engines for targeted transactional search
Search engines create awareness; LLMs close the sale
questions.explanation: Slide 29 (Puntoni 2026): social media creates awareness of a need, LLMs are used for early information search, and search engines for targeted transactional search.

questions.stem: SEO optimises rank. According to slide 31, GEO optimises which of the following?
options: Number of backlinks from LLM providers
Page load time and crawl frequency
Paid placement inside chatbot responses
Being included in the LLM answer, word count or share of answer, position-adjusted word count, subjective impression, and being recommended
questions.explanation: Slide 31 lists GEO's optimisation targets: inclusion (yes/no), word count (share of the answer), position-adjusted word count (earlier citations weigh more), subjective impression (relevance, influence, uniqueness) and being recommended. See Aggarwal et al. (2024).
questions.trap: GEO does not optimise 'rank'.

questions.stem: Slide 32 compares LLM search with search engines. Which row is correct?
options: Unit of relevance – LLM: the whole page; search engine: a passage
Retrieval – LLM: synthesises a handful of passages into one narrative answer with citations; search engine: ranks pages and returns a list of links
Archiving – LLM: an index of keywords mapped to URLs; search engine: frozen training snapshot
Crawling – only search engines crawl
questions.explanation: Slide 32: LLMs crawl for pre-training and live retrieval, hold two memories (frozen snapshot and live retrieval), retrieve passages and synthesise one cited answer; the unit of relevance is a passage or sentence. Search engines index keywords to URLs, rank whole pages and return links.
questions.trap: The planted distractor reverses the unit of relevance (page vs passage).

questions.stem: Slide 33 names two key challenges of GEO. They are:
options: Technical (the LLM must be able to retrieve our content) and content (the LLM must include us in its answer)
Mobile and desktop
Legal and ethical
Budget and talent
questions.explanation: Slide 33: the LLM should be able to retrieve information from our website (technical) and should include us in its answer (content). Slide 34 covers the technical side; slides 35–37 the content side.

questions.stem: Which technical GEO recommendation did slide 34 make?
options: Move all content into images
Block AI crawlers to protect content
Ensure content is crawlable, do not block good AI crawlers, use semantic HTML and reduce latency; LLMS.txt is not necessary
Create an LLMS.txt file; it is essential
questions.explanation: Slide 34: ensure content is crawlable, don't block the good AI crawlers, use semantic HTML, reduce latency, and LLMS.txt or other AI-oriented formats are not necessary. Many of these tips apply to SEO as well.
questions.trap: LLMS.txt is explicitly called unnecessary.

questions.stem: Does SEO work for GEO? Slide 35's answer is 'yes and no'. Which statement reflects it?
options: Keyword stuffing is the most effective GEO tactic
Neither on-page nor off-page SEO has any effect on GEO
On-page relevance still matters but keyword stuffing hurts; off-page links have a weak direct effect, and being discussed matters more than being linked
Off-page backlinks are the main GEO driver; on-page content is irrelevant
questions.explanation: Slide 35: on-page SEO – relevance still matters, keyword stuffing hurts and leads to low-quality writing; off-page SEO – weak direct effect, though higher rank may help; it is more important to be discussed than merely linked.

questions.stem: According to Aggarwal et al. (2024), the top three GEO techniques are:
options: Quotation addition, statistics addition, citing sources
Images, videos, infographics
Keyword stuffing, backlinks, meta tags
Paid placement, sponsorship, affiliate links
questions.explanation: Slide 36: top techniques are quotation addition, statistics addition and cite sources. Good techniques are fluency optimisation, technical terms, authoritative tone and easy-to-understand writing.

questions.stem: Aggarwal et al. report that the best GEO technique improves position-adjusted word count by about how much, and for whom is the visibility change greatest?
options: 10%; for top-ranked websites
41%; for lower-ranked websites
75%; equally for all sites
41%; only for e-commerce sites
questions.explanation: Slide 36: the best technique gives a 41% improvement in position-adjusted word count, and the visibility change is greater for lower-ranked websites. This is why GEO is attractive for smaller brands like State Property.

questions.stem: The iterative GEO method on slide 37 works by:
options: Buying ads inside the LLM
Submitting your sitemap to OpenAI
Feeding an LLM your content and competitors' content, asking it to recommend one option, revising your content and repeating until recommended
Waiting for real search-ranking changes after each edit
questions.explanation: Slide 37: feed both your and competitors' content to an LLM, ask for a recommendation, revise, re-feed and iterate. It turns the LLM into a simulated customer, so there is no need to wait for market response as with SEO. Guardrails: avoid false information.

questions.stem: In the State Property GEO exercise, why did the original bespoke page come LAST in the first LLM test for a 45-year-old lawyer seeking a S$5,000 heirloom signet ring?
options: It had too many statistics
The page loaded too slowly
It used LLMS.txt incorrectly
It gave no price range, never mentioned men, signet rings or heirlooms, and charged a separate design fee
questions.explanation: The LLM said State Property had 'no mention of pricing beyond contact our team' and 'no mention of signet rings, men's jewellery or heirloom framing'. Orient Atelier won because it alone named a men's ring category. Relevance to the customer's words still matters.

questions.stem: After the rewrite, State Property moved from last to first. Which additions were responsible, according to the LLM's own reasoning?
options: A new logo and colour scheme
Explicit customer naming (bankers, lawyers, doctors in their 40s), a price range of S$2,700–8,420, a founder quote on 18K gold for heirlooms, and cited sources
A list of 50 keywords repeated across the page
Removing all competitor comparisons
questions.explanation: The LLM praised the rewrite for naming the customer, fitting the budget with a stated price range, explaining 18K gold's heirloom durability via a founder quotation, and matching the 'not in a hurry' timeline. Quotations, statistics and citations – the top three GEO techniques – did the work.
questions.source: S3 GEO exercise doc, sections 3 and 5

questions.stem: In the stress test where the son's birthday was in 10 weeks, State Property lost to B.P. de Silva because of its honest 5–6 month timeline. What was the lesson?
options: Attack B.P. de Silva's claims in the write-up
Speed is a real product gap that copy cannot fix; solve it with an express track or a ready-to-wear fallback, never a false claim
Remove all timelines from the website
Shorten the stated timeline in the copy to win the recommendation
questions.explanation: The exercise concluded that iteration reveals real product gaps. GEO needs guardrails against false information (slide 37), so the fix was to point time-pressed buyers to 41 ready-to-wear signet rings with engraving, not to invent a faster timeline.
questions.trap: Tempting to 'optimise' by lying; the slides forbid false information.
questions.source: S3 GEO exercise doc, section 5; slide 37

questions.stem: Slide 38 ('Beyond GEO', Acar and Schweidel 2026) raises several futures. Which is NOT among them?
options: Mandatory government licensing of all LLM search
A 'dual internet' and whether we still need a website for humans
Brands offering their own dedicated agents, with full control but adoption challenges
Consumers using third-party LLM agents, raising questions about branding and price
questions.explanation: Slide 38 lists brand-owned agents (expensive, how to get adoption), third-party agents (how to compete, role of branding and price), agent–agent interaction, a dual internet, and the idea of paying LLMs to recommend products (LLM advertising). Licensing is not mentioned.

questions.stem: Session 7 says firms must write for customers' AI agents (Bot2Bot) with structured, factual, machine-readable answers. Which Session 3 idea does this extend?
options: Bots as customers and the LLM's preference for quotable, factual passages
Crawl budget management
Keyword stuffing for crawlers
Paid search bidding
questions.explanation: Puntoni's 'bots as customers' (slide 28) and the passage-level unit of relevance (slide 32) mean content must be precise and citable. Session 7's Bot2Bot advice – exact prices, specs and policies, consistent across channels – is the same logic applied to commerce.

questions.stem: The iterative GEO method uses an LLM as a simulated customer, just as Session 2 uses LLMs as synthetic participants. Which shared caution applies to both?
options: The LLM's judgement may not match real humans, so results are hypotheses to validate, and outputs must not contain false claims
Both require paying the LLM provider for placement
Both replace the need for a website
Both only work for luxury goods
questions.explanation: In both cases the LLM stands in for a human. Session 2 lists hallucination and regression to the mean; the GEO exercise noted the LLM itself wanted to 'verify claims independently'. Treat the LLM's recommendation as a signal, keep citations real, and confirm with market data.

questions.stem: In the traditional advertising workflow taught in Session 4, which is the correct order of the five steps?
options: Strategy & Concept → Brief → Production → Measurement → Media Planning & Buying
Brief → Production → Strategy & Concept → Media Planning & Buying → Measurement
Strategy & Concept → Production → Brief → Measurement → Media Planning & Buying
Brief → Strategy & Concept → Production → Media Planning & Buying → Measurement
questions.explanation: The client briefs the agency first, planners and creatives then find the big idea, the ad is produced, media is planned and bought, and measurement reports at the end. Any order that puts strategy before the brief fails because the agency cannot plan without the objectives, audience and budget; and measurement cannot precede media buying.
questions.trap: Swapping the order of brief and strategy.

questions.stem: Advertising is part of which P of the marketing mix, and which three decisions does that P involve?
options: Place: channel, coverage, logistics
Product: functionality, packaging, brand
Promotion: message, media, budget
Price: list price, discounts, allowances
questions.explanation: Advertising sits under Promotion, which involves deciding the message, the media and the budget. Place decisions concern channels and distribution, not communication.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the strategic difference between advertising and SEO/GEO?
options: Advertising captures existing demand; SEO/GEO creates new demand
Advertising creates demand (push); SEO/GEO captures demand people already have (pull)
Both capture existing demand but at different funnel stages
SEO/GEO works at awareness; advertising works only at purchase
questions.explanation: SEO/GEO only works when someone is already searching, so it is pull and sits at consideration/purchase. Advertising is push: it creates awareness and desire among people not yet looking. 'Advertising captures existing demand; SEO/GEO creates new…' reverses the roles, the planted near-miss.
questions.trap: Reversing push and pull.

questions.stem: According to the slides, in-house creative teams grew between 2008 and 2023 from roughly:
questions.explanation: In-house creative teams rose from 42% in 2008 to 82% in 2023. The 12% to 85% figure is CDO adoption from Session 8, and 60% to 83% is ad executives deploying AI in creative (IAB 2024 to 2026).
questions.trap: Confusing with CDO adoption (S8) or IAB AI-deployment figures.

questions.stem: Nutella Unica used an algorithm to generate 7 million unique jar labels that sold out in a month. This is the clearest example of:
options: Mass customisation
Hyperpersonalisation
Dynamic Creative Optimisation
Co-creation
questions.explanation: Mass customisation produces huge volumes of unique variations without tying each variant to an identifiable person. Hyperpersonalisation, the planted near-miss, requires that a specific variant be linked to a specific individual or micro-segment using data.
questions.trap: Calling any large number of variants 'hyperpersonalisation'.

questions.stem: Coca-Cola's 'Create Real Magic' let digital artists make brand art with GPT-4 and DALL·E, with winners displayed at Times Square. Which Gen-AI opportunity does this illustrate?
options: Co-creation: consumers become part of the story
Hyperpersonalisation at the individual level
Programmatic media buying
Static personalisation with pre-set rules
questions.explanation: Co-creation moves the brand from 'crafting narratives to be consumed' to 'designing platforms for shared storytelling', as CMR puts it. No individual data tailoring or real-time assembly was involved, so it is not hyperpersonalisation or DCO.

questions.stem: What distinguishes hyperpersonalisation from mass customisation?
options: Hyperpersonalisation uses far more variants
Mass customisation requires Gen-AI; hyperpersonalisation does not
Mass customisation happens in real time; hyperpersonalisation is batch-produced
Hyperpersonalisation ties the specific variant to an identifiable person or micro-segment using data
questions.explanation: The defining feature of hyperpersonalisation is that the variant is tied to a specific identifiable person or micro-segment, with Gen-AI making this economically viable. Volume alone ('Hyperpersonalisation uses far more variants') is mass customisation's trait, and neither definition hinges on real-time delivery.
questions.trap: Thinking the difference is volume.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts the static approach to personalisation with Dynamic Creative Optimisation (DCO)?
options: Static uses AI; DCO uses human copywriters
Static sets rules before serving; DCO assembles approved components per impression in real time
Static changes brand elements; DCO locks only the headline
Static happens in real time; DCO batch-produces variants in advance
questions.explanation: In the static approach Gen-AI batch-produces variants or fixed rules decide the swap before ads are served. DCO modularises the ad, locks brand elements, and assembles the best combination per impression while learning from results. 'Static happens in real time; DCO batch-produces variants…' reverses the two.
questions.trap: Reversing which approach is real-time.

questions.stem: In a DCO setup, which elements are typically locked rather than varied?
options: Headline and call-to-action
Logo, brand colours, fonts and legal claims
Hero image and offer
Product shown and social proof
questions.explanation: Core brand elements such as logo, colours, fonts and legal claims are locked so every assembled version stays on-brand; headline, image, offer and CTA are the modules that vary. Locking the headline would defeat the purpose of optimisation.

questions.stem: Meta Advantage+ (launched March 2022) automates targeting, placements and creatives and claims about 22% higher return on ad spend. It is the course's main example of:
options: Co-creation platforms
Synthetic ad testing
In-house agency replacement
Dynamic Creative Optimisation
questions.explanation: Advantage+ auto-creates versions and adapts them across placements per impression, the hallmark of DCO. It is not a co-creation platform (consumers do not create content) and it replaces media-buying labour, not the agency as such.

questions.stem: According to the IAB 2026 survey, what share of ad executives believe young consumers feel positive about AI ads, versus the share who actually do?
questions.explanation: 82% of executives believe Gen Z and Millennials are positive, but only 45% actually are, a 37-point gap that widened from 32. '45% vs 82%' reverses the figures; 73% vs 27% refers to purchase likelihood after disclosure.
questions.trap: Reversing who is more positive.

questions.stem: In the IAB 2026 data, which generation was more negative about AI ads, and by roughly how much?
options: Millennials, 39% negative vs Gen Z 20%
Gen Z and Millennials equally, about 30% each
Gen Z, 39% negative vs Millennials 20%
Gen Z, 82% negative vs Millennials 45%
questions.explanation: Gen Z were 39% negative versus 20% of Millennials; the 30% figure is the blended average. 'Gen Z, 82% negative vs Millennials 45%' misuses the executive-versus-consumer gap percentages.
questions.trap: Assuming the younger group is more positive about AI.

questions.stem: Why does the IAB say the executive–consumer perception gap on AI ads is likely to keep widening?
options: Consumers are becoming unable to detect AI ads
Disclosure rules have been abolished in most markets
Gen Z has stopped using social media
Advertisers' concerns have turned inward (cost, implementation) and away from consumer perception
questions.explanation: Advertisers' top benefit shifted to cost efficiency (64%) and their worries moved to internal issues, so they stop measuring how consumers feel. Consumers are actually more likely to think they have seen an AI ad (71%), which rules out 'Consumers are becoming unable to detect AI ads'.

questions.stem: In the IAB 2026 study, what share of young consumers said knowing an ad was AI-made would increase or not change their purchase likelihood?
questions.explanation: 73% said disclosure would increase or not change purchase likelihood; only 27% said less likely. 60% is the share of executives in the separate IAB/Aymara study who say AI ads should always be disclosed.
questions.trap: Confusing the consumer 73% with the executive 60%.

questions.stem: The IAB/Aymara 2025 study found what share of marketers had experienced at least one AI incident (hallucinated content, loss of brand tone, biased output)?
questions.explanation: 70% had at least one incident; only 30% had none. 51% is the share relying on human review as a safeguard, and about 90% is the share who nonetheless feel prepared, the 'false sense of security'.
questions.trap: Picking 30%, which is the share with no incident.

questions.stem: Kim (CMR, 2025) argues that Gen-AI in advertising is a 'paradigmatic evolution'. Which claim best reflects that argument?
options: Prompting becomes a strategic meta-skill and the operations, talent and organisation of advertising change
AI is a new production tool that leaves roles and organisation unchanged
Agencies will disappear within two years
Creativity is fully automated, so human judgement is no longer needed
questions.explanation: Kim frames prompting as a strategic communication skill needing rhetorical precision, domain knowledge and critical evaluation, and shows the whole system changing, not just the tools. 'AI is a new production tool that leaves roles and organis…' is exactly what 'paradigmatic' denies, and Kim never predicts agencies vanish.

questions.stem: Which is a key RISK of relying on LLMs for strategy and copy, as highlighted on the slides?
options: Copy cannot be A/B tested cheaply
LLMs write too slowly for digital culture
Outputs drift toward generic 'average' language unless prompted carefully
Production costs per asset rise sharply
questions.explanation: The slides warn that LLM outputs converge to the average unless carefully prompted (the 'higher floor, not higher ceiling' point). Speed and low cost per asset are strengths of Gen-AI, and copy variants can be A/B tested cheaply, so the other three statements reverse the facts.

questions.stem: Timperio's aggregate results table shows AI-only with 36,447 interactions at $0.0046 each, agency-only 32,288 at $0.0052, and AI-Agent 29,501 at $0.0057. Adding the agency's €350 fee, the agency's true cost per interaction is closest to:
options: $0.0052, unchanged, because fees are sunk
$0.010, about double AI-only
$0.017, about 3.6 times AI-only
$0.054, about 12 times AI-only
questions.explanation: Including the ~US$367 fee on top of the equal media spend raises the agency's cost to roughly $0.017 per interaction, about 3.6 times AI-only. '$0.0052, unchanged, because fees are sunk' ignores a real cost; $0.054 is the cost per interaction for persuasive images, not the agency aggregate.
questions.trap: Treating the agency fee as sunk and comparing media cost only.
questions.source: Timperio case Exhibit 8, Table 3; Q5 class answer

questions.stem: In Timperio's format table, reels generated about 88,600 interactions versus about 9,600 for images. The main lesson the class drew was:
options: Agency content always beats AI content
Format mattered more than who created the ad
Images produce more meaningful engagement than video
Informative content beats persuasive content in every format
questions.explanation: Reels earned roughly nine times more interactions at far lower cost, dwarfing differences between creators. Informative beat persuasive only for images (3.1:1), not for videos, which rules out 'Informative content beats persuasive content in every format'.

questions.stem: Timperio's results by cell show that for informative IMAGE ads the agency-only version earned 4,010 interactions at $0.010 versus AI-only's 713 at $0.060. The best reading is:
options: AI content is generally inferior to agency content
Human craft still won on product-accurate, informative visuals even though AI won overall
Informative content should never be made with AI
The agency fee made this cell the cheapest
questions.explanation: The agency clearly won this one cell while AI-only led both video objectives and total likes, so the right conclusion is a hybrid: humans for informative, product-accurate images; AI for high-volume reels. 'AI content is generally inferior to agency content' overgeneralises from one of twelve cells.
questions.trap: Generalising one cell to the whole experiment.
questions.source: Timperio Exhibit 8, Tables 1–2; Q5–Q6 class answers

questions.stem: Which caveat about the Timperio experiment did the class consider MOST important when reading the results?
options: The ads ran for six months in three countries
The agency used was a global network with a large budget
The experiment used unequal budgets per ad
Interactions mixed cheap video views with likes and clicks, and no sales data was collected
questions.explanation: 'Interactions' were inflated by video views and the test lacked conversion data, so results are directional. The experiment ran 14 days in one market with equal ~US$42 budgets and a single freelancer as 'agency', which contradicts the other options.
questions.source: Timperio case; Q5 class answer caveats

questions.stem: Timperio's team found that AI image tools could not reliably reproduce the real bottle and label. Which prompting challenge does this illustrate?
options: Convergence to average language
Lack of cultural nuance in captions
Brand fidelity: AI renders product details, text and labels unreliably
Inconsistent tone across a set of twelve ads
questions.explanation: Brand fidelity is the challenge: generic bottles appeared instead of Timperio's, so real product shots must be composited or brand-trained models used. The other options are real challenges too, but they concern copy and consistency rather than product rendering.
questions.source: S4 Q4 class answer; Timperio case

questions.stem: Which recommendation for Timperio best matches BOTH the Exhibit 8 numbers and the IAB governance findings?
options: Go fully AI-only to minimise cost per interaction
Keep the agency for all content to protect the heritage brand
AI-first in-house co-pilot for everyday reels, agency for flagship/informative visuals, human review and disclosure
Stop advertising and rely on GEO
questions.explanation: AI was cheapest and won likes and reels, but the agency won informative images and 70% of marketers report AI incidents, so a hybrid with human review and disclosure fits all the evidence. Pure AI-only ignores both the informative-image result and governance risk.
questions.trap: Taking the cost result alone as the decision.
questions.source: S4 Q6 class answer; IAB & Aymara (2025)

questions.stem: The group-project brief says randomly changing a colour or a model's face is NOT personalisation. Which Session 4 concept makes a creative difference genuinely personalised?
options: Using more variants per campaign
Adding a disclosure label
Switching from images to reels
A link between the segment's underlying motivation and the specific creative choices
questions.explanation: Personalisation requires that composition, palette, copy and imagery trace to the segment's Maslow need, occasion or experience level, with identifiable segments to deliver to. More variants alone is mass customisation; disclosure and format are separate decisions.
questions.trap: Equating variety with personalisation.

questions.stem: Timperio chose which ads worked by comparing interactions across cells. Which Session 8 warning applies most directly to that reading?
options: Meta's delivery algorithm chose who saw each ad, so gender differences may reflect delivery, not creative appeal
Analytics should be centralised under a CDO
Unstructured data has no predefined format
Low-level image features should be extracted first
questions.explanation: Because Meta's algorithm decided exposure (one reel reached 84% women), audience differences are partly a delivery effect, a competing explanation that breaks the third causality condition. This is the descriptive-versus-causal discipline from Session 8.

questions.stem: According to Haenlein et al. (2020), as used in Session 5, an influencer is best defined as:
options: Any celebrity who endorses a product for a fee
A brand employee who posts on social media
A computer-generated character with a backstory
A person with a large, engaged following whom you would not know unless you followed them
questions.explanation: The definition stresses an engaged following built on social media rather than fame from elsewhere, which is why a traditional celebrity ('Any celebrity who endorses a product for a fee') is not the same thing. 'A computer-generated character with a backstory' describes a virtual influencer, a subtype defined later in the session.
questions.trap: Equating influencers with celebrities.

questions.stem: Why does influencer marketing work, according to the slides?
options: It is cheaper than any other media
It guarantees reach to the whole population
It feels like advice from a friend, gets around ad-blindness and reaches niche communities
It allows full brand control over the message
questions.explanation: Influencer marketing borrows trust: a recommendation from someone you chose to follow feels like a friend's tip, not an ad. Full brand control ('It allows full brand control over the message') is exactly what human influencers do not offer and what virtual influencers add.

questions.stem: The key tension in influencer marketing, as framed in Session 5, is between:
options: Brands wanting authenticity versus influencers wanting higher fees
Brands wanting control, consistency and scale versus human influencers wanting authenticity and creative freedom
Influencers wanting scale versus brands wanting niche reach
Platforms wanting disclosure versus brands wanting secrecy
questions.explanation: Brands want control, consistency and scale; human influencers want authenticity, creative freedom and their own schedule. Virtual influencers resolve this by giving full control at the cost of some authenticity. 'Brands wanting authenticity versus influencers wanting hi…' swaps who wants what.
questions.trap: Swapping which side wants authenticity.

questions.stem: Which is a CON of human influencers listed on the slides?
options: They lack real lived experience
They cannot build loyal communities
They are available in unlimited supply
Scandal and reputation risk, unpredictability and high cost
questions.explanation: Human influencers bring scandal risk, may refuse the script, are expensive and in limited supply. Lacking lived experience ('They lack real lived experience') is a drawback of virtual influencers, the planted reverse.
questions.trap: Mixing up human and virtual drawbacks.

questions.stem: Lil Miquela and Lu do Magalu differ mainly in that:
options: Miquela is cartoon-like; Lu is photorealistic
Miquela is brand-owned by Dior; Lu is independent
Miquela is independent (created by Brud); Lu is brand-owned by Magazine Luiza
Miquela posts only in Portuguese; Lu posts in English
questions.explanation: Miquela is an independent virtual influencer created by Brud that takes brand deals (Dior, Prada, BMW); Lu is owned by the Brazilian retailer Magazine Luiza, keeps all brand equity and doubles as a service assistant. 'Miquela is brand-owned by Dior; Lu is independent' reverses ownership.
questions.trap: Calling Lu independent or Miquela brand-owned.

questions.stem: In the HBR study (Hwang et al., 2024), how did paid posts change engagement for virtual versus human influencers?
options: Virtual –13.3%; human +2.1%
Both rose by about 13%
Virtual +13.3%; human –2.1%
Virtual +2.1%; human –13.3%
questions.explanation: Virtual influencers' paid posts earned 13.3% more engagement than their organic posts, while humans' paid posts earned 2.1% less. 'Virtual –13.3%; human +2.1%' flips the signs, the classic near-miss.
questions.trap: Flipping the signs.

questions.stem: Why do PAID posts by virtual influencers earn MORE engagement while paid posts by humans earn LESS?
options: Virtual influencers have more followers than humans
A virtual influencer is already seen as a brand creation, so an ad is no betrayal of authenticity; for humans, sponsorship feels like selling out
Platforms boost virtual influencer posts algorithmically
Paid posts by humans are usually lower quality
questions.explanation: Followers expect humans to be 'real', so a sponsored post violates authenticity; a virtual influencer has no authenticity to lose, and brand deals bring novelty and polish. Humans actually have more followers on average (2.8M vs 1.1M), so 'Virtual influencers have more followers than humans' is wrong.
questions.source: S5 Q5 class answer; Hwang et al. (2024)

questions.stem: In which category was the paid-post engagement advantage of virtual influencers largest, according to the HBR data?
options: Automotive: +22% virtual vs –5% human
Food and beverage: +13.3% virtual vs –2.1% human
Fashion and beauty: +16.3% virtual vs –2.3% human
Technology: +9% virtual vs 0% human
questions.explanation: Fashion and beauty, an image-led category CGI does well, showed +16.3% for virtual and –2.3% for human. The +13.3% / –2.1% figures in 'Food and beverage: +13.3% virtual vs –2.1% human' are the overall averages, not a category.
questions.trap: Attributing the overall figure to a specific category.

questions.stem: The CMR 'Layer Coherence Triad' (Saxena, 2025) says authenticity in the AI age requires which three things together?
options: Reach, frequency, recency
Novelty, consistency, scale
Likes, comments, shares
Information credibility, disclosure transparency, reputation trust
questions.explanation: People judge 'real' by multiple cues: can facts be checked, is AI use disclosed plainly, and does the source have a track record. 'Novelty, consistency, scale' lists what brands want from virtual influencers, not what makes them feel authentic.

questions.stem: The CMR article stresses that the three authenticity signals are 'multiplicative, not additive'. What does this imply?
options: Having only one or two signals feels hollow; all three together are rare (<9%) but succeed about 82% of the time
Having any one signal is enough to be seen as authentic
Each signal adds a fixed amount of trust
Transparency alone outweighs the other two
questions.explanation: Multiplicative means a weak signal drags down the whole judgement; one or two present feels suspicious. All three appear in fewer than 9% of cases but then yield a positive outcome 82% of the time. 'Having any one signal is enough to be seen as authentic' is the additive misreading.
questions.trap: Treating one signal as sufficient.

questions.stem: The 'uncanny valley' (Mori, 1970) describes:
options: The drop in engagement after a virtual influencer is revealed to be fake
The gap between executive and consumer views of AI
The cost difference between human and virtual influencers
A spike in eeriness when something looks almost, but not quite, human
questions.explanation: Eeriness spikes when a figure is almost human, so brands should go clearly stylised or fully polished; 'almost human with glitches' (Vodafone's moving mole) is the danger zone. 'The gap between executive and consumer views of AI' is the IAB perception gap from Session 4.
questions.trap: Confusing with the S4 perception gap.

questions.stem: Meta changed its blunt 'Made with AI' label to a clickable 'AI Info' label. What lesson does the CMR article draw?
options: Labels should be removed because they reduce engagement
Any small edit should be labelled the same as a fully synthetic image
Disclosure must be understandable and proportionate, not merely present
Only video needs AI labels
questions.explanation: The first label tagged a minor edit the same as a fully fake image, so it confused users; the fix made disclosure understandable. The lesson is that disclosure must be comprehensible (test for 80% understanding), not that labels should go.

questions.stem: Vodafone Germany ran a TikTok ad with an AI presenter; viewers spotted a mole moving between frames. Vodafone openly admitted it was an experiment. Which lesson fits best?
options: Honest disclosure after detection can turn a crisis into a conversation, but near-human glitches are the uncanny-valley danger zone
AI presenters should never be used in telecom ads
Viewers cannot detect AI video, so disclosure is unnecessary
The ad failed because it was in German
questions.explanation: Vodafone's openness converted backlash into dialogue, while the moving mole shows how 'almost human' realism invites scrutiny. Viewers clearly could detect the AI, which contradicts 'Viewers cannot detect AI video, so disclosure is unnecessary'.

questions.stem: Shudu, a CGI supermodel created by a white male photographer, is used on the slides to illustrate which ethical concern?
options: The uncanny valley
Commodification of Blackness: renting diversity without hiring or paying real people from that group
Algorithmic collusion
Input data leakage
questions.explanation: Shudu raises the concern that surface diversity can hide old power, race and gender patterns, since the creator profits rather than people from the community portrayed. Collusion and data leakage belong to Sessions 6 and 9.

questions.stem: What share of US social media users already follow a virtual influencer, according to the slides?
questions.explanation: 52% of US social media users follow a virtual influencer. 15% is the share who highly trust AI influencers (CMR), and $32B is the industry size, not a percentage.
questions.trap: Confusing with the 15% high-trust figure.

questions.stem: Which statement about the cost of influencers is supported by the readings?
options: Virtual influencers cost more because CGI production is expensive
Both cost roughly the same per post
A human influencer with 1M+ followers can charge $250K+ per post; Lil Miquela charges about $9,000
Virtual influencers are free because they are software
questions.explanation: HBR contrasts the $250K+ fee of a 1M-plus-follower human with Miquela's roughly $9,000 per post. Virtual influencers are not free: a human team, production and continuous investment sit behind them.
questions.trap: Assuming software means zero cost.

questions.stem: HBR reports humans average 2.8M followers versus 1.1M for virtual influencers, yet still recommends virtual influencers for some brands. Why?
options: Because virtual influencers will soon overtake humans in followers
Because followers and engagement have an inverted-U relationship, and for lesser-known brands follower count matters little
Because reach is irrelevant in influencer marketing
Because virtual influencers post more often
questions.explanation: Follower count and engagement follow an inverted U, so bigger is not always better, and for brands like Misbhv or Moschino reach mattered little compared with engagement. Reach is not irrelevant; it is just not decisive.

questions.stem: HBR's four principles for deciding whether to use a virtual influencer include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Replace all human influencers with virtual ones to cut risk
Recognise consumers' desire for novelty
Look at public engagement data for your category and competitors
Experiment, measure ROI and learn
questions.explanation: HBR recommends a portfolio: brands adding virtual influencers still use humans. Wholesale replacement contradicts the portfolio principle. The other three options are the remaining principles.
questions.trap: The portfolio principle versus replacement.

questions.stem: Nars dropped a human influencer after 'Dramageddon' and launched three virtual influencers. This illustrates which comparison factor from HBR?
options: Reach
Reputation risk: virtual influencers are drama-free
Cost
Diversity
questions.explanation: The Nars case shows the reputation-risk advantage of controllable characters. Cost and diversity are separate HBR factors illustrated by the $250K fee and by Hauli or Blu respectively.

questions.stem: In the class pipeline for building a virtual influencer, why must you save the prompt, settings and seed in the image tool?
options: To comply with EU AI Act labelling
To reduce the cost of generation
To speed up voice synthesis in ElevenLabs
So you can recreate the same face across posts; otherwise each generation changes it
questions.explanation: Face consistency was the biggest build challenge: new generations change the face unless the seed and prompt are reused. Labelling and voice are separate steps in the pipeline.

questions.stem: Which is the correct order of the class pipeline for making a virtual-influencer video?
options: Voice → Image → Script → Editing → Animation
Image → Script → Voice → Animation → Editing
Script → Animation → Image → Voice → Editing
Editing → Image → Voice → Script → Animation
questions.explanation: Generate the image (Leonardo), write a ≤15-second script, synthesise the voice (ElevenLabs), animate by linking voice to photo (Vidnoz/HeyGen/Hedra), then edit in CapCut with captions and ambient sound. Animation needs both image and voice first.

questions.stem: According to the Built In reading, a key DRAWBACK of AI influencers is:
options: They cannot post around the clock
They cannot be customised for different markets
They are limited by time, place and physics
They have no real lived experience, so endorsements can feel shallow and are harder to trust
questions.explanation: 'What does a cartoon know about skincare?' captures the experience gap, and realistic ones are mistaken for people, hurting trust. The other three statements are the opposite of the benefits Built In lists: 24/7 posting, versatility across markets, and creative freedom beyond time, place and physics.
questions.trap: Reversing benefits and drawbacks.

questions.stem: Will virtual influencers replace human influencers? Which answer matches the readings' conclusion and its reasoning?
options: No, coexistence: human lived experience cannot be fully copied and brands that add virtual influencers still use humans
Yes, because they are cheaper and drama-free
Yes, because regulation now bans paid human endorsements
No, because virtual influencers are illegal in the EU
questions.explanation: Built In concludes 'coexistence, not replacement', and HBR's data show brands keep a portfolio. The EU AI Act requires labels, not a ban, so 'No, because virtual influencers are illegal in the EU' is wrong.
questions.source: Built In (2025); Hwang et al. (2024); Q9 class answer

questions.stem: Meta's 'AI Info' label (S5), New York's algorithmic-pricing notice (S6) and the EU AI Act's chatbot disclosure (S9) share which principle?
options: Disclosure of AI must be understandable, and hidden AI later discovered costs more trust than disclosed AI
AI use should be banned in consumer-facing contexts
Only images need to be labelled
Disclosure is unnecessary when engagement is high
questions.explanation: Across sessions the course argues for disclosure that people can understand, because being found out is costlier than being open, as Lil Miquela's 2018 reveal and Vodafone showed. None of these frameworks bans AI.
questions.source: S5 slide 30; S6 slides 30–31; S9 slide 34

questions.stem: A brand chooses a hyper-realistic virtual influencer to endorse a skincare product with claims like 'this cured my acne'. Which combination of course concepts flags the problem?
options: Explore vs exploit and framing
RAG and fine-tuning
Uncanny valley plus failed information credibility in the CMR triad, since a CGI character has no skin to treat
Descriptive vs causal analytics
questions.explanation: Near-human realism risks the uncanny valley, and an uncheckable personal-experience claim fails information credibility, so trust collapses. The other options are frameworks from Sessions 6, 7 and 8 that do not address this.

questions.stem: Which set lists the four Ps that define dynamic pricing in Kopalle et al. (2023)?
options: Product, Price, Place, Promotion
Personal, Public, Peak, Promotional
People, Products, Periods, Places
Price, Periods, Platforms, Profiles
questions.explanation: Kopalle defines dynamic pricing as prices varying with four demand drivers: People, Products, Periods and Places; static pricing is the special case where none vary. The marketing-mix 4Ps in 'Product, Price, Place, Promotion' are the professor's planted near-miss.
questions.trap: Confusing Kopalle's 4 Ps with the marketing-mix 4Ps.

questions.stem: Why is price described on the slides as different from the other Ps of the marketing mix?
options: It is the only P that makes money directly; the others first cost money
It is the only P regulated by law
It cannot be changed once set
It is the only P customers notice
questions.explanation: Price generates revenue directly while promotion, product and place are costs before they pay back. Prices can change instantly online, so 'It cannot be changed once set' is wrong.

questions.stem: Kopalle's Hyderabad vegetable seller visits rich areas first, poorer areas later at lower prices, and sells wilting stock near cost late in the day. Which Ps does this cart illustrate?
options: People, Periods, Places and Products (freshness)
Only Periods
People and Places only
Only Products
questions.explanation: One cart shows all four: who is buying (People), time of day (Periods), neighbourhood (Places) and freshness (Products). The example exists precisely to show all four at once.

questions.stem: Which pricing strategy is dynamic pricing essentially 'value-based pricing done at scale', according to the class answer?
options: Cost-plus pricing
Competitive pricing
Penetration pricing
Value-based pricing, with price discrimination as the economic idea behind it
questions.explanation: Cost-plus sets the floor, competitors set the range, and value sets the ceiling; dynamic pricing tries to find each customer's or moment's ceiling. Price discrimination is the underlying economics. Cost-plus ignores willingness to pay entirely.

questions.stem: 'Surveillance pricing' is the critical term for which practice?
options: Surge pricing during peak demand
