Personalised pricing based on tracked personal and behavioural data
Markdown pricing for perishable goods
Regional pricing by location
questions.explanation: Surveillance pricing is the critics' name for people-based pricing using tracked personal data. Surge, markdown and regional pricing use market data (periods, products, places) and are broadly accepted.
questions.trap: Labelling market-data pricing as surveillance pricing.

questions.stem: Delta announced AI revenue management for 20% of domestic fares, faced backlash and told Congress it would not set personalised fares. The main lesson drawn in class was:
options: Airlines may not use algorithms for pricing
Delta's AI produced discriminatory prices
Perception alone can hurt: customers assumed personal-data pricing even though it was not implemented
AI pricing is illegal in the United States
questions.explanation: Delta never implemented personal fares yet still had to back down, showing perception equals reality in pricing. Airlines have always priced on demand and season, which is accepted; the fear was the jump to personal data.
questions.trap: Thinking Delta actually implemented personalised fares.

questions.stem: Uber's surge pricing rose to about 4x during the 2014 Sydney café siege. What does this case teach?
options: Surge pricing should be abolished
An algorithm can be economically logical but morally tone-deaf in a crisis, so firms need ethical circuit breakers
Customers prefer surge pricing in emergencies
Surge pricing attracted enough drivers so the outcome was acceptable
questions.explanation: Surge is designed to attract drivers, but during a hostage crisis it looked like gouging and Uber called it 'the wrong decision'. The fix is caps or switch-offs in emergencies, not abolition.

questions.stem: RealPage allowed landlords to feed private data into one shared pricing tool. The US DOJ alleged this amounted to:
options: Surge pricing
Privacy breach of tenants' browsing data
Deceptive 'was' pricing
Algorithmic collusion resembling price-fixing
questions.explanation: Competitors using the same third-party algorithm with private, competitively sensitive data can turn independent pricing into coordinated price-fixing. The lesson is to audit vendors and keep final decisions in-house.

questions.stem: Which of the following is PERSONAL data in the slides' classification of pricing inputs?
options: Competitor prices scraped in real time
Weather, local events and seasonality
Inventory and supply limits
Purchase history, browsing behaviour and device-level geolocation
questions.explanation: Personal data covers purchase history, browsing (time on page, cart), device location, loyalty data and broker profiles. Competitor prices, weather and inventory are non-personal market data used for undercutting rivals and expiry discounts.

questions.stem: How does reinforcement learning differ from ordinary machine learning in pricing?
options: RL makes sequential, linked decisions and learns from its own actions and rewards to maximise long-run reward; ML makes independent one-off predictions
RL needs more historical data than ML
ML learns from rewards; RL predicts from history
RL removes the need for human oversight
questions.explanation: In RL an agent observes a state, acts, gets a reward and updates its policy; today's price changes tomorrow's stock. ML predicts outcomes independently from past data. 'ML learns from rewards; RL predicts from history' reverses the two.
questions.trap: Thinking RL is just ML with more data.

questions.stem: In RL terminology applied to pricing, which mapping is correct?
options: State = the price set today; Action = profit
Agent = the pricing algorithm; State = day, weather, stock, rival price; Action = today's price; Reward = profit minus waste
Policy = the market; Environment = the pricing rule
Reward = the competitor's price; Agent = the customer
questions.explanation: The agent is the decision-maker, the state is the current situation, the action is the price chosen, the reward is the feedback (profit minus penalties), and the policy is the rule 'in state X charge Y'. 'State = the price set today; Action = profit' swaps state and action.

questions.stem: Which statement about the explore–exploit trade-off matches the class answer?
options: Once the best price is found, never explore again
Always explore; exploitation wastes information
Explore only when the competitor is closed
Explore more at the start, exploit more over time, but keep a small share of ongoing exploration because markets change
questions.explanation: This is the epsilon-greedy idea: learn early, then use the best-known price while still testing a little (e.g., 10% of traffic) since a new competitor or season can change the best price. Never exploring again ('Once the best price is found, never explore again') risks locking in a stale price.
questions.source: S6 slide 26; Q6 class answer; Kopalle et al.

questions.stem: Which tools does Kopalle et al. name for balancing exploration and exploitation in practice?
options: Regression and ARIMA
Focus groups and surveys
A/B tests and multi-armed bandits such as Thompson Sampling
Cost-plus rules and price floors
questions.explanation: Kopalle cites A/B tests and multi-armed bandits (Thompson Sampling), plus Deep Q-Networks that beat manual markdown rules. ARIMA and Prophet are forecasting tools, not explore-exploit methods.

questions.stem: In Dubé and Misra's ZipRecruiter study, raising the single uniform price from $99 to $327 changed profit by roughly:
questions.explanation: The optimal uniform price lifted profit 55% even though sign-ups fell from 25% to 12%. +19% is the additional gain from personalisation, +86% is personalisation versus the $99 base, and 25% is the fall in sign-ups when the price doubled.
questions.trap: Mixing up the +55% uniform gain and the +19% personalisation gain.

questions.stem: At ZipRecruiter, MOST of the profit gain came from:
options: Fixing the underpriced uniform price (+55%)
Personalised prices (+19%)
Lowering prices for small firms
Removing personal data from the model
questions.explanation: The biggest and safest win came from correcting the basic price; personalisation added +19% on top. This is why the class concluded 'get the basic price right before personalising'.
questions.trap: Attributing the main gain to personalisation.

questions.stem: What did Dubé and Misra find about consumers under personalised pricing?
options: Total consumer surplus rose and every customer paid less
Total consumer surplus fell and almost all customers paid more
Consumer surplus was unchanged
Total consumer surplus fell, but more than 60% of individual customers were better off
questions.explanation: The firm captured more value in aggregate, yet over 60% of customers, mostly smaller, less-advantaged firms, paid below the uniform price. High-WTP customers paid more. 'Total consumer surplus rose and every customer paid less' overstates the consumer benefit.

questions.stem: Dubé and Misra report that consumer surplus is 'non-monotonic' in the amount of data used. What does this imply for regulators?
options: More data always hurts consumers, so all personal data should be banned
Less data always helps consumers
Removing some data can hurt consumers more, so privacy rules must be designed carefully
Data quantity has no effect on consumers
questions.explanation: Consumer surplus moves up and down as data is added or removed, so a blunt restriction can make consumers worse off. Giansiracusa adds that algorithms could also find people who need lower prices, another reason not to ban everything.

questions.stem: The framing slide shows Frame A: 'Your price is $120' while another shopper pays $100, and Frame B: 'You get $20 off' a $140 list price while another gets $40 off. Why do customers react differently?
options: Frame B gives a lower final price
Customers believe a fair reference price exists; a discount respects it while a higher personal price breaks it
Frame A is illegal in all jurisdictions
Customers cannot do the arithmetic
questions.explanation: Both frames yield the same money outcome, but a discount feels like a gain against the reference while a higher price feels like a loss versus another shopper (prospect theory). This is why laws target price increases and why the baseline must be real.
questions.trap: Assuming the frames differ in money outcome.

questions.stem: Kopalle's worked example sets a shelf price of $2,000 with a $400 coupon for the price-sensitive segment. Dayen notes some Amazon sellers raise list prices ~23% to make discounts look bigger. Together these show:
options: Coupons are always deceptive
List prices should never be shown
Discount framing can implement optimal two-tier pricing, but inflated or fake 'was' prices are deceptive and backfire
Price-sensitive customers prefer higher prices
questions.explanation: The coupon delivers the optimal two prices in a frame customers accept, yet FPF and FTC rules require the baseline to be bona fide. An inflated list price turns a fair frame into deception.

questions.stem: New York's algorithmic pricing law requires what disclosure?
options: A list of all competitors' prices
The firm's profit margin on each sale
Nothing; New York bans personalised pricing outright
'THIS PRICE WAS SET BY AN ALGORITHM USING YOUR PERSONAL DATA'
questions.explanation: New York requires the capitalised notice; Connecticut requires a readily visible notice whenever personal data raises a price. Neither state bans the practice outright.
questions.trap: Thinking the laws ban rather than require disclosure.

questions.stem: Which of the following is one of the Future of Privacy Forum's seven recommendations for responsible data-driven pricing?
options: Apply extra safeguards for essential products, such as caps in disasters and human review when prices jump
Remove race and gender from inputs, which guarantees fair outcomes
Never disclose personalisation to avoid confusing customers
Use fake 'was' prices to make discounts attractive
questions.explanation: FPF's seven steps include extra safeguards for essentials (housing, food, health). FPF explicitly warns that removing race or gender does NOT guarantee fair outcomes, and requires bona fide baseline prices and clear disclosure.
questions.trap: Believing input-blindness ensures fairness.

questions.stem: In the Roast & Reward game you receive 5,000 cups every Monday, pay $1 per cup sold, and face a $1.50 penalty per cup unsold on Sunday. Why did the case warn that the ML price adviser 'may not work well'?
options: It always suggests the maximum price
It uses competitor data illegally
It predicts today's demand from past patterns but ignores remaining stock and the end-of-week penalty, which is a sequential problem
It cannot read weather data
questions.explanation: The ML adviser makes one-off predictions; it does not pace stock across the week or plan for the Sunday waste penalty. That sequential dependency is exactly what RL is built for.
questions.source: Roast & Reward case; Q7 class answer

questions.stem: In Roast & Reward, a cup sold at $2 earns $1 profit; a cup left unsold on Sunday costs $1.50. On Saturday you are well behind the ~714 cups/day pace. The RL-consistent move is to:
options: Cut the price to clear stock, since selling at $2 beats a $1.50 penalty by $2.50 per cup
Raise the price to protect margin
Keep the ML-suggested price regardless of stock
Stop selling to avoid cost
questions.explanation: Clearing stock late in the week avoids the waste penalty; the swing per cup is $2.50. Raising the price when behind pace would leave more unsold cups on Sunday.
questions.trap: Protecting margin when the real cost is waste.

questions.stem: Which Session 9 idea does a cost-minimising pricing or ad-delivery algorithm that quietly disadvantages a group illustrate?
options: Input data leakage
Optimising the wrong metric as a source of bias, requiring fairness constraints and subgroup monitoring
Inherited IP risk
The uncanny valley
questions.explanation: An objective such as revenue or cost can create harm with perfectly clean data, the same mechanism as the STEM-ads case. FPF's bias testing and S9's subgroup disaggregation are the matching controls.

questions.stem: How does the Session 6 lesson 'explore then exploit' connect to Session 8's analytics discipline?
options: Both say to trust descriptive conversion rates
Both reject experimentation as too costly
Both apply only to video advertising
Both rely on deliberate experiments (random price cells, holdout groups) to learn causal effects before scaling a decision
questions.explanation: ZipRecruiter explored with ten random price cells before exploiting $327; Session 8's prospecting-versus-retargeting case needs holdout groups to measure incremental lift. Both trade a little short-term performance for causal information.
questions.source: S6 Q6 class answer; S8 slides 29–31

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a rule-based (flowchart) chatbot?
options: A model fine-tuned on company data so it keeps brand tone
A deterministic decision tree that matches input to pre-written answers
A voice agent that handles interruptions and keeps a task thread
A generative model that writes a new reply to any open-ended input
questions.explanation: Rule-based bots are built on decision trees with pre-written answers; the same input always gives the same output. The generative description is the AI chatbot, which is probabilistic and needs no script.
questions.trap: Mixing up deterministic rule-based bots with probabilistic generative bots.

questions.stem: According to the CMR reading, roughly how much does a chatbot save a firm per customer interaction?
options: About $70
About $0.70
About $0.07
About $7.00
questions.explanation: Ren & Zhang (CMR 2026) cite a saving of about $0.70 per interaction. The point of the article is that this visible saving hides a cost pushed onto customers, agents and society, so the number is small but the frustration cost is large.
questions.trap: Decimal-place swap on a well-known number.

questions.stem: Which 1960s program is the ancestor of today's chatbots, using simple pattern matching to act like a therapist?
options: Retell
ELIZA
IVR
LUIS
questions.explanation: ELIZA (1960s) matched patterns to play a therapist. IVR phone trees came in the 1970s–90s, Microsoft LUIS is a mid-2010s NLU tool, and Retell AI is a modern real-time voice-agent platform.
questions.trap: Other names on the history slide placed in the wrong decade.

questions.stem: Which two problem groups does the session use to classify what goes wrong with rule-based chatbots?
options: Crawling and indexing; relevance and importance
Hallucination and bias; IP and privacy
Cost and latency; privacy and security
Understanding and complexity; handover, humanisation and personalisation
questions.explanation: The slides split chatbot problems into (1) understanding and complexity and (2) handover, humanisation and personalisation. Crawling/indexing are Session 3 search terms; hallucination/bias/IP/privacy are Session 2 and 9 risk terms.
questions.trap: Borrowing taxonomies from S3 or S9.

questions.stem: Which problem did generative AI largely FIX compared with rule-based bots?
options: Rising customer expectations
Breaking on typos, slang and multi-intent messages
Refusing to hand over to a human
Customers' psychological bias against bots
questions.explanation: Gen-AI understands open-ended input, handles typos, slang and multi-intent messages and keeps context, so the understanding problems were largely fixed. Handover refusal, expectations and the bias against bots persist; they are design and psychology problems, not technology problems.
questions.trap: Assuming Gen-AI also solved handover and trust.

questions.stem: Per HBR, what share of customers still find chatbots frustrating, and what share prefer a human?
options: 14% frustrated; 70% prefer a human
53% frustrated; 64% prefer a human
77% frustrated; 88% prefer a human
88% frustrated; 77% prefer a human
questions.explanation: HBR (McKinlay, Puntoni & Saka, 2025) reports 77% frustrated and 88% preferring a human. 64% and 53% are Gartner figures from the CMR article (prefer no AI; would consider switching); 14% is the share of issues fully solved in self-service.
questions.trap: Swapping the two headline percentages or mixing in the CMR Gartner numbers.

questions.stem: The architecture comparison table lists three approaches. Which one is described as 'knowledge frozen until retrained, high cost, high need for ML talent'?
options: Privately trained (fine-tuned) model
Off-the-shelf LLM plus RAG
Off-the-shelf LLM with light prompting
Classic IVR phone tree
questions.explanation: The privately trained (fine-tuned) column is slowest to deploy, high cost, deep brand knowledge but frozen until retrained, and needs ML talent. Off-the-shelf + RAG is the column with 'always current' knowledge and low-medium cost. IVR is from the Microsoft voice-tier table, not the architecture table.
questions.trap: Thinking fine-tuning keeps knowledge current.

questions.stem: In the same table, which approach has the main risk 'only as good as the documents and the retrieval'?
options: Off-the-shelf only
Real-time speech-to-speech
Off-the-shelf + RAG
Privately trained
questions.explanation: RAG grounds answers in retrieved chunks of company documents, so its weakness is garbage in, garbage out and poor retrieval. Off-the-shelf alone risks generic answers and hallucination; fine-tuned risks cost and staleness.
questions.trap: Attributing hallucination as RAG's main risk rather than document quality.

questions.stem: What is the key technical difference between RAG and fine-tuning?
options: RAG only works with voice; fine-tuning only with text
RAG updates the model's parameters; fine-tuning does not
RAG needs more ML talent than fine-tuning
RAG retrieves documents at question time without changing parameters; fine-tuning updates parameters
questions.explanation: RAG pastes retrieved passages into the prompt and leaves model weights unchanged, so content can be updated by editing a document. Fine-tuning retrains parameters on company data, which is costly and goes stale. The reversed option (RAG updates parameters) swaps the two approaches.
questions.trap: Reversing which approach changes parameters.

questions.stem: What are the two phases of RAG described by McKinsey?
options: Training and inference
Explore and exploit
Crawling and indexing
Ingestion and retrieval
questions.explanation: Ingestion chunks documents into embeddings stored in a vector database; retrieval matches the question to relevant chunks and pastes them into the prompt. Crawling/indexing is search-engine language (S3); explore/exploit is RL (S6).
questions.trap: Search-engine terms from Session 3 as a near-miss.

questions.stem: Why is RAG compared to an 'open-book exam'?
options: The model can answer only yes or no
The model is graded by a human after every answer
The model memorises the whole book before answering
The model looks up the relevant page first and answers from it, often with a citation
questions.explanation: A plain LLM answers from memory (closed book) and may be outdated or invent facts; RAG retrieves the right passage and answers from it with a citation. If the book is wrong or the wrong page is opened, the answer is still wrong.
questions.trap: Confusing retrieval with memorisation.

questions.stem: A regional retailer with weekly-changing promotions and no ML team wants a service chatbot. Which approach does the session recommend?
options: Classic IVR phone tree
Off-the-shelf LLM with light prompting only
Privately trained model, retrained each week
Off-the-shelf LLM plus RAG on its FAQs and promo pages
questions.explanation: Fast-changing content with no ML team points to off-the-shelf + RAG: update a document, not the model, and answers stay current and citable. Fine-tuning would go stale and cost too much; off-the-shelf alone would hallucinate company facts.
questions.trap: Choosing fine-tuning for brand depth despite fast-changing content.

questions.stem: In HBR's study, identical conversations were rated how much lower in satisfaction when people knew they were talking to a chatbot?
options: 17% lower
37% lower
23% lower
8.5% lower
questions.explanation: Knowing it was a bot cut satisfaction by 8.5%. The 37% figure is the gain when the bot's benefits (instant, 24/7) were highlighted; 23% is the satisfaction drop for angry customers facing a human-like bot; 17% is the lift from the 'constantly learning' label.
questions.trap: All four numbers come from the same HBR article.

questions.stem: HBR says the chatbot problem is 'psychological, not technical'. Which evidence best supports this claim?
options: RAG reduces hallucination by grounding answers
Gen-AI adoption in service teams rose from 5% to over 80%
73% of people mistook GPT-4.5 for a human, yet customers still dislike chatbots
Chatbots save about $0.70 per interaction
questions.explanation: If 73% cannot tell GPT-4.5 from a human and people still dislike chatbots, realism is not the bottleneck; the dislike is a bias triggered by knowing it is a bot. The other options are true but concern adoption, cost or architecture, not the psychology argument.
questions.trap: Picking a true statement that does not support the specific claim.

questions.stem: Which HBR strategy is matched with the correct evidence?
options: Prove accuracy with real success stats → 8% higher firm rating
Label the bot 'constantly learning' → up to 17% more likely to follow its advice
Use flattery carefully → 35% fewer lies
Deliver good news in a human way → 22% higher expected accuracy
questions.explanation: 'Constantly learning' lifts advice-following by up to 17%. Proving accuracy raises trust by up to 22%; human-style good news raises firm ratings 8%; acting human reduces unethical behaviour by about 20% (people are 35% more likely to lie to a bot). Flattery lifts recommendation acceptance by up to 12.5%.
questions.trap: Numbers shuffled across the six strategies.

questions.stem: A customer writes: 'This is the THIRD time my order is late!!!' According to HBR, how should the bot respond?
options: Short, direct, machine-like steps and a quick route to escalation
Warm small talk and emojis to calm the customer
A long apology with a survey link
Flattery about the customer's patience
questions.explanation: Angry or hurried customers are 23% less satisfied with a human-like bot; they want efficiency. Detect anger, drop the small talk, give short clear steps and escalate. Warmth is for good news and long problem-solving, not anger.
questions.trap: Assuming more humanisation is always better.

questions.stem: A bot handles refund claims. HBR suggests it should sound MORE human in this flow. Why?
options: People are up to 35% more likely to lie to a bot; human-like cues raise guilt and cut unethical behaviour by about 20%
Human phrasing speeds up the refund process
Human-sounding bots are cheaper to run
Regulators require human-sounding bots for payments
questions.explanation: HBR strategy 4: customers are up to 35% more likely to lie (for example about a refund) to a bot; human-like phrasing such as 'Oh no!' or 'I see' raises the feeling of guilt and reduces unethical behaviour by roughly 20%. The humanisation dial goes up in fraud-risk moments.
questions.trap: Generic answers about speed or cost instead of the fraud mechanism.

questions.stem: According to CMR, what is the single biggest irritant in chatbot interactions?
options: No easy path to a human
Too many emojis
Slow response time
Pretending to be human
questions.explanation: Ren & Zhang identify 'no easy path to a human' as the number one irritant; users type 'speak to a human' or even 'chicken nuggets' to break out of loops. Pretending to be human is a separate source of frustration (lack of or fake humanisation).
questions.trap: Other real CMR frustration sources offered as the 'single biggest'.

questions.stem: CMR pairs five sources of frustration with five best practices. Which pairing is correct?
options: Can't solve complex problems → set expectations with a clear self-introduction
Lack of personalisation → be like a human but don't pretend to be one
Poor integration with humans → active listening
Failure to understand → seamless handover protocol
questions.explanation: 'Can't solve complex problems' is answered by setting expectations: say what the bot can and cannot do. Failure to understand pairs with active listening (repeat back); poor human integration pairs with a seamless handover protocol; lack of humanisation pairs with 'be like a human, don't pretend'; lack of personalisation pairs with streamlined personalisation.
questions.trap: Shuffled source–practice pairs.

questions.stem: Which is NOT one of the reasons the session gives for voice being harder than text?
options: Customers cannot scroll back to re-read
Customers expect split-second responses
Voice agents cannot connect to business data
Customers interrupt and change topic
questions.explanation: Voice is harder because replies must be near-instant, customers interrupt (barge-in), there is no scroll-back, and emotion lives in the voice. Voice agents can and should ground answers in systems of record (Microsoft behaviour 2), so 'voice agents cannot connect to business data' is the false statement and therefore the answer.
questions.trap: A plausible-sounding technical limitation that the materials contradict.

questions.stem: Microsoft's three-tier table for voice agents calls which tier the 'mainstream sweet spot' for order tracking, billing and appointments?
options: A human call centre
Tier 3 real-time speech-to-speech
Tier 2 generative AI voice grounded in business data
Tier 1 classic IVR
questions.explanation: Tier 2 (generative AI voice) is the mainstream sweet spot: flexible, grounded, needs guardrails. Tier 1 IVR suits simple high-volume tasks like balance checks; Tier 3 real-time speech-to-speech is for premium experiences where the conversation is the brand. Over-engineering is its own unreliability.
questions.trap: Assuming the most advanced tier is always best.

questions.stem: A voice agent says: 'Cancel the blue jacket, refund $89 to Visa ending 4412 – shall I go ahead?' Which Microsoft reliability behaviour is this?
options: Keeping a clear task thread
Handing off with context
Confirming the 'receipt' before acting
Explaining what it is doing during a pause
questions.explanation: Repeating key details and asking for confirmation before any action is the 'receipt' behaviour; it matters in voice because customers cannot scroll back. Task thread is about returning to a parked question; latency messages cover silence; hand-off passes a summary to a human.
questions.trap: Other behaviours from the same list of seven.

questions.stem: Microsoft says operational facts like delivery dates must come from systems of record, never model guesses. Which course idea is this closest to?
options: Grounding via RAG and APIs to avoid hallucination
Explore vs exploit in reinforcement learning
Disaggregating performance by subgroup
Importance as a ranking pillar
questions.explanation: A confident wrong delivery date is a hallucination; grounding answers in retrieved documents (RAG) or live database/API calls is the fix (McKinsey lists database queries and API calls as RAG sources). The other options are S6, S9 and S3 ideas.
questions.trap: Cross-session terms that sound related.

questions.stem: In a Bot2Bot world where the customer's own AI agent (e.g., Meta's Muse) shops for them, how should a firm's answers change?
options: Hide prices so the agent must call a human
Become structured, factual and machine-readable with consistent data across channels
Switch entirely to voice
Add more emotional storytelling and flattery
questions.explanation: An AI buying agent is unmoved by flattery; it compares exact prices, stock, specs and policies, so persuasion shifts to information quality and consistency, which links to GEO in Session 3. The human behind the agent still matters for trust, but the message must be machine-readable.
questions.trap: Applying human-persuasion tactics to a bot customer.
questions.source: S7 slide 38; links to S3 slide 38

questions.stem: The Chatling exercise applied 'one rock-solid scenario beats five shaky ones'. Which earlier-session idea does this echo?
options: Start narrow and test, like the Timperio experiment's controlled 12-cell design in S4
Keyword stuffing from S3
Price discrimination from S6
Regression to the mean from S2
questions.explanation: Microsoft's advice to start with one high-volume scenario, test a dozen messy cases and rerun after every change is the same experimental discipline as Timperio's controlled test cells and the course's explore-then-exploit thread. Keyword stuffing hurts GEO and is unrelated; regression to the mean and price discrimination are different concepts.
questions.trap: Unrelated course terms used as distractors.
questions.source: S7 exercise; Microsoft five passes; S4 Timperio

questions.stem: The course definition of marketing analytics (Palmatier, Petersen & Germann) ends with which words, and why does the professor stress this?
options: '...machine learning methods' – because AI is now required
'...customer and market data' – because data volume is the goal
'...marketing dashboards' – because reporting is the output
'...enhance marketing decision making' – because analytics exists to improve decisions, not insight
questions.explanation: The definition is 'a technology-enabled and model-supported approach to harness customer and market data to enhance marketing decision making'. The ending matters: more data or more answers is not the aim, better decisions are. Dashboards and ML are tools, not the purpose.
questions.trap: Treating data or insight as the end point.

questions.stem: What does the session mean by 'citizen analysts'?
options: Non-analysts who can now query data because AI gives them access
External consultants embedded in brand teams
Government statisticians who audit marketing claims
Customers who rate products online
questions.explanation: AI gives non-analysts access to coding help, data cleaning, visualisation and analysis, creating a larger group of 'citizen analysts'. Tadelis warns that treating this as an access problem alone makes bad analytics worse.
questions.trap: Reading 'citizen' literally.

questions.stem: Which organisational model is DBS's '2-in-a-box' best described as?
options: Purely embedded with no central unit
Purely centralised under a CDO
Outsourced to an external AI vendor
Hybrid: a separate analytics unit deeply embedded with stakeholders and sharing their KPIs
questions.explanation: DBS keeps analytics as a separate unit but embeds it deeply with business stakeholders and shares the same KPIs, fixing the old 'service centre' problem where analysts never understood the business question. That is a hybrid, not pure centralised or embedded.
questions.trap: Labelling it centralised because the unit is separate.

questions.stem: Which is a disadvantage of the EMBEDDED analytics model?
options: Consistent standards that stifle creativity
Slow to respond to local market needs
Duplicated work and inconsistent metric definitions across teams
Drifts away from business needs and is seen as a cost centre
questions.explanation: Embedded analysts sit inside brand or market teams, giving context and speed but duplicating work and defining metrics inconsistently, which makes enterprise-wide AI harder. Drifting from the business, being seen as a cost centre and slow local response are the centralised model's weaknesses.
questions.trap: Swapping the pros and cons of the two models.

questions.stem: Chief Data Officer adoption rose from what to what, according to the session?
questions.explanation: CDO adoption rose from 12% in 2012 to 85% in 2025 (Davenport & Bean). 42%→82% is the in-house creative team figure from Session 4; 5%→80% is chatbot adoption in service teams from Session 7; 33% is the share of firms with a CAIO.
questions.trap: Other 'rose from X to Y' statistics from neighbouring sessions.

questions.stem: Which is one of the ways Tadelis says AI can make analytics WORSE?
options: AI cannot process unstructured data
AI refuses to answer causal questions
AI slows down data cleaning
AI gives an answer before anyone checks the question
questions.explanation: Tadelis lists: treating AI analytics as an access problem, answering before the question is checked, polished output raising confidence not truth, scaling a flawed metric, and loss of transparency. AI will happily answer causal questions with the wrong method, which is the danger.
questions.trap: Options that contradict the course (AI speeds cleaning and handles unstructured data).

questions.stem: Which is NOT one of Tadelis's six principles for decision-grade analytics?
options: Reward truth-seeking, not persuasion
Start with the decision
Democratise answers before governing metrics
Label the question as descriptive, predictive or causal
questions.explanation: Tadelis says the opposite: 'before companies democratise answers, they need to govern what the answers mean' (Airbnb Minerva). The six principles are: start with the decision, label the question, expose assumptions and counterfactuals, govern the metrics, validate high-stakes and causal claims, reward truth-seeking.
questions.trap: A reversed principle that sounds pro-innovation.

questions.stem: Different Airbnb teams gave different answers to the same question because metric definitions differed, so Airbnb built the Minerva platform. Which Tadelis principle does this illustrate?
options: Govern the metrics
Validate high-stakes claims
Expose assumptions and counterfactuals
Start with the decision
questions.explanation: Minerva is a single source of truth for metric definitions: define once, use the same way everywhere, track changes. That is principle 4, govern the metrics. Self-service analytics needs more governance, not less.
questions.trap: Other principles from the same list.

questions.stem: eBay's branded-keyword search ads looked highly effective until holdout experiments showed most of the value was not incremental. What was the flaw?
options: eBay used the wrong colour palette
Customers who searched 'eBay' would have come anyway, so conversion rate overstated causal impact
The ads had poor creative quality
The holdout group was too large
questions.explanation: People searching for 'eBay' already intended to visit, so attributing their purchases to the ad confuses association with causation. Holdouts revealed low incrementality. This is the same selection-bias trap as retargeting vs prospecting.
questions.trap: Generic creative explanations instead of the causal-inference point.

questions.stem: 'Which customers are likely to churn next month?' is which type of question?
options: Causal
Descriptive
Exploratory
Predictive
questions.explanation: It asks what is likely to happen, which is predictive. 'Whose behaviour will change if we intervene?' would be causal. Descriptive asks what happened. 'Exploratory' is a Session 2 research type, not one of the S8 question types.
questions.trap: Churn questions are often mislabelled causal; 'exploratory' imports S2 vocabulary.

questions.stem: Which of the three conditions for causality do most 'AI insights' meet, and which do they usually fail?
options: Meet: X before Y; fail: association
Meet: association; fail: no competing explanations
Meet all three but fail statistical significance
Meet: no competing explanations; fail: X before Y
questions.explanation: The three conditions are X happens before Y, X and Y are associated, and no competing explanations. AI tools easily find associations (condition 2) but rarely rule out rival explanations such as selection bias, so they fail condition 3.
questions.trap: Rearranging the three conditions.

questions.stem: The in-class table showed prospecting converting at 3% and retargeting at 10%. A typical LLM says 'shift budget to retargeting'. What kind of error is this?
options: Ignoring the cost of prospecting
Giving a descriptive answer to a causal question
A rounding error in the conversion rates
Giving a causal answer to a descriptive question
questions.explanation: The budget decision is causal (which campaign creates extra conversions), but raw conversion rates are descriptive. Retargeted users already visited the site and many would buy anyway, so the comparison fails the 'no competing explanation' condition.
questions.trap: Reversing descriptive/causal.

questions.stem: With control groups added, prospecting shows 1.0% (control) vs 3.0% (exposed) and retargeting 9.5% vs 10.0%. What is the incremental lift of each?
options: Prospecting +2.0 pp; retargeting +0.5 pp
Prospecting +200%; retargeting +100%
Prospecting +3.0 pp; retargeting +10.0 pp
Prospecting +0.5 pp; retargeting +2.0 pp
questions.explanation: Incremental lift is exposed minus control: prospecting 3.0 − 1.0 = +2.0 percentage points; retargeting 10.0 − 9.5 = +0.5 pp. Prospecting creates four times the lift per person reached; 95% of retargeting conversions would have happened anyway.
questions.trap: Reading raw rates as lift, or swapping the two campaigns.

questions.stem: Using the same control-group table, what share of retargeting's 10% conversions would have happened anyway, and what should the final budget decision also consider?
options: About 5%; consider only total conversions
About 95%; shift 100% of budget to prospecting immediately
About 95%; consider cost per incremental conversion, diminishing returns and margin
About 50%; consider brand awareness
questions.explanation: 9.5 of the 10 percentage points occur in the control group, so about 95% is not incremental. The A+ caveat: retargeting audiences are cheaper to reach, so compare cost per incremental conversion, check diminishing returns as prospecting scales, consider margin, and keep some retargeting if still profitable. It is not all-or-nothing.
questions.trap: Jumping from the lift numbers to an all-or-nothing decision.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of unstructured data in marketing?
options: Instagram images and free-text reviews
Customer ages in a CRM column
A table of weekly sales by SKU
Conversion rates by campaign
questions.explanation: Unstructured data has no predefined format: text, images, sound, video. Ad creatives, packaging, reviews, social posts and chatbot logs are marketing examples. Sales tables, age columns and conversion rates are structured.
questions.trap: Numeric but messy data mistaken for unstructured.

questions.stem: Li & Xie's image-analytics framework has three feature levels. Detecting a logo or a human face in an image belongs to which level?
options: Mid-level
Low-level
Meta-level
High-level
questions.explanation: Low-level features are pixel properties such as colour, brightness and contrast; mid-level features are what is in the image, objects, people, logos; high-level features are how people interpret it, emotion, aesthetics, brand meaning. There is no 'meta-level'.
questions.trap: Calling logo detection low-level because it is 'basic'.

questions.stem: A brand wants to know whether its ads convey a 'premium, high-performance' feel. Which image feature level should it extract, and why?
options: Low-level, because colour is objective and fast to compute
Mid-level, because counting products is most reliable
All features at every level, to be safe
High-level, because it captures interpretation and matches marketing theory, trained on human judgements
questions.explanation: Li & Xie: choose the feature level that matches the decision; 'premium feel' is interpretation, so high-level features (emotion, aesthetics, brand meaning), typically CNNs trained on human ratings. Extracting every feature is explicitly discouraged.
questions.trap: 'Extract everything' sounds thorough but violates the framework.
questions.source: Li & Xie framework: outcome → feature level → measure → validate

questions.stem: In the Boost Juice exercise, VADER scored 'Product's great but no system: 15 + 30 min waits' as +0.81 while a contextual reading gave −0.4. What does this show?
options: The review was actually positive
LLMs always inflate negative sentiment
Sentiment analysis cannot be used on short reviews
Lexicon models handle mixed reviews and context poorly, so scores must be validated
questions.explanation: A dictionary model counts positive words like 'great' and misses the 'but', the wait complaint and negation. The exercise showed both methods ranked outlets the same way but the lexicon hid how bad Outlet 1 was. Tadelis principle 3: check the method before trusting the number.
questions.trap: Blaming the LLM or the data instead of the method.

questions.stem: In the Chanel vs Dior exercise, students compared nine Instagram images per brand. The A+ caveat about engagement differences was that they are:
options: Causal proof that colour drives likes
Irrelevant because luxury brands do not use Instagram
Descriptive only; follower count, posting time or paid boosting are competing explanations, so causal claims need controlled tests
Reliable because nine posts is a large sample
questions.explanation: Nine posts is a snapshot and engagement differences may come from follower counts, timing or paid promotion rather than image features. Label the comparison descriptive (Tadelis principle 2) and prove causality with A/B tests. Li & Xie also note product images may drive purchase intent while people images drive social interaction.
questions.trap: Treating a small descriptive comparison as causal.
questions.source: S8 Q6 Chanel vs Dior; Li & Xie

questions.stem: According to Davenport & Bean, what share of leaders say culture and change management are the main barrier to becoming data-driven?
questions.explanation: 92% cite culture and change management as the main barrier; technology alone is not enough. 43%→33% is the fall in self-reported data-driven culture; 58% of leaders claim 'exponential' GenAI gains without measuring them.
questions.trap: Other percentages from the same five-trends article.

questions.stem: P&G's 'AI factory' is best described as:
options: An external vendor contract for GenAI
A consumer-facing app for product recommendations
A shared platform of data, tools, methods and security that cuts deployment time by about six months, used by mostly embedded data scientists
A centralised team that does all analysis for the company
questions.explanation: P&G's several hundred data scientists are mostly embedded in business units but share a common platform, the AI factory, which cuts deployment time by about six months, a hybrid model. One team builds the factory, another scales the models. Pampers My Perfect Fit is one application, not the factory itself.
questions.trap: Describing it as pure centralised.

questions.stem: In P&G's 'cybernetic teammate' experiment with 776 staff, what was found?
options: AI reduced collaboration between R&D and commercial staff
An individual using AI performed as well as a team without AI, and teams with AI performed best
AI had no measurable effect on performance
Teams without AI outperformed individuals with AI
questions.explanation: The HBS–P&G experiment found an individual with AI matched a team without AI, teams with AI did best, and AI broke down silos between R&D and commercial staff. This is also an example of Davenport & Bean's call to measure GenAI results with controlled experiments.
questions.trap: Reversing the comparison.

questions.stem: Davenport & Bean say early agentic-AI wins will most likely come from:
options: Fully autonomous marketing campaigns
Small, structured, low-money internal tasks such as password resets
Replacing the CDO role
Customer-facing spending decisions
questions.explanation: Agents still predict the next word and make errors, so humans stay in the loop and early wins are small structured internal tasks (password resets, leave booking), not customer-facing spending. 37% of IT leaders think they already have agentic AI; the authors call that hype.
questions.trap: Hype-driven options.

questions.stem: Tadelis's warning that polished AI output raises 'confidence, not truth' is closest to which idea from another session?
options: Session 6: Kopalle's four Ps of pricing
Session 2: 'do you believe the results?' – validity checks on synthetic data
Session 5: the uncanny valley
Session 3: the importance pillar in search ranking
questions.explanation: Both say an AI answer is a confident draft, not evidence; validate in proportion to the stakes. This is the course's 'AI is fast; check it' thread running through S2, S4, S7, S8 and S9. The other options are unrelated frameworks.
questions.trap: Cross-session names with no logical link.
questions.source: Tadelis; S2 slide 35; P2 thread A

questions.stem: Which Session 6 idea is closest to Session 8's holdout/control-group logic?
options: Exploration via A/B tests and multi-armed bandits before exploiting the best price
Framing a price as a discount
Surveillance pricing
The Hyderabad vegetable seller
questions.explanation: Both are deliberate experimentation to learn causal effects: holdouts measure incremental lift; A/B tests and bandits (Kopalle; ZipRecruiter's ten random prices) explore before exploiting. Framing, surveillance pricing and the vegetable seller are different S6 concepts.
questions.trap: Familiar S6 terms without the experimental logic.
questions.source: S8 slides 29–31; S6 slide 26; P2 thread B

questions.stem: How does the session define AI risk?
options: The legal penalties a firm faces for using AI
Any error an AI model makes in production
The probability and impact of deliberate or accidental harm to individuals, organisations or society from AI
The impact of harm from AI, regardless of how likely it is
questions.explanation: Risk is probability × impact, intent is deliberate or accidental, and the victim can be an individual, organisation or society. Impact alone ignores likelihood; an error is not a risk unless it can cause harm.
questions.trap: Dropping probability from the definition.

questions.stem: The inherited-vs-added risk table lists who creates each type. Which pairing is correct?
options: Inherited: the regulator; Added: the customer
Inherited: your prompts; Added: the vendor's training data
Inherited: the vendor's training data and objective; Added: your prompts, pasted data and publishing choices
Inherited: risks you can see; Added: risks you cannot see
questions.explanation: Inherited risk is baked in by the vendor (training data, labelling, optimisation objective, safety tuning) and usually invisible to you; added risk is introduced by you through prompts, data and what you publish, and is under your control. The 'risks you can see vs cannot see' option reverses visibility: inherited risk is the black box, added risk is visible.
questions.trap: Reversing the two columns of the table.

questions.stem: 'We didn't build or train the model, so the bias is the vendor's problem.' According to the session, this statement is:
options: Correct, if the vendor provides indemnification
Wrong, only if you fine-tuned the model
Correct, because inherited risk belongs to the vendor
Wrong, because not building the model does not remove your responsibility; inherited and added risk both land on you
questions.explanation: The key line of slide 8: 'Not building or training the model does not remove your responsibility.' You chose the vendor and chose to publish; customers and regulators blame the brand (NEDA was blamed for Tessa, not the vendor). Indemnification helps with IP cost but not with reputation or responsibility.
questions.trap: Indemnification offered as a get-out.
questions.source: S9 slide 8; MIT SMR NEDA case

questions.stem: Which list correctly names the three sources of algorithmic bias from the session?
options: Biased training data, non-representative data, optimising the wrong metric
Hallucination, bias amplification, regression to the mean
Input leakage, inference, profiling
Misuse, misapply, misrepresent
questions.explanation: The three sources are biased training data (health-cost proxy), non-representative data (Gender Shades) and optimising the wrong metric (STEM ads). The 'hallucination, bias amplification, regression to the mean' list is Session 2's cons of synthetic participants; 'misuse, misapply, misrepresent' are three of HBR's 4 Ms; 'input leakage, inference, profiling' is privacy vocabulary.
questions.trap: Other three-item lists from S2 and S9 readings.

questions.stem: A US health algorithm used health cost as a proxy for health need and under-flagged Black patients even though race was excluded. Which bias source is this?
options: Biased training data via a biased proxy label
Accidental misadventure
Optimising the wrong metric
Non-representative data
questions.explanation: The data accurately reflected an unfair world: less is spent on Black patients at the same sickness level, so predicting cost reproduced the inequality. Removing race did not help because the label and other proxies carry the bias. The fix is to change the target variable, not to drop a column.
questions.trap: Calling it 'wrong metric' because cost is a metric; in the slides it is filed under biased data/proxy.

questions.stem: MIT's Gender Shades study found face-analysis tools had far higher error rates for darker-skinned women than lighter-skinned men. Which bias source and which fix?
options: Wrong metric; add a fairness constraint to the objective
Biased proxy label; change the target variable
Input leakage; restrict which data staff may paste
Non-representative data; rebalance or collect data and test each subgroup
questions.explanation: Training sets had mostly lighter-skinned male faces, so the model did well on average but poorly on under-represented groups. The fix is to rebalance the data and test performance by subgroup. The other fixes belong to sources 1 and 3 or to privacy risk.
questions.trap: Fix mismatched to source.

questions.stem: A gender-neutral STEM job ad was shown to more men than women because young women are a more expensive audience to reach. The algorithm was:
options: Trained on sexist data (biased training data)
Minimising cost per impression, so discrimination was a side effect (optimising the wrong metric)
Deliberately programmed to exclude women
Missing women in its training set (non-representative data)
questions.explanation: The data were fine; the cost-minimising objective 'bought' cheaper male impressions. Perfect data plus the wrong objective still produces bias. Fix: parity constraints or minimum delivery by group and monitoring delivery reports by demographic. This is the same mechanism as the slide 36 exercise's cost-vs-reach algorithm.
questions.trap: Filing it under biased data.

questions.stem: A model has excellent overall accuracy. According to slide 17, what is the only way to see whether it is biased?
options: Ask the vendor for its fairness certificate
Disaggregate performance by subgroup (race, gender, age, geography)
Remove sensitive variables such as race from the inputs
Increase the training data size
questions.explanation: In all three bias cases the aggregate score can look excellent: the model accurately predicts a biased label, the majority dominates the average, or it hits its objective with harm as a side effect. Only disaggregating by subgroup reveals it. Removing race fails because proxies remain ('fairness through blindness').
questions.trap: 'Remove race' sounds like fairness but the health case shows it fails.

questions.stem: In Getty Images v. Stability AI (UK), what was the outcome described in the session?
options: The claim was dismissed entirely
No copyright liability (training outside the UK; weights are not a copy) but trademark infringement because outputs reproduced Getty's watermark
Getty won on copyright because model weights are a copy of the images
Stability was fined US$1.5bn
questions.explanation: The UK court found no jurisdiction over training done abroad and that model weights are not a 'copy', but held Stability liable for trademark infringement because generated images reproduced the Getty watermark. The US$1.5bn figure is the Bartz v. Anthropic settlement.
questions.trap: 'Getty won on copyright' is the planted near-miss; it won on trademark.

questions.stem: What did Bartz v. Anthropic establish, according to the session?
options: Training on legally acquired books is fair use, but using pirated copies is not; this drove a US$1.5bn settlement
Authors cannot sue AI companies
All AI training on books is illegal
AI outputs are always copyrightable by the user
questions.explanation: The ruling split acquisition from use: legally acquired books for training qualified as fair use; pirated copies did not, leading to a US$1.5bn settlement with authors. The session's line: 'fair use is not a get-out-of-jail-free card.'
questions.trap: All-or-nothing readings of the case.

questions.stem: A marketing team publishes an AI-generated hero image. Which statement about IP is correct?
options: Because the vendor trained the model, any infringement is purely inherited risk
Using 'in the style of' a living artist removes legal risk
Publishing infringing output is your added IP risk, and purely AI-generated content may not be copyrightable in the US
AI output is automatically copyrighted to the firm that prompted it
questions.explanation: Whether published output infringes is a risk you fully own because you chose to publish. US copyright needs human authorship, so purely AI output may be unprotected and competitors could reuse it. 'In the style of' a living artist raises legal and reputational issues rather than removing them.
questions.trap: Assuming ownership of AI output, or offloading all IP risk to the vendor.

questions.stem: Which is a recommended way to manage IP risk, per the session and the HBR IP article?
options: Review vendor terms for licensed training data and indemnification, and keep records of prompts, sources and the human role
Delete all prompt records so there is no evidence
Prompt with living artists' names so style is clearly attributed
Only use free, open-source image tools
questions.explanation: Controls include monitoring cases, vendor terms with licensed-data tiers and indemnification (e.g., Microsoft's Copilot Copyright Commitment), and keeping provenance records of prompts, sources and human input to support authorship and show no wilful copying. Deleting records and 'in the style of' prompts increase exposure.
questions.trap: Options that sound protective but increase risk.

questions.stem: Samsung banned staff use of ChatGPT after engineers pasted code into it. This illustrates which privacy risk?
options: Inference of sensitive attributes
Input leakage of confidential data into a public AI tool
Algorithmic collusion
Non-representative training data
questions.explanation: Pasting customer or company data into public AI tools means it can be retained, used for training or exposed: input leakage, an added privacy risk. Inference is the Target case; collusion is Session 6 (RealPage).
questions.trap: Mixing up the two privacy mechanisms.

questions.stem: Target predicted a teenage girl's pregnancy from shopping patterns and sent baby coupons before her family knew. No data was leaked. Why is this still a privacy harm?
options: Because the firm created and acted on a sensitive attribute the customer never disclosed (inference), failing the reasonable-expectations test
It is not a privacy harm since the data was collected legally
Because coupons are a form of discrimination
Because Target violated GDPR
questions.explanation: Privacy risk includes data the system infers, not just data that leaks. Target manufactured sensitive information and acted on it, revealing it to family. Legality may be grey, but it fails the 'creepiness' test and damages trust. Controls: flag sensitive inferred categories and require opt-in.
questions.trap: 'No leak, no harm' reasoning.

questions.stem: Which privacy control from slide 30 is most directly aimed at the Samsung-type problem?
options: Monitoring sensitive profiles
Restrict which data categories staff may put into which AI tools
Federated learning
Transparent opt-outs for customers
questions.explanation: A data-classification policy (public / internal / confidential / personal → which tool is allowed) plus approved enterprise tools and data-loss prevention addresses input leakage. Federated learning and anonymisation reduce the need to move raw data; opt-outs and profile monitoring address inference and transparency.
questions.trap: All options are real controls; only one matches the mechanism.

questions.stem: In AI governance, deliberate risks and accidental risks call for different control types. Which pairing is correct?
options: Deliberate → policy, incentives and accountability; Accidental → detection, monitoring and review
Deliberate → insurance; Accidental → legal disclaimers
Both → red teaming only
Deliberate → detection and monitoring; Accidental → policy and incentives
questions.explanation: A deliberate risk is a choice or accepted trade-off, so it needs a named owner, policy and incentives; an accidental risk emerges unintended, so it needs detection, monitoring and review such as red teaming and subgroup audits. The option that gives deliberate risks detection and accidental risks policy reverses the pairing.
questions.trap: Reversed pairing.

questions.stem: Management knowingly accepts that a cost-minimising ad algorithm under-delivers to costlier demographic groups because it lowers CPM. The right control is:
options: A privacy impact assessment
Pre-launch red teaming of the image generator
A written fairness requirement, a named owner and KPIs that include reach parity (policy and accountability)
A four-eye review of ad copy
questions.explanation: This is a deliberate trade-off, so it needs policy, incentive and accountability controls: fairness requirements, an accountable owner, and KPIs beyond cost. Red teaming and four-eye review are detection/review controls for accidental risks; a privacy impact assessment addresses data use, not delivery bias.
questions.trap: Choosing a review control for a deliberate risk.

questions.stem: In the MIT SMR Ethical Matrix, what are the rows and columns?
options: Rows = sessions; columns = readings
Rows = likelihood; columns = impact
Rows = stakeholders (including subgroups); columns = concerns, positive and negative
Rows = risks; columns = control types
questions.explanation: The Ethical Matrix lists every affected stakeholder as a row (splitting subgroups with different concerns) and their concerns as columns, colour-coded red (grave harm or hard constraint), yellow (some worry), green (no worry or benefit). A likelihood × impact grid is a separate severity tool.
questions.trap: Confusing the matrix with the likelihood × impact grid.
questions.source: O'Neil, Appel & Tyner-Monroe (MIT SMR, 2024); S9 slide 33

questions.stem: Severity in the risk map is defined as:
options: Impact only, because likelihood cannot be estimated
Likelihood × impact, with harm to vulnerable groups or a legal hard constraint treated as automatically high
The cost of the control
The number of stakeholders affected
questions.explanation: Severity = likelihood × impact (how many people, how badly), and MIT SMR adds that grave harm to vulnerable people or breaking a legal hard constraint is a red cell regardless of probability. This is how the slide 36 exercise scores risks 1–9.
questions.trap: Impact-only definitions.

questions.stem: How do red teaming and benchmarking differ as ways to evaluate an LLM?
options: Benchmarking covers only bias; red teaming covers only accuracy
They are the same technique under two names
Benchmarking tests inputs against desired outputs with metrics; red teaming deliberately tries to make the model misbehave
Red teaming is automated; benchmarking is manual
questions.explanation: Benchmarking compares test inputs with desired outputs on accuracy, robustness, fairness and bias, but suffers data contamination and Goodhart's law. Red teaming adversarially provokes misbehaviour and should cover at least every red cell of the Ethical Matrix, but is subjective and cannot find risks nobody imagined. NEDA's Tessa would likely have been caught by both.
questions.trap: Narrowing each technique to one dimension.

questions.stem: NEDA replaced its human eating-disorder helpline with the vendor-built 'Tessa' chatbot, which gave dieting advice and was taken down. What is the main governance lesson?
options: Chatbots should never be used by charities
The problem was a server outage
NEDA should have used a bigger model
Red cells in the Ethical Matrix (vulnerable users harmed) should have triggered red teaming and benchmarking before launch, and the deployer, not the vendor, was blamed
questions.explanation: Identifying failure scenarios for vulnerable users would have made 'harmful dieting advice' an obvious red cell; red teaming and benchmarking would likely have caught it. NEDA was blamed, not the vendor X2AI, illustrating that inherited risk still lands on the deployer.
questions.trap: Technical or blanket-ban answers.
questions.source: MIT SMR NEDA case; S9 Q1

questions.stem: HBR's 2×2 of Gen-AI risk crosses intent with usage. Knowingly spreading dubious AI content made by others (e.g., a fake Cybertruck crash video) is which cell?
options: Misuse (deliberate × creating)
Misadventure (accidental × consuming)
Misapply (accidental × creating)
Misrepresent (deliberate × consuming)
questions.explanation: The consumer knowingly spreads others' dubious content: deliberate × consuming = misrepresent. Misuse is deliberately creating harmful content (scams, deepfakes); misapply is accidentally trusting a hallucination; misadventure is unknowingly sharing a fake (Pentagon explosion image).
questions.trap: Misrepresent vs misadventure swapped.

questions.stem: In the same 2×2, a marketer trusts ChatGPT's false claim that a radio host embezzled funds and publishes it. Which cell, and which mitigation family?
options: Misrepresent; mitigate with damage-mitigation plans
Misuse; mitigate with watermarking
Misadventure; mitigate with awareness training
Misapply (accidental × creating); mitigate creation risk with aligned AI principles, watermarking and a controlled gen-AI environment
questions.explanation: Trusting a hallucination you then create content from is accidental × creating = misapply. HBR's creation-side mitigations are aligning AI principles with company values, watermarking AI output and a controlled in-house gen-AI environment. Consumption-side mitigations are training, labelling/validation with a four-eye rule, and damage-mitigation plans.
questions.trap: Pairing the right cell with the consumption-side mitigations.

questions.stem: Which statement about the EU AI Act and the NIST AI RMF is correct?
options: NIST is voluntary (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage); the EU AI Act is binding with risk tiers based on how and where a system is used, not on the technology
Both are binding law in the EU and US
NIST classifies systems into unacceptable, high, limited and minimal tiers
The EU AI Act bans all chatbots
questions.explanation: NIST AI RMF is a voluntary process framework: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage. The EU AI Act is binding and sorts systems into unacceptable, high, limited and minimal tiers by use context; chatbots and deepfakes fall under limited-tier transparency duties, not bans. The option attributing the four tiers to NIST confuses the two frameworks.
questions.trap: Swapping which framework has the tiers.

questions.stem: The STEM-ads bias (cost-minimising objective) is the same mechanism as which other course case?
options: Lil Miquela pretending to be human until 2018
The PNAS 11–20 game showing LLMs reason less deeply
RAG retrieving the wrong document chunk
Uber's surge pricing during the Sydney siege: an algorithm faithfully optimising its objective with harmful side effects
questions.explanation: Both are 'wrong objective' failures: the ad algorithm minimised cost and excluded women; Uber's surge maximised driver supply during a hostage crisis. Neither had biased data; the metric produced the harm. This is the course's optimisation-bias thread (also retargeting's conversion-rate trap in S8).
questions.trap: Other famous cases with different mechanisms.
questions.source: S9 slide 16; S6 slide 16; P2 thread D

questions.stem: The group project brief states the core business problem that motivates personalised advertising. Which option captures it?
options: People buy the same product for different reasons, so one average message converts poorly
Static images perform worse than video
Consumers dislike all forms of advertising
Ad platforms charge too much for broad reach
questions.explanation: The brief's logic is customer heterogeneity: different emotional triggers need different visual and textual cues, so one average message speaks to nobody. This is STP from Session 1 pushed to the creative level.

questions.stem: According to the brief, which of the following is NOT personalisation?
options: Randomly changing a colour or a model's face between segments
Choosing a CTA that matches each segment's stated preference
Showing a different usage occasion tied to each segment's motivation
Changing the Maslow need the ad appeals to for each segment
questions.explanation: The brief explicitly says randomly changing a colour or a model's face is not personalisation; a genuine link between the segment's underlying motivation and the creative choices is required. The other three options trace a creative lever to segment evidence.
questions.trap: Cosmetic variation looks like personalisation but is not.

questions.stem: Which four criteria make a segment usable for the project, according to the prompt pack's segment-selection phase?
options: Awareness, interest, desire, action
Colour, composition, copy, tone
Size, value, distinctiveness of response, identifiability on the ad platform
Age, gender, income, location
questions.explanation: Segments are scored on size in the real market, value, distinctiveness (would a different message change their response?) and identifiability on Meta Ads. The brief says a psychologically interesting but untargetable segment is unusable.
questions.source: Group Project Master Prompt Pack, Phase 2

questions.stem: Which of these is a concrete Meta Ads route that makes a segment identifiable?
options: A synthetic respondent's verbatim quote
The segment's Maslow level
Custom audiences from CRM lists, interest targeting, life events and lookalike seeds
The segment's favourite colour palette
questions.explanation: Identifiability means the platform can actually deliver the ad to that group: core signals (age, location), detailed interests, life events, custom audiences (pixel, CRM), lookalikes or Advantage+ self-selection. Psychological traits alone cannot be targeted.
questions.source: Group Project Master Prompt Pack, Phase 2; Nespresso pack Part 1

questions.stem: In the Nespresso project, the same machine was sold to three segments with three different needs. Which pairing is correct?
options: Gen-Z iced café aspirants – safety/value
Value-driven switchers – esteem and status
All three – belonging
Time-poor home ritualists – self-care and reliability
questions.explanation: S1 Gen-Z Iced Café-Culture Aspirants = belonging/esteem; S2 Time-Poor Home Ritualists = safety via reliability and self-care ('Your 10 minutes, sorted'); S3 Value-Driven Switchers & Upgraders = safety/value (fair price, trade-in). The product did not change; only the message did.
questions.source: Nespresso A+ Prompt Pack v2, Part 1

questions.stem: The review of the Nespresso draft flagged that the headline 'Upgrade your mornings' for the value segment carried the wrong need. Why?
options: It used British spelling
It mentioned a competitor
It was too long for Instagram
It is an esteem/aspiration message while the segment's need is safety/value; the badge did the value work but the headline did not
questions.explanation: Each creative element should trace to the segment's motivation. 'Upgrade your mornings' signals aspiration, not 'better coffee at a fair price'. Alternatives like 'Better coffee. Same budget.' fix the mismatch.
questions.source: Nespresso A+ Prompt Pack v2, Part 2 (issue 4)

questions.stem: Why did the project hold brand elements (logo, product with capsules, 4:5 format) constant across all three ads?
options: To save design time
To make the ads look like competitors'
Because Meta requires identical layouts
So that the visible differences between ads are clearly segment logic, not three random designs
questions.explanation: Holding brand elements constant and varying only need, scene, people, palette, tone and offer proves that differences are personalisation rather than arbitrary variation. It also mirrors DCO, where brand elements are locked and components vary.
questions.source: Nespresso A+ Prompt Pack v2, Prompt C 4.1; S4 slide 28

questions.stem: The brief requires the synthetic research section to be reproducible. Which elements must be reported?
options: The team's personal opinions of the brand
The names of the LLM's training data sources
Which questions were asked, how many participants, how the data were analysed, and limitations
Only the final segment names
questions.explanation: The rubric asks for exact questions, number of participants, analysis method and reproducibility from the appendix, plus an honest validity discussion (hallucination, stereotype amplification, regression to the mean, trained positivity) and the statement that results are simulated.
questions.source: Nespresso A+ Prompt Pack v2, Prompt G; S2 slide 25

questions.stem: The Nespresso team reported an 85% female skew and halal mentions only among Malay personas, and decided NOT to use gender or ethnic targeting. Which Session 2 concern does this reflect?
options: Bias amplification – the LLM reproduced stereotypes, so demographic patterns in the synthetic data are untrustworthy
Trained behaviour
Regression to the mean
Hallucination of prices
questions.explanation: Stereotyped demographic patterns are bias amplification. Treating them as real would risk discriminatory targeting and also raise Session 9 risks, so the team chose behaviour- and interest-based signals instead.
questions.source: Nespresso A+ Prompt Pack v2, Part 2; S2 slide 25

questions.stem: The optional 'synthetic ad test' asked segment personas to choose among the three ads. What result counts as strong, and what should the team do if a segment prefers another ad?
options: 100% agreement; otherwise rerun until it agrees
At least 60% of each segment choosing 'its' ad; if not, report honestly and explain what was changed
Any result above 30%; delete the losing ad
Likes above 1,000; otherwise buy media
questions.explanation: The pack sets ≥60% as a strong result and says to report an unexpected preference honestly and describe the iteration, because the professor rewards reflection more than perfect numbers. Rerunning until it agrees would be data manipulation.
questions.source: Nespresso A+ Prompt Pack v2, Prompt E

questions.stem: How should a real Nespresso team validate the three personalised ads, according to the project's conclusion?
options: Ask the LLM whether it likes the ads
Run a Meta A/B test with each ad in its audience plus a control 'average' ad, measured on CTR, cost per add-to-cart and incremental sales, plus human interviews per segment
Launch all three to everyone and pick the one with the most comments
Count Instagram likes for a week
questions.explanation: Because the research data are simulated, validation needs real humans and causal measurement: A/B tests with a control ad and incremental outcomes (Session 8's conversion ≠ incrementality lesson), plus 10–15 interviews per segment and Audience Insights for size.
questions.trap: Likes are not incremental sales.
questions.source: Nespresso A+ Prompt Pack v2, Prompt F; S8 slides 29–31

questions.stem: Which appendix disclosures did the project require that connect to Session 9 risk management?
options: A list of team members' hobbies
AI tool disclosure with human checks performed, a note that the logo is used for academic purposes and offers are illustrative, and image prompts with iteration counts
A copy of Meta's terms of service
The LLM's full chat logs printed in colour
questions.explanation: The AI disclosure table (tool, use, human check, who), the IP note on the real logo, the invented-offer caveat and logged prompts are exactly the IP and governance controls from Session 9: keep records of prompts and the human role, and be transparent.
questions.source: Nespresso A+ Prompt Pack v2, Prompt F; S9 slides 24, 30

shorts.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
shorts.stem: Explain how marketing 'creates value' using Maslow and Levitt, and give one example from the course.
shorts.model: Concept: the AMA defines marketing as creating, communicating, delivering and exchanging offerings that have value. Value is created by satisfying a need, and Maslow's hierarchy shows needs run from physiological and safety up to belonging, esteem and self-actualisation, with lower needs prioritised first. Mechanism: Levitt's 'people buy a quarter-inch hole, not a drill' means the firm should think about the consumer's problem and sell the solution; the same product can satisfy different needs. Example: Session 1 asks whether we sell clothing or a sense of belonging or self-esteem. In the Nespresso group project the same machine was sold as an iced café treat (belonging/esteem), ten quiet minutes (self-care) and a fair-price upgrade (value/safety). Limitation: the need a firm intends to serve (identity) may not be the need customers perceive (image), so positioning must be checked with research rather than assumed.
shorts.minimum: Value = a need satisfied (Maslow). Sell solutions, not products (Levitt's drill and hole). Example: clothing as belonging; Nespresso's three needs for one machine.
marking: Maslow: needs at different levels, lower prioritised
Limitation or link to identity vs image

shorts.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
shorts.stem: Why does customer heterogeneity lead firms to the STP framework, and what does each letter involve?
shorts.model: Concept: customers differ in demographics, personality, life experience, purchase history and location, so one message or offer fits nobody well. Mechanism: the two extremes, treating everyone the same or treating each person differently, are either ineffective or too costly, so STP sits in between. Segmentation identifies a small set of groups of similar customers. Targeting evaluates those segments on size, growth, alignment and competition and picks the ones with the highest ROI. Positioning decides how the brand should be perceived against competitors, remembering identity is not the same as image. Example: Nespresso in the group project found six segments by synthetic research and targeted three with different Maslow needs and different ads. Limitation: a segment is only useful if it is reachable; the project brief states that a psychologically interesting but unidentifiable segment is unusable, and AI-driven personalisation can push STP so far that privacy and trust issues appear (Sessions 6 and 9).
shorts.minimum: Customers differ → one message fits nobody. STP = segment similar groups, target by size/growth/alignment/competition for ROI, position vs competitors. Segments must be reachable.
marking: Explains the two extremes STP sits between

shorts.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
shorts.stem: Distinguish market research from marketing analytics and say where each appears later in the course.
shorts.model: Concept: both are ways firms learn about the market, alongside experience and intuition ('all others bring data'). Market research is the systematic design, collection and analysis of data relevant to a specific marketing problem, using primary or secondary and qualitative or quantitative data; it is essential for new product development, STP and the 4Ps. Marketing analytics is the constant measuring, monitoring and analysing of marketing data and performance: dashboards, forecasting, optimisation and machine learning. Mechanism: research is project-based and problem-specific, analytics is continuous. Example: Session 2's synthetic market research (100 persona responses on consideration and price) is research done with LLM personas; Session 8's prospecting-vs-retargeting incrementality test is analytics that should end in a decision. Limitation: AI blurs the line, since LLMs can both generate research data and analyse performance, but the validity concerns differ: hallucination and regression to the mean in research, descriptive answers to causal questions in analytics.
shorts.minimum: Research = systematic study of a specific problem (S2 synthetic research). Analytics = constant measuring and monitoring of performance (S8). One is project-based, the other continuous.

shorts.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
shorts.stem: Is AI a marketing friend or foe? Give the structured answer the Session 1 exercise asked for.
shorts.model: Concept: the professor wants a structured analysis across the course concepts, not a verdict. Mechanism: analyse the impact on (1) marketing vs other functions, where marketing is one of the heaviest users of AI for copy, images, targeting and chatbots; (2) revenues vs costs, where AI cuts production and service cost (e.g., about $0.70 saved per chatbot interaction) and can lift revenue through personalisation; (3) strategy, marketing mix, research and analytics, where synthetic research speeds segmentation, dynamic pricing and personalised ads change the mix, and analytics becomes faster but not automatically better; and (4) consumer behaviour, where consumers gain convenience and bots as buyers appear, but face surveillance pricing, inauthentic content and privacy inference. Example: the IAB perception gap, 82% of executives vs 45% of young consumers positive about AI ads, shows benefit to firms and scepticism among consumers. Conclusion with a condition: friend when governed (human review, disclosure, causal testing), foe when unchecked. Limitation: evidence is early and often vendor-reported.
shorts.minimum: Structure: functions, revenue vs cost, strategy/mix/research/analytics, consumer behaviour. Opportunities and threats in each. Conditional verdict: friend if governed, foe if unchecked.
marking: Uses the four-part structure from the exercise
Opportunities and threats in each part
At least one course number or case

shorts.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
shorts.stem: Describe the AIDA funnel and the customer journey, and explain how AI tools from later sessions touch each stage.
shorts.model: Concept: AIDA (Attention, Interest, Desire, Action) is the canonical purchase funnel from about 1898 (St. Elmo Lewis). The customer journey widens this into physical and digital touchpoints on the way to purchase and beyond, often described with personas. Mechanism: consumers start unaware and may end by purchasing; marketers need tools at every stage.
