Example: advertising and virtual influencers (S4, S5) create attention and interest; GEO (S3) captures early information search when consumers ask LLMs; chatbots and conversational commerce (S7) remove friction at purchase and serve customers after it; dynamic pricing (S6) acts at the purchase moment; analytics (S8) measures the whole journey. Limitation: the funnel is a simplification. In Session 3 the professor notes that LLMs now sit between social media (need awareness) and search engines (transactional search), and bots may soon buy on the consumer's behalf, so the journey itself is changing.
shorts.minimum: AIDA = Attention, Interest, Desire, Action (1898). Journey = touchpoints before and after purchase. Ads/influencers at the top, GEO mid, chatbots and pricing at purchase, analytics throughout.
marking: AIDA stages named with date or author
At least three sessions mapped to stages
Notes the journey is changing (LLMs, bots)

shorts.sessionName: Introduction – Key Marketing Concepts and AI
shorts.stem: Explain the 4Ps of the marketing mix and show how this course maps AI onto them.
shorts.model: Concept: after STP, the tactical stage decides the marketing mix, usually the 4Ps attributed to Borden (1964): Product (functionality, quality, packaging, brand), Price (list price, discounts, financing), Place (channels, coverage, logistics, service levels) and Promotion (advertising, selling, PR, message, media, budget). Mechanism: the course applies AI to each. Promotion receives four sessions: synthetic market research to know the customer, GEO to be found in LLM answers, AI-generated and personalised advertising, and virtual influencers. Price is Session 6 on dynamic pricing with reinforcement learning. Place and service are Session 7 on chatbots, voice agents and RAG. Product insight comes from research and image analytics in Session 8. Example: Nespresso in the project held product constant and varied the Promotion message by segment. Limitation: Kopalle's dynamic-pricing definition also uses four Ps (People, Products, Periods, Places), a frequent confusion, and AI also changes the learning layer (analytics, risk) that sits around the mix.
shorts.minimum: 4Ps = Product, Price, Place, Promotion (Borden 1964). Course: Promotion S2–S5, Price S6, Place/Service S7, with analytics and risk around them. Not Kopalle's People/Products/Periods/Places.
marking: Four Ps named with examples of decisions

shorts.stem: Name the four validity concerns about synthetic participants and give one control for each.
shorts.model: Concept: synthetic participants are LLMs prompted to answer as personas; they are fast, scalable and cheap, but Session 2 lists four validity concerns. Hallucination: the model invents facts and misreads prompts (e.g., assuming 'more expensive = higher quality'); control by clearly separating prompt facts from assumptions and benchmarking against real data. Bias amplification: stereotypes in training data are exaggerated; control by instructing independence ('do not infer attitudes from age or income alone') and checking subgroup patterns, as the Nespresso team did when it dropped gender and ethnic targeting. Regression to the mean: answers cluster on the average internet opinion; control by allowing dissent and rare views and comparing the spread with any human benchmark. Trained behaviour: safety tuning makes respondents polite and agreeable; control by asking for honest negatives and treating positivity as inflated. Example: the PNAS 11–20 game showed LLM distributions differ from humans'. Limitation: the professor's conclusion is 'apply but remain cautious'; results are hypotheses to validate with humans.
shorts.minimum: Hallucination, bias amplification, regression to the mean, trained behaviour. Controls: separate facts from assumptions, independence instructions, allow dissent, benchmark against real data; treat as hypotheses.
marking: Each con explained in one line

shorts.stem: Distinguish synthetic participants from digital twins and explain when a firm should use each.
shorts.model: Concept: a synthetic participant is an LLM told to adopt a persona defined by age, gender, income, attitudes and so on; it answers as that person and can be scaled to thousands of respondents instantly with zero attrition. A digital twin is a model calibrated on a specific real person's actual prior survey or interview answers, used to predict that same person's reaction to new stimuli. Mechanism: participants rely on the model's general knowledge of such people; twins rely on recorded human data, so their accuracy depends on the richness and recency of that data. Use participants for exploratory work, niche segments, sensitive topics and rapid concept screening (the 'fill gaps' and 'replace' roles). Use twins to 'make a first impression twice', track a fixed panel over time or run what-if simulations (the 'create new' role). Example: the Session 2 exercise used 100 persona participants; a firm with an existing panel could build twins. Limitation: twins drift as people change, participants regress to the mean; both are simulated, not findings.
shorts.minimum: Participant = persona-prompted LLM, instant scale. Twin = calibrated on a real person's past answers, predicts their future responses. Participants for exploration; twins for repeat testing on a known panel.
marking: Correct definition of twin including calibration on real data
Accuracy depends on human data richness/recency

shorts.stem: What did the PNAS 11–20 money request study show about LLMs as human surrogates, and what prompting fixes were tested?
shorts.model: Concept: the 11–20 game asks players to request 11–20 shekels with a bonus for asking exactly one less than the other player; it measures reasoning depth and has known human results. Mechanism: the authors compared LLM answers with human distributions. Findings: LLMs showed lower reasoning levels than humans, their distribution did not match the human one, patterns varied across LLMs and task designs, and some design changes made them less human-like. Fixes tested: zero-shot tricks (chain-of-thought, 'take a deep breath', demographics) did not help, and changing language or role made results unstable; few-shot examples drove results toward the samples given, not toward humans; RAG with the original paper made answers more human-like but still significantly different; fine-tuning on many human answers made them statistically indistinguishable. Example: an LLM still chose 19 'because of loss aversion' when payouts were fixed, so its self-explanations are unreliable. Limitation: if fine-tuning needs the human data anyway, the slides ask why use synthetic participants at all.
shorts.minimum: LLMs reason less deeply, distributions differ. Zero/few-shot did not fix it; RAG closer but different; fine-tuning matched humans. Self-explanations unreliable.
marking: Describes the game as a reasoning test
Key findings on reasoning and distribution
The 'why use synthetic data then?' point

shorts.stem: Explain the four roles AI can play in market research (Korst, Puntoni and Toubia) with an example of each.
shorts.model: Concept: AI does not only replace surveys; it can change market research in four ways. Support: speed up and scale existing methods, for example auto-transcribing interviews, coding open-ended answers, drafting survey items and summarising findings. Replace: use synthetic participants instead of human respondents, as in the Session 2 exercise with 100 persona responses. Fill gaps: generate insight where human data is unavailable, such as niche segments, sensitive or stigmatised topics and rapid concept screening. Create new: research that did not exist before, chiefly digital twins, virtual replicas of real customers used to test strategies. Mechanism: the further right you move, from support to create new, the more you rely on the model rather than on humans, so validity risk rises. Example: the Nespresso project used replace (synthetic segments) and planned human validation. Limitation: the four cons apply most strongly to replace and create new, so the professor advises applying with caution.
shorts.minimum: Support (transcribe, code), replace (synthetic participants), fill gaps (niche, sensitive topics), create new (digital twins). Validity risk rises left to right.
marking: Attributed to Korst, Puntoni and Toubia
Link to course exercise or project

shorts.stem: Why does Session 2 say that asking the right question of a synthetic participant may be harder than asking a human?
shorts.model: Concept: good market research depends on asking the right question; with synthetic participants the prompt is the question, the sample and the respondent all at once. Mechanism: small prompt choices change results. The Tesla Model Y example prompt steered respondents towards EVs and hybrids; adding instructions about independence, allowing petrol preferences and separating facts from assumptions corrects that, but slide 37 asks whether it steers participants too much. Language and role changes made PNAS results highly unstable, and few-shot samples pulled answers toward the examples given. The model may also hallucinate the meaning of a persona attribute (income implies premium taste) and will politely agree because of training. Example: in the Nespresso project the team used six independent chats and explicit independence instructions, then reported template repetition and a female skew as limitations. Limitation: there is no human to clarify or push back, so the researcher must iterate prompts, document them and treat outputs as hypotheses.
shorts.minimum: The prompt is question, sample and respondent in one; small wording changes steer results (Tesla EV focus, unstable language/role effects). Must iterate, document and treat as hypotheses.
marking: Steering example from the Tesla prompt

shorts.stem: Classify exploratory, descriptive and causal research and explain how a firm should choose a sampling technique.
shorts.model: Concept: research types differ by how well the problem is defined. Exploratory research handles ambiguous problems ('is there a market for customised wine?'; 'why don't non-buyers buy: taste, image, price, packaging?'). Descriptive research applies when the firm is aware of the problem and wants to profile it ('what kind of consumers buy our product; is it more popular among women?'). Causal research tests a clearly defined cause-and-effect question ('do we sell more with white labels?'). Mechanism: the type drives design, data-collection method and sample. Sampling draws a sample from the population, with each customer an element. Probability techniques (simple random, stratified, cluster) let you use inferential statistics to generalise; non-probability techniques (convenience, judgmental, quota, snowball) are cheaper and fit exploratory work but limit generalisation. Example: the Session 2 exercise was explicitly exploratory with a defined segment, a quota-like approach. Limitation: synthetic 'samples' are not drawn from a population at all, so inference to real customers is weak; Session 8's descriptive/predictive/causal analytics labels echo this typology.
shorts.minimum: Exploratory = ambiguous problem; descriptive = profile a known problem; causal = test an effect. Probability sampling (random, stratified, cluster) generalises; non-probability (convenience, quota, snowball) does not.
marking: Synthetic sample limitation or S8 link

shorts.stem: How does search in an LLM differ from search in a search engine, and why does that change what marketers optimise?
shorts.model: Concept: a search engine crawls and indexes pages, then ranks whole URLs by relevance (query–text match, length-controlled) and importance (number and quality of inbound links) and returns a list of links. An LLM has two memories, a frozen training snapshot and what it retrieves live; it pulls a handful of passages and synthesises them into one narrative answer with citations, so the unit of relevance is a quotable passage, not a page. Mechanism: because the output is one answer, there is no 'rank' to win; GEO optimises inclusion in the answer, word count or share of answer, position-adjusted word count, subjective impression and being recommended (Aggarwal et al. 2024). Example: in the State Property exercise the LLM ignored a page that lacked a price range and never mentioned men or heirlooms; adding a founder quote, a market statistic and cited sources moved it from last to first. Limitation: LLMs may still cite incorrectly or prefer well-discussed brands, and consumers may never visit the website ('learning without websites').
shorts.minimum: Engine: index, rank pages by relevance + links, list of links. LLM: retrieve passages, one cited answer. GEO optimises inclusion/share/recommendation, not rank.
marking: LLM: two memories, passage synthesis, citations

shorts.stem: Do SEO techniques still work for GEO? Explain which do, which do not, and what works instead.
shorts.model: Concept: slide 35 answers 'yes and no'. On-page SEO still matters because relevance to the customer's words is required for retrieval, but keyword stuffing hurts: it produces low-quality writing that LLMs do not quote. Off-page SEO (links) has only a weak direct effect; a higher search rank may help retrieval, but being discussed across the web matters more than being linked. Mechanism: LLMs select passages that are fluent, authoritative and verifiable, so Aggarwal et al. found the top techniques are adding quotations, adding statistics and citing sources, with fluency, technical terms, authority and easy-to-understand writing as good secondary techniques; the best gives about 41% more position-adjusted word count, with larger gains for lower-ranked sites. Technical basics still apply: crawlable content, do not block good AI crawlers, semantic HTML, low latency; LLMS.txt is not necessary. Example: State Property's rewrite used all three top techniques. Limitation: guardrails against false claims, since the LLM itself flagged celebrity claims as marketing copy to verify.
shorts.minimum: Yes and no. Relevance still matters, keyword stuffing hurts; links weak, being discussed beats being linked. Works: quotations, statistics, citations (41%), fluency, authority.
marking: Technical basics incl. LLMS.txt not needed

shorts.stem: Describe the iterative GEO method and its advantages and risks compared with traditional SEO.
shorts.model: Concept: the iterative method (slide 37, inspired by Kartik Hosanagar) feeds an LLM your write-up and competitors' write-ups, instructs it to use only those texts, poses a customer scenario and asks it to recommend one label. You read why others were preferred, revise your content and repeat until you are recommended, then stress-test with new scenarios. Mechanism: the LLM becomes a simulated customer, so you learn in minutes rather than waiting weeks for search rankings and traffic to respond as in SEO; it also changes the optimisation objective from rank to being recommended. Example: State Property went from fifth to first in one round by adding a price range, explicit men's signet and heirloom language, a founder quotation and cited sources; a second scenario with a 10-week deadline showed a real product gap on speed. Risks: the LLM is one judge whose preferences may differ from real buyers or other models; it rewards confident claims, so guardrails against false information are essential; and over-fitting copy to the test prompt can hurt real readers. Limitation: results should be confirmed with actual LLM visibility tracking and sales.
shorts.minimum: Feed own + competitor content → ask LLM to recommend → revise → iterate. Fast simulated customer, no waiting for market. Risks: one judge, false claims, over-fitting.
marking: LLM as simulated customer, speed advantage

shorts.stem: Explain the two 'key developments' from Puntoni (2026) and what they mean for a brand's marketing strategy.
shorts.model: Concept: slide 28 names two developments. First, learning without websites: customers ask LLMs instead of Google and often get the answer without visiting the site the answer relies on. Second, bots as customers: consumers outsource the decision itself to LLM agents. Mechanism: the website stops being the destination and becomes a source; visibility means being quoted and recommended inside an answer, and persuasion shifts from design and emotion to information quality. Slide 29 places LLMs in early information search between social media (need awareness) and search engines (transactional search). Implications (slide 38): brands may build their own agents (control and data, but costly and hard to drive adoption), must compete inside third-party agents where branding and price play new roles, face agent-to-agent interaction and a dual internet, and may even see LLM advertising. Example: State Property's bespoke page had to literally contain the customer's words to be considered. Limitation: evidence is early; current advice is to keep a human website and add machine-readable precision, which Session 7's Bot2Bot discussion repeats.
shorts.minimum: Learning without websites + bots as customers. Website becomes a source, not destination; compete inside answers; own agents vs third-party agents; branding and price change.
marking: At least two strategic implications from slide 38

shorts.stem: Explain the two pillars search engines use to rank results and how on-page and off-page SEO address each.
shorts.model: Concept: after crawling and indexing, a search engine judges match quality on two pillars. Relevance is the overlap between query and page text, weighted so that some words count more, controlled for text length and allowing for spelling errors, synonyms and word order. Importance is authority measured by the number and quality of inbound links; the World Bank outranks 'Jason's blog' for similar content, and a Forbes link boosts importance strongly. Secondary factors include click-through rate (+), a suspiciously fast rise in importance (−), malware (−) and slow loading (−). Mechanism: on-page SEO raises relevance by researching the keywords consumers actually use (Google Trends, 'anniversary gift ideas') and building helpful, non-commercial content around them that differs from competitors'. Off-page SEO raises importance by promoting content so other sites link to it and by monitoring links. Example: State Property's case was originally an SEO strategy before the GEO rewrite. Limitation: for GEO, links matter less and being discussed matters more, and keyword stuffing backfires.
shorts.minimum: Relevance = query–text match (weighted, length-controlled). Importance = number and quality of inbound links. On-page SEO → relevance; off-page SEO → importance.
marking: On-page vs off-page mapped to pillars

shorts.stem: Classify the three types of search queries, link them to the customer journey, and explain why the distinction matters for SEO and GEO.
shorts.model: Concept: informational queries seek knowledge ('what to buy before baby arrives', 'is Babyzen Yoyo good for everyday use'); transactional queries aim to buy ('buy DeLonghi coffee machine online', 'promo DeLonghi'); navigational queries seek a specific site or page ('DBS contact number', 'Singapore Airlines website'). Mechanism: these roughly follow the journey from early consideration to purchase to loyalty, and each needs different content: guides and comparisons for informational, product and offer pages for transactional, and a findable brand page for navigational. Slide 29 adds that LLMs are now used for early informational search while search engines keep targeted transactional search, so GEO matters most for informational prompts. Example: the State Property exercise chose an informational prompt early in the journey ('which jeweller for a bespoke signet ring?') because that is where the LLM shapes the consideration set. Limitation: spelling variations ('dlongi expresso') and mixed intents blur categories, and engines must infer intent.
shorts.minimum: Informational (learn), transactional (buy), navigational (find a site). Map to journey stages; LLMs dominate early informational search, so GEO targets those prompts.

shorts.stem: Should a firm keep advertising once it has done SEO and GEO well? Explain the strategic roles of each.
shorts.model: Advertising and SEO/GEO do different jobs. SEO/GEO is demand capture: it works only when someone is already searching or asking an AI assistant, so it sits at the consideration and purchase stages of the journey. Advertising is demand creation: it pushes a message to people who were not looking, building awareness and desire, and it gives the firm control over message and timing. The two reinforce each other. Ads raise branded searches that SEO then captures, and they generate the brand mentions and authority signals that generative engines rely on when deciding whom to recommend. For Timperio, GEO gets the brand recommended when a user asks for 'the best Italian olive oil', but advertising is what makes people think of Molise olive oil in the first place. Cutting advertising slowly drains the pool of demand that SEO/GEO fishes from. The limitation is budget: a small firm must balance cheap in-house AI content against paid media spend and measure incremental effect, not just clicks.
shorts.minimum: Yes. SEO/GEO = pull, captures existing demand at consideration/purchase. Advertising = push, creates awareness and desire. They reinforce each other: ads create the searches and mentions that SEO/GEO capture.
marking: Push vs pull distinction stated clearly
Funnel stages: GEO at consideration/purchase, advertising at awareness
Reinforcement: ads drive branded search and brand mentions

shorts.stem: Explain the difference between the static approach to ad personalisation and Dynamic Creative Optimisation. Give an example of each.
shorts.model: Both approaches tailor an ad to a person or segment, but they differ in when the decision is made. In the static approach, Gen-AI batch-produces many variants up front, or fixed rules decide the swap, for example 'show the product the user viewed last'. The rules are set before any ad is served. In Dynamic Creative Optimisation the ad is broken into modules: image, headline, description, offer and call-to-action. Brand elements such as logo, colours and fonts are locked, a pool of approved components fills each slot, and the platform assembles the best combination per impression in real time, learning from results as ads keep serving. Meta Advantage+ (2022) is the course example: it automates targeting, placements and creatives and claims about 22% higher return on ad spend. Gen-AI's role is to fill the component pool cheaply; the human role is to define the objective and lock the brand. The limitation is that DCO is only as good as its component pool, and optimising for clicks can drift towards generic creative unless quality is monitored.
shorts.minimum: Static: variants or rules fixed before serving (e.g., show last-viewed product). DCO: modular ad, brand elements locked, platform assembles best combination per impression in real time (Meta Advantage+, ~22% higher ROAS).
marking: DCO = modules assembled per impression, real time, learns
Example: Meta Advantage+ with the 22% claim

shorts.stem: The IAB finds a widening gap between how advertisers and young consumers feel about AI ads. Describe the gap, explain why it exists, and say what bridges it.
shorts.model: The IAB 2026 survey shows 82% of ad executives believe young consumers feel positive about AI-made ads, while only 45% of Gen Z and Millennials actually do, a 37-point gap up from 32. Negative sentiment is highest among Gen Z (39% vs 20% of Millennials), who describe AI-using brands as inauthentic, disconnected and unethical. The gap exists because the two sides judge AI by different criteria. Advertisers judge it by internal benefits, and their top benefit has shifted to cost efficiency (64%), with concerns turning inward to implementation and creativity rather than consumer perception. Consumers judge the ad by how it feels, and 'cheaper, not better' content risks AI slop. The bridge is disclosure, the one point where both sides agree: 60% of executives say AI ads should always be disclosed, and 73% of consumers say knowing an ad was AI-made would increase or not change purchase likelihood. Clear disclosure is also the third biggest attention driver. The limitation: disclosure helps only if the creative is good and the category is appropriate; it matters most for health, finance and politics.
shorts.minimum: 82% of execs think young consumers are positive; only 45% are (Gen Z 39% negative). Execs judge by cost and speed, consumers by feel. Disclosure bridges it: 73% say it would not reduce purchase intent.
marking: Gen Z more negative than Millennials
Reason: advertisers' concerns turned inward / cost-efficiency mindset
Disclosure as the bridge with 73% or 60% figure
Caveat on where disclosure matters most or quality

shorts.stem: What do the Timperio Exhibit 8 results teach a small firm about using AI versus an agency for social media advertising?
shorts.model: Timperio ran 12 Instagram ads over 14 days: three creation strategies (AI-only, AI plus human, agency-only) times two objectives (informative, persuasive) times two formats (post, reel), each with about US$42 of media. AI-only produced the most interactions (36,447) at the lowest cost ($0.0046) and the most likes (2,373). The agency's true cost was about 3.6 times higher once its €350 fee was included. However, format mattered more than creator: reels generated roughly nine times more interactions than images. And the agency clearly won on informative images (4,010 interactions at $0.010 versus AI-only's 713 at $0.060), where product-accurate craft matters. The lesson is a hybrid: an AI-first in-house co-pilot for high-volume, low-stakes content such as reels and seasonal posts, with human or agency craft for flagship and product-accurate pieces, human review before publishing because 70% of marketers have had an AI incident, and disclosure where AI is material since Gen Z is sceptical. The evidence is directional only: one market, tiny budgets, one freelancer as 'agency', interactions inflated by video views, and no sales data.
shorts.minimum: AI-only cheapest and most likes; agency ~3.6× cost but won informative images; format (reels) mattered most. Recommend hybrid with human review. Caveat: 14 days, small budgets, no sales data.
marking: AI-only cheapest / most likes with a number
Agency fee changes the cost comparison
Format effect and agency's informative-image win
shorts.source: Timperio case Exhibit 8; Q5–Q6 class answers

shorts.stem: List and explain the main challenges of prompting AI tools to create brand advertising, using the Timperio exercise.
shorts.model: Prompting is a skill, not a button, as Kim (CMR, 2025) argues. The Timperio exercise exposed several challenges. First, brand fidelity: image tools could not reliably reproduce the real bottle and label, so the AI-only ads used generic bottles; real product shots must be composited or brand-trained models used. Second, specificity: vague prompts give stock-photo 'average' results, the convergence risk on the slides, so good prompts state objective, audience, brand voice, palette, composition, mood and what to avoid. Third, local and cultural nuance: Italian wording and heritage tone needed human iteration. Fourth, text in images and small details such as hands and typography render badly, so captions are added separately. Fifth, consistency across a set: twelve pieces must share one look and voice, so parameters must be documented as the case's Exhibit 6 insists. Sixth, evaluation discipline: judging when output is good enough and checking for hallucinated claims, such as invented health benefits, and IP or likeness risks. The limitation is that these challenges shift effort from production to direction and review; the 'higher floor' does not raise the ceiling without skilled humans.
shorts.minimum: Brand fidelity (generic bottles), specificity (avoid average output), cultural nuance, text/detail rendering, consistency across a set (document parameters), evaluation for hallucinated claims and IP. Prompting is a strategic skill (Kim).
marking: Brand fidelity problem named with Timperio example
Convergence to average / need for specific prompts
Checking for hallucinated or risky claims
shorts.source: S4 Q4 class answer; Timperio case; Kim (CMR, 2025)

shorts.stem: 'Why hire an agency when I can do the same job with ChatGPT?' Evaluate this claim and explain how the agency business model must change.
shorts.model: ChatGPT lets a firm do a job, not necessarily the same job. Gen-AI raises the floor, so anyone can produce competent copy and visuals quickly and cheaply, which is why in-house creative teams rose from 42% in 2008 to 82% in 2023. But it does not raise the ceiling. Agencies still add the big idea and storytelling that AI outputs tend to flatten into average, brand consistency across years and channels, cultural nuance and taste, media negotiation, legal and IP cover, and accountability when things go wrong; 70% of marketers have already had an AI incident. The agency model must therefore shift from selling hours and production, which AI commoditises, to selling strategy, creative direction, prompt and AI orchestration, governance and measurement: from 'we make the ads' to 'we design the system that makes the ads'. Pricing moves from hourly and asset fees towards retainers, performance fees or licensed AI workflows, as McCann and FCB are doing by positioning AI as augmentation for award-winning work. The limitation is that the Timperio data show AI already matching or beating agency output on cheap, high-volume formats, so agencies must prove value on the high-stakes work.
shorts.minimum: AI raises the floor (42%→82% in-house) but not the ceiling: big ideas, consistency, nuance, accountability remain. Agencies must sell strategy, orchestration and governance, not production hours.
marking: What agencies still add (ideas, consistency, accountability, IP)
Business model shift to strategy/orchestration/governance and new pricing
shorts.source: S4 slide 19; Q2 class answer; Kim (CMR, 2025)

shorts.stem: Explain the key tension between brands and human influencers, and how virtual influencers resolve it. What is lost in the process?
shorts.model: Brands want control, consistency and scale: they want the message said as briefed, the same look every time, and content in many places and languages. Human influencers want authenticity, creative freedom and their own schedule; they may refuse the script, bring scandal risk, cost $250K or more per post at 1M-plus followers, and exist in limited supply, especially diverse talent. Virtual influencers are computer-generated characters with their own personality, backstory and accounts. They give brands full control: no private life, no scandals, fully customisable words and looks, present in five places at once, changeable with a prompt. Lil Miquela (independent, Brud) earns about $2M a year from Dior, Prada and BMW; Lu do Magalu is brand-owned by Magazine Luiza and keeps all the equity. What is lost is authenticity grounded in lived experience: a CGI character cannot really try the skincare, only 15% of consumers highly trust AI influencers, and near-human realism risks the uncanny valley. HBR's answer is a portfolio, not a swap: humans for trust- and experience-heavy categories, virtual for high-concept, scalable or risk-sensitive campaigns.
shorts.minimum: Brands want control, consistency, scale; humans want authenticity and freedom. Virtual influencers give full control (Miquela, Lu). Lost: lived-experience authenticity and trust (only 15% highly trust them). Use a portfolio.
marking: Both sides of the tension named correctly
Human cons: scandal, unpredictability, cost, supply
Virtual benefits: control, consistency, scale, with an example
What is lost: authenticity, trust, uncanny valley

shorts.stem: Paid posts by virtual influencers earn more engagement than their organic posts, while for humans the reverse holds. Explain this finding and its implication.
shorts.model: Hwang et al. (HBR, 2024) analysed over a million posts from 551 human and 13 virtual influencers across 112 brands. Virtual influencers' paid posts earned 13.3% more engagement than their organic posts; humans' paid posts earned 2.1% less. In fashion and beauty the gap was wider: +16.3% versus –2.3%. The mechanism is expectations. Followers expect a human to be real, so a sponsored post feels like selling out, an authenticity violation. A virtual influencer is already understood as a brand creation, so an ad is no betrayal; there is no authenticity to lose. Brand deals also bring novelty, such as Miquela with BMW, and higher production polish, and fashion and beauty are image-led categories that CGI does well. The implication is that disclosure does not kill performance for virtual influencers, because people engage knowing they are virtual, and that they are a low-risk, high-engagement option for sponsored content. The limitation is category fit: for experience-based products where credibility of the claim matters, a character that cannot use the product may underperform, and only 15% of consumers highly trust AI influencers.
shorts.minimum: +13.3% for virtual paid posts, –2.1% for human (fashion/beauty +16.3% vs –2.3%). Humans lose authenticity when paid; virtual influencers have none to lose. Novelty and polish help. Implication: disclosure doesn't hurt them.
marking: No authenticity to lose for virtual influencers
Supporting mechanisms: novelty, polish, category fit
shorts.source: S5 slide 27; Q5 class answer; Hwang et al. (2024)

shorts.stem: How can a brand make a virtual influencer feel authentic? Use the CMR Layer Coherence Triad.
shorts.model: Saxena (CMR, 2025) argues that in the 'Perceived Era', when AI can fake anything, people judge authenticity by a set of signals, about 3.9 on average, not by one proof. The triad has three layers that work multiplicatively: information credibility (can people check the facts?), disclosure transparency (is AI use stated in plain language?) and reputation trust (does the source have a good track record?). All three appear together in fewer than 9% of cases, but when they do the outcome is positive 82% of the time; one or two alone feels hollow or suspicious. For a virtual influencer this means sticking to checkable claims such as fabric, origin and price rather than fake personal experiences; labelling clearly as AI in the bio and on each post, as Meta's clickable 'AI Info' label does after the blunt 'Made with AI' tag confused users; and anchoring the character to a trusted brand and real human voices such as designers and customers. Avoid the uncanny valley by going clearly stylised or fully polished; Vodafone's presenter with a moving mole shows the danger zone. The limitation is that authenticity is a relationship, not a compliance checklist, and only 15% of consumers highly trust AI influencers today.
shorts.minimum: Triad: information credibility, disclosure transparency, reputation trust, multiplicative (<9% have all three; 82% success when present). Checkable claims, clear AI label, attach to a trusted brand; avoid the uncanny valley.
marking: Concrete application of each layer to a virtual influencer
shorts.source: S5 slide 28; Saxena (CMR, 2025); Q6 class answer

shorts.stem: Are virtual influencers ethical? Give a balanced answer with mitigations.
shorts.model: Virtual influencers raise three ethical concerns. First, representation: Shudu, a CGI Black supermodel created by a white male photographer, is criticised as commodification of Blackness, since brands can rent diversity without hiring or paying real people from that group, and surface diversity can hide old power, race and gender patterns. Second, beauty standards: most are young, thin and female, projecting impossible bodies to young audiences. Third, deception: realistic characters are mistaken for humans, and Lil Miquela pretended to be human until 2018. Mitigations follow from each concern: involve and pay creators from the community in designing the persona and share credit or revenue; avoid hyper-sexualised or impossible body types; and disclose AI clearly, which the EU AI Act and TikTok and Instagram rules now require. The counterpoint is that the human influencer pool is 68% white, so virtual influencers can widen representation (Ralph and Russo's Hauli reached 19.4M views). The ethical question is therefore not the character itself but who controls and profits from it. The limitation: disclosure rules are new and enforcement is uneven, so brands must self-govern.
shorts.minimum: Concerns: commodification of diversity (Shudu), unrealistic beauty standards, deception if undisclosed. Mitigate: involve and pay real creators, avoid impossible bodies, disclose AI. Counterpoint: can widen representation (68% white human pool).
marking: Counterpoint on widening representation with the 68% figure
Judgement on who controls and profits
shorts.source: S5 slide 29; Q7 class answer; Built In; HBR

shorts.stem: Should brands always disclose that an influencer is virtual? Argue with evidence.
shorts.model: Yes. Three arguments support mandatory disclosure. First, it is becoming law and policy: the EU AI Act requires AI-generated content to be labelled, and TikTok and Instagram now require AI labels. Second, being found out costs more trust than disclosing: Lil Miquela's 2018 reveal and Vodafone Germany's moving-mole presenter both show that audiences notice, and Vodafone recovered only by openly admitting the experiment. Third, disclosure does not kill performance: the HBR data show virtual influencers' paid posts earn 13.3% more engagement even though followers know they are virtual, because there is no authenticity to betray. In the CMR triad, disclosure transparency is one of three multiplicative signals, so hiding it undermines the whole judgement. The design point is that the label must be understandable: Meta's first 'Made with AI' tag treated a small edit like a fully synthetic image and confused users, so it became a clickable 'AI Info' label; CMR recommends testing for 80% comprehension. The limitation is that disclosure alone does not make a weak or deceptive claim acceptable; information credibility and reputation must also be present.
shorts.minimum: Yes: law and platform policy (EU AI Act, TikTok/Instagram); being found out costs more (Miquela 2018, Vodafone); performance holds (+13.3% paid posts). Label must be understandable (Meta 'AI Info').
marking: Evidence that disclosure does not hurt engagement
Limitation: disclosure is not sufficient alone
shorts.source: S5 slide 30; Q8 class answer; Saxena (CMR, 2025)

shorts.stem: What are the main practical challenges in building a virtual influencer, and what do they reveal about where the real work lies?
shorts.model: The class pipeline is image generation (Leonardo), a script of 15 seconds or less, voice synthesis (ElevenLabs), animation linking voice to photo (Vidnoz, HeyGen or Hedra) and editing in CapCut. The challenges appear at every step. Face consistency: each new generation changes the face, so the prompt, settings and seed must be saved to recreate the same character across posts. Uncanny valley: lip-sync, blinking, eyes and teeth look slightly off, so calm, low-movement shots and short scripts work better. Voice match: the voice must fit face, age and accent, which takes several attempts. Free-tool limits: watermarks, credits, no commercial rights and no auto captions. Realism details: total silence feels fake, so soft ambient sound and captions for muted viewing are needed. Authenticity and ethics: claims must be checkable and an 'AI-generated' label added, following the CMR triad and the EU AI Act. Persona depth: a face is not an influencer; a real one needs a backstory, a posting plan and a human team, as Built In and the Miquela and Lu examples show. The lesson is that making the video took under an hour; making it believable and trustworthy is the real work, and that is a strategy problem, not a tool problem.
shorts.minimum: Pipeline: image → script → voice → animation → editing. Challenges: face consistency (save the seed), uncanny valley, voice match, free-tool limits, realism details, disclosure, persona depth and a human team. Real work = trust and strategy.
marking: Conclusion that trust/strategy is the real work

shorts.stem: Define dynamic pricing using Kopalle et al.'s framework and explain why the public reacts differently to its different forms.
shorts.model: Kopalle et al. (2023) define dynamic pricing as prices that vary with four demand drivers: People (does this customer have higher willingness to pay?), Products (does this configuration change value, such as bundles or first class?), Periods (is demand higher now, as in surge or weekend rates?) and Places (does location change cost or value?). Static pricing is the special case where none vary, so it is a question of degree. The Hyderabad vegetable seller shows all four from one cart. Pricing on Products, Periods and Places uses market data and is broadly accepted; nobody is shocked by off-peak fares or outlet prices. Pricing on People using personal data, which critics call surveillance pricing, is where trust breaks. Giansiracusa explains why: information inequality, since the seller knows your whole online life while you know nothing, and the sense that your 'pain point' is being found. Delta only announced AI revenue management and still had to promise Congress no personalised fares, showing perception alone can hurt. The limitation is that the line is blurry: a loyalty discount is people-based yet accepted, so what matters is whether the data were knowingly shared and the frame is a discount.
shorts.minimum: Dynamic pricing = prices vary by People, Products, Periods, Places (Kopalle); static is the special case. Market-data pricing (periods, places, products) is accepted; people-based pricing on personal data ('surveillance pricing') breaks trust (Delta).
marking: Four Ps named correctly with one example each
Static as special case / question of degree
Distinction between market-data and personal-data pricing
shorts.source: S6 slides 11–15; Kopalle et al. (2023); Harvard Law Today (2025)

shorts.stem: Using the ZipRecruiter evidence, explain who wins and who loses from personalised pricing, and what a manager should do first.
shorts.model: Dubé and Misra (JPE, 2023) ran the first field test of machine-learning personalised pricing at ZipRecruiter, a B2B job-ad platform charging $99 a month. In 2015, 7,867 new customers each saw one of ten random prices between $99 and $399, and a Bayesian LASSO model learned which registration answers predicted price sensitivity. Demand was far less sensitive than expected: doubling the price cut sign-ups only 25%. The best single price was $327, raising profit 55% even though sign-ups fell from 25% to 12%. Personalised prices added a further 19% (86% versus the $99 base). The firm wins. Consumers lose in aggregate, since total consumer surplus falls, yet more than 60% of individual customers are better off, mostly smaller and less-advantaged firms that pay below the uniform price; high-WTP customers pay more, so fairness-weighted welfare can rise. A manager should first fix the uniform price, the large low-risk gain, then consider personalisation framed as discounts with a real baseline, protected essentials and human review. Limits the authors admit: one B2B monopoly, customers who cannot fake their type, and no long-term backlash, which Delta and Amazon's 2000 DVD episode suggest is real.
shorts.minimum: Uniform price $99→$327 = +55% profit; personalisation +19% more. Total consumer surplus falls but >60% of customers pay less. Do the safe step first: fix the uniform price, then personalise discounts.

shorts.stem: Why does framing matter in personalised pricing? What makes a discount frame legitimate rather than deceptive?
shorts.model: The same money outcome can feel fair or unfair depending on the frame. 'Your price is $120' when another shopper pays $100 feels like discrimination; 'you get $20 off' a $140 list price when another gets $40 off feels like a deal. The mechanism is the reference price: customers believe a fair price exists, a discount respects it and gives a gain, while a different higher price breaks it and creates a loss relative to someone else, and losses hurt more than gains (prospect theory). This is why New York and Connecticut laws target price increases based on personal data, and why Dubé himself notes that '$3.99 for everyone plus a $2 coupon for you' is accepted while '$1.99 for you, $3.99 for him' is not. Kopalle's worked example delivers the optimal two prices as a $2,000 shelf price plus a $400 coupon for the price-sensitive segment. The frame is legitimate only if the baseline is real: FTC rules and FPF recommendation 5 require discounts from a bona fide list price, and Dayen reports Amazon sellers inflating list prices about 23% to fake bigger discounts, which destroys trust when discovered. The limitation, per the American Prospect, is that discount framing can simply hide discrimination, so some argue for rules on the data itself.
shorts.minimum: Same outcome, different feeling: a discount keeps the reference price (gain); a higher personal price breaks it (loss). Laws target increases. Legitimate only with a real, bona fide baseline; inflated 'was' prices are deceptive.
marking: The two frames with the same money outcome
Link to disclosure laws targeting increases
Bona fide baseline requirement with FPF/FTC or Amazon example
shorts.source: S6 slides 33–34; FPF (2026); Dayen (2024); Kopalle et al.

shorts.stem: Explain how reinforcement learning differs from machine learning in pricing and why the Roast & Reward case warned against relying on the ML price adviser.
shorts.model: Machine learning learns patterns from historical data and makes independent one-off predictions, such as 'what will demand be tomorrow?'. Reinforcement learning has an agent acting in an environment: it observes a state (day of week, weather, event, competitor open and its price, remaining stock), chooses an action (a price from $1 to $10), receives a reward (profit minus penalties) and updates its policy to maximise long-run cumulative reward. The decisions are sequential: today's price changes tomorrow's stock and customers' expectations. The core trade-off is explore versus exploit, which firms handle with A/B tests and bandits. In Roast & Reward, 5,000 cups arrive every Monday and are not carried over, each cup costs $1, unsold cups cost $1.50 each on Sunday, and a daily minimum must be met. A price that maximises today's profit can sell out before a busy Saturday or leave waste on Sunday. The ML adviser predicts today's demand from past patterns but ignores stock pacing (about 714 cups a day) and the end-of-week penalty, so the case says it 'may not work well in sequential decision-making'. The lesson for managers: algorithms learn what price works; humans decide what price is fair, adding framing, crisis caps and disclosure.
shorts.minimum: ML = independent predictions from history; RL = agent, state, action, reward, policy, sequential, long-run reward, explore vs exploit. ML adviser ignores stock pacing and the $1.50 Sunday penalty, so it fails the sequential problem.
marking: ML as one-off prediction vs RL as sequential decision
RL terms mapped to the game (state, action, reward, policy)
Game rules used to show why ML adviser fails

shorts.stem: Should firms be required to disclose algorithmic pricing? Discuss with reference to recent laws and the limits of disclosure.
shorts.model: Yes, for pricing based on personal data. Disclosure is becoming law: New York requires the notice 'THIS PRICE WAS SET BY AN ALGORITHM USING YOUR PERSONAL DATA' and survived a court challenge; Connecticut requires a readily visible notice whenever personal data raises a price; the EU's GDPR and Consumer Rights Directive require telling people when a price is personalised; and US states are filing 60 to 70 bills a year while California's Attorney General swept retailers, grocers and hotels in 2026. Hidden personalisation discovered later costs more trust, as Delta, Amazon's 2000 DVD prices and Orbitz's Mac-user hotel prices show. FPF recommends layered, just-in-time notices at checkout, explaining why ('thank-you code for your recent purchase', 'surge due to few drivers'), and showing the factors or a price history where no single baseline exists. But the label must be understandable, the same lesson as Meta's 'AI Info' label, and a scary label may push firms toward discount framing, which is fine only if the baseline is real. The limitation, argued by Dayen, is that disclosure alone is weak: firms hide personalisation in friendly words and private app coupons, so privacy rules on the data and anti-discrimination price rules are also needed, and FPF adds extra safeguards for essentials.
shorts.minimum: Yes for personal-data pricing: NY notice law, Connecticut visible notice, EU rules. Hidden pricing costs more trust (Delta). Labels must be understandable; disclosure alone is weak, so add data and price rules and protect essentials.
marking: NY and/or Connecticut law described correctly
FPF best practice on how to disclose

shorts.stem: Who is responsible when a shared pricing algorithm leads to collusion, and how should firms govern algorithmic pricing vendors?
shorts.model: The firms are responsible, not only the vendor; 'the software did it' is no defence. RealPage let landlords feed private, competitively sensitive data into one shared rent-setting tool, and in 2024 the DOJ and eight state attorneys-general alleged algorithmic coordination amounting to price-fixing that harmed millions of renters; a settlement followed and New York and California have banned shared rent algorithms. Kopalle adds that even independent AI pricing bots can learn to keep prices high without communicating (Calvano et al. 2020), so the risk is structural. Governance follows FPF's recommendations: map and track all pricing data and its sources; avoid feeding private competitor-sensitive data into shared tools; keep final pricing decisions in-house with humans approving algorithm suggestions, which Kopalle notes is standard practice; document why prices were set; test for bias; and align vendors through contracts on data use (recommendation 7). Add circuit breakers for crises and essentials. The limitation is that detecting tacit algorithmic collusion is hard, since no one 'agreed' to anything, so regulators and firms need monitoring of outcomes, not just intentions.
shorts.minimum: Firms are responsible. RealPage: shared tool plus private data = alleged price-fixing; bots can collude tacitly (Calvano). Govern: no private rival data in shared tools, humans decide, document, audit and contract with vendors (FPF #7).
marking: Concrete governance steps incl. vendor contracts
shorts.source: S6 slides 17, 32; Q9 class answer; FPF (2026); Kopalle et al.

shorts.stem: Chatbot technology is far better than five years ago, yet 77% of customers remain frustrated. Explain why and give three fixes.
shorts.model: Concept: generative AI fixed the rule-based bot's understanding problems (typos, slang, multi-intent, context) but not the human ones. Mechanism: expectations rose faster than ability, so failures disappoint more; HBR shows identical conversations score 8.5% lower when people know it is a bot; firms deploy bots to cut cost (about $0.70 saved per interaction) and over-trust them, so bots interrogate, apologise uselessly and refuse to hand over, and 'no easy path to a human' is CMR's number one irritant; bots often lack authority and data. Example: HBR found 88% still prefer a human even though 73% could not tell GPT-4.5 from a person. Fixes: (1) set expectations and disclose it is AI, label it 'constantly learning' (+17%) and show accuracy (+22%); (2) ground answers in company data with RAG and systems of record; (3) treat humanisation as a dial, machine-like for angry customers, warm for good news, with clear escalation triggers and a context summary on handover. So what: the chatbot is a brand ambassador; the fix is design and psychology, not model power.
shorts.minimum: Tech fixed understanding, not trust and expectations (8.5% bot bias). Over-trust and no handover are the irritants. Fix: set expectations, ground with RAG, tone dial plus seamless handover.
marking: Separates rule-based problems (fixed) from persisting human problems
Names over-trust, interrogation or handover refusal (CMR)
Gives three concrete fixes with HBR/CMR evidence

shorts.stem: Compare the three technical approaches to building an AI chatbot and state when a firm should choose each.
shorts.model: Concept: every AI chatbot does three steps, understand input, ground knowledge, generate a reply; the big design choice is step two, where the knowledge comes from. Mechanism: an off-the-shelf LLM with light prompting is fastest and cheapest but generic, with knowledge frozen at training and a hallucination risk. A privately trained (fine-tuned) model learns deep brand and domain knowledge but is slow, expensive, needs ML talent and goes stale until retrained. Off-the-shelf plus RAG ingests company documents as embeddings and retrieves the relevant chunks at question time, so answers are current, cheap and citable, with the risk that it is only as good as the documents and retrieval. Example: the session's rule is start-up or SMB, off-the-shelf or RAG; large regulated enterprise with stable expertise, fine-tune (plus RAG); fast-changing content, RAG, which is where most firms land. Limitation: RAG and fine-tuning are complements, not rivals; fine-tuning teaches how to talk, RAG supplies what is true today, and RAG shifts the work to content governance.
shorts.minimum: Off-the-shelf: fast, generic, hallucinates. Fine-tuned: deep but costly and stale. RAG: current, cheap, citable; most firms land here. Choose by content change rate and team.
marking: Explains knowledge currency: frozen vs retrieved live
States the decision rule by firm type
Notes RAG and fine-tuning are complements; garbage in, garbage out

shorts.stem: Explain RAG using the open-book exam analogy, its two phases, and its main limitation.
shorts.model: Concept: retrieval-augmented generation lets an LLM look up company knowledge before answering, like an open-book exam, instead of answering from memory like a closed-book exam. Mechanism: in the ingestion phase, FAQs, manuals and policies are cut into chunks and turned into embeddings, numbers that capture meaning, stored in a database searchable by meaning; in the retrieval phase the question is embedded, matched to the most relevant chunks, which are pasted into the prompt so the LLM answers grounded in that content, often with a citation. McKinsey's library analogy: ingestion stocks the shelves and builds the index; retrieval is the librarian finding the right pages. It can also reach live sources through database queries and API calls. Example: Amazon, DoorDash and Thomson Reuters use LLMs plus RAG; the Chatling exercise's knowledge base is RAG ingestion. Limitation: garbage in, garbage out. If the documents are wrong or outdated, or retrieval opens the wrong page, the answer is still wrong, so data quality, multimodal content, bias, licensing and privacy need governance.
shorts.minimum: Open book: look up the right page, then answer with a citation. Ingestion (chunks to embeddings) then retrieval (match and paste into prompt). Limitation: garbage in, garbage out.
marking: Ingestion phase with chunks and embeddings
Retrieval phase pasted into the prompt, grounded answer with citation
Garbage in, garbage out and governance needs
A course example (McKinsey cases or Chatling)

shorts.stem: Humanisation is 'a dial, not a switch'. Explain when a chatbot should sound more human and when less, with evidence.
shorts.model: Concept: how human a bot sounds should change with the moment, and it should never pretend to be human. Mechanism: HBR shows warmth and human cues work in some contexts and backfire in others. Turn the dial down for angry or hurried customers, who are 23% less satisfied with a human-like bot and want fast, direct, machine-like replies; also for young, time-pressed users (CMR: Gen Z and millennials want efficiency). Turn it up when delivering good news, where 'Hi, I'm Ava, great news!' lifts firm ratings by 8% because people credit good news to themselves; in long problem-solving chats and with older customers who want empathy; and in fraud-risk flows such as refunds, where people are up to 35% more likely to lie to a bot and human-like phrasing cuts unethical behaviour by about 20%. Keep flattery factual (up to 12.5% more acceptance) because too-human flattery feels manipulative. Example: the Chatling system prompt switched to short direct steps when the user sounded angry. Limitation: always disclose it is AI; CMR's rule is be like a human, but don't pretend to be one, and disclosure is becoming law (EU AI Act).
shorts.minimum: Less human for angry/hurried/young customers (−23%). More human for good news (+8%), long problem-solving, older customers and fraud-risk refunds (35% more lies to bots). Never pretend to be human.
marking: States the dial principle and 'never pretend'
Up: good news, fraud-risk with figures
Segment adaptation (young vs older) from CMR
shorts.source: HBR strategies 3–6; CMR practices 4–5; S7 slide 33

shorts.stem: Why is a voice agent harder to build than a text chatbot, and how does Microsoft's guide design for reliability?
shorts.model: Concept: in voice, capability gets attention but reliability earns trust; a reliable voice agent consistently completes the task, survives interruptions and escalates with context. Mechanism: voice is harder because customers expect split-second replies, they interrupt (barge-in), they cannot scroll back, emotion sits in the tone of voice, and lines are noisy. Microsoft's design answers: latency messages ('give me ten seconds'), barge-in handling with a clear task thread, 'receipts' that repeat key details and confirm before acting, keypad (DTMF) fallbacks and silence re-prompts, grounding facts in systems of record rather than guesses, knowing boundaries and escalating with a context summary. Example: the clothing-retailer agent parks 'where's my order', fixes the double charge, returns to the order, and confirms 'cancel the blue jacket, refund $89 to Visa ending 4412, shall I go ahead?'. Limitation: match the tier to the job, IVR for simple high-volume tasks, generative voice as the sweet spot, real-time speech-to-speech only where conversation is the brand; and start with one high-volume scenario, test a dozen messy calls and rerun after every change.
shorts.minimum: Harder: instant replies, interruptions, no scroll-back, emotion in voice. Design: receipts, latency messages, barge-in, keypad fallback, grounded facts, escalate with context. Pick the right tier.
marking: At least three reasons voice is harder

shorts.stem: Chatbots are moving into sales and into 'Bot2Bot' interactions. What changes for firms, and what risks remain?
shorts.model: Concept: chatbots now generate leads, recommend and complete purchases (conversational commerce), and increasingly talk to the customer's own AI agent rather than to a person. Mechanism: in sales the same frustration risks apply but the stakes rise, because a frustrated prospect is lost revenue, not just a service cost; recommendations must be grounded in the real catalogue, flattery factual, and hot leads passed to a human with context, measured on conversion and lead quality. In Bot2Bot, an AI buying agent such as Meta's Muse compares exact prices, stock, specs and policies, so persuasion shifts from emotion to information quality: answers must be structured, factual and machine-readable and consistent across website, feeds and chatbot, which links to GEO in Session 3. Example: B2B buyer agents already place orders and negotiate; Muse partners include Walmart, Sephora and Best Buy. Limitation and risks: firms must detect whether they are talking to a human or an agent, set authentication and spending limits, decide liability if an agent buys the wrong item, and guard price negotiation, which connects to personalised pricing in Session 6; the human behind the agent still judges brand trust and fair terms.
shorts.minimum: Sales bots: same frustration risks, higher stakes; ground in catalogue, hand hot leads to humans. Bot2Bot: structured, factual, machine-readable answers (GEO link). Risks: detection, authentication, liability, pricing.
marking: Conversational commerce and why stakes rise
Grounding, factual flattery, human handover for leads
Bot2Bot shift to information quality, Muse example
Names new rules: detection, limits, liability

shorts.stem: Prospecting converts at 3%, retargeting at 10%. The CMO wants to move budget to retargeting. Advise, using the session's framework.
shorts.model: Concept: the budget split is a causal question, which campaign creates extra conversions per dollar, but the conversion rates are descriptive. Mechanism: retargeted users have already visited the site and many would buy anyway, so prior intent is a competing explanation and condition 3 for causality fails; it is the same selection-bias trap as eBay's branded search ads, where holdouts showed little incremental value. Run randomised holdout or control groups inside each campaign. Example: with the slide's control data, prospecting lifts from 1.0% to 3.0% (+2.0 pp) while retargeting lifts from 9.5% to 10.0% (+0.5 pp), so 95% of retargeting conversions were not incremental and prospecting creates four times the lift per person reached. Limitation and so-what: compare cost per incremental conversion, since retargeting is cheaper to reach; account for diminishing returns as prospecting scales and for margin; keep some retargeting if it is still profitable. The quality of the answer came from the question design and data, not from the AI (Tadelis).
shorts.minimum: Causal question, descriptive data; selection bias (eBay). Use control groups: prospecting +2.0 pp vs retargeting +0.5 pp, 95% not incremental. Compare cost per incremental conversion.
marking: Labels the question causal vs the data descriptive
Computes +2.0 pp vs +0.5 pp and 95% non-incremental
Caveats: cost per incremental conversion, diminishing returns, not all-or-nothing

shorts.stem: AI makes analytics faster, cheaper and more accessible. Does that mean better analytics? Use Tadelis's argument.
shorts.model: Concept: no; faster and cheaper improve efficiency, not decision quality, and better analytics means better decisions. Mechanism: Tadelis shows how AI can make bad analytics worse: firms treat it as an access problem, AI answers before anyone checks the question, polished output raises confidence rather than truth, a flawed metric gets scaled across thousands of campaigns, and the method becomes invisible. His six principles are the guardrails: start with the decision, label the question (descriptive, predictive, causal), expose assumptions and counterfactuals, govern the metrics, validate high-stakes and causal claims, and reward truth-seeking over persuasion. Example: the retargeting question answered confidently and wrongly from raw conversion rates; Airbnb's Minerva built because teams defined metrics differently. Limitation and so-what: 'answers are not evidence, and evidence is not a better decision'; add friction where the cost of being wrong is high, use triage like banks' model-risk validation, and remember Davenport & Bean's finding that 92% see culture, not technology, as the barrier. P&G shows the upside when platform, culture and upskilling in 'how models go wrong' come together.
shorts.minimum: No: efficiency ≠ decision quality. AI answers wrong questions confidently, hides methods, scales bad metrics. Apply the six principles; add friction where stakes are high.
marking: Names at least three ways AI worsens analytics
Lists the six principles (or most of them)

shorts.stem: Should marketing analytics be centralised or embedded? Recommend a structure and the C-suite roles, with course evidence.
shorts.model: Concept: a hybrid hub-and-spoke model with one accountable data and AI leader. Mechanism: the hub owns the platform, metric definitions, validation of high-stakes and causal claims, and talent standards; the spokes sit in brand or market teams and share their KPIs so analysis stays decision-first and fast. Pure centralised drifts from the business, is seen as a cost centre and responds slowly; pure embedded duplicates work and defines 'churn' three different ways, which blocks enterprise-wide AI. Example: P&G's AI factory, a shared platform that cuts deployment time by about six months, with several hundred data scientists mostly embedded in business units; DBS's '2-in-a-box', a separate analytics unit deeply embedded with stakeholders and sharing their KPIs, which fixed the service-centre problem. Roles: one business-facing CDAO reporting to the CEO or COO (Bean's view) rather than four tech chiefs, since role proliferation confuses internal customers; the CIO keeps infrastructure; a separate CAIO only where AI is core and high-risk. Limitation: CDO adoption is 85% yet under half of data leaders call their function successful and 92% cite culture as the barrier, so the org chart matters less than culture and shared KPIs.
shorts.minimum: Hybrid: central platform and metric governance plus embedded analysts sharing KPIs (P&G, DBS). One CDAO, not four roles. Culture is the real barrier.
marking: Recommends hybrid with reasons against both pure models
Hub responsibilities include metric governance and validation
P&G AI factory and DBS 2-in-a-box examples
One business-facing CDAO; CAIO only if AI core

shorts.stem: Distinguish descriptive, predictive and causal questions and state the three conditions for causality, with a marketing example of each.
shorts.model: Concept: analytics questions come in three types and each needs a different method, which is why Tadelis's second principle is to label the question before answering. Mechanism: descriptive asks what happened ('which campaign had the highest CTR?'); predictive asks what is likely to happen ('who will churn next month?'); causal asks what happens if we change something ('did the price cut cause the sales lift?'). Causality requires three conditions: X happens before Y, X and Y are associated, and there is no competing explanation. Most 'AI insights' meet only the second. Example: 'who is at risk of churn' is predictive, but 'whose behaviour will change if we offer a discount' is causal, and they need different data (an experiment, not a model score). The retargeting case met association but failed the no-competing-explanation test because prior intent explained the 10% conversion rate. Limitation and so-what: AI will answer any of the three confidently even when the method is wrong, so validate causal claims in proportion to the stakes, with experiments, holdouts or quasi-experimental designs such as difference-in-differences.
shorts.minimum: Descriptive = what happened; predictive = what will happen; causal = what if we change X. Causality: X before Y, associated, no competing explanation. AI usually only shows association.
marking: Correct definitions of all three types
Churn predictive vs causal trap or retargeting example
Method implication: experiments for causal claims

shorts.stem: Explain Li & Xie's framework for turning images into marketing variables and why 'extract every feature' is the wrong approach.
shorts.model: Concept: unstructured data such as images comes with no ready-made variables, so someone must decide which features matter and how to extract them; Li & Xie's framework is business outcome → choose feature level → measure → validate. Mechanism: low-level features (colour in HSV space, brightness, clarity, composition) are objective, fast and scalable via tools like Pillow or k-means; mid-level features (objects, faces, logos) use pretrained vision APIs or fine-tuned CNNs such as ResNet; high-level features (emotion, aesthetics, quality) use CNNs trained on human judgements and map directly onto marketing theory. Effects depend on context: faces lift engagement on Twitter but not Instagram; consumer selfies get likes while brand selfies drive purchase intent; warmer, clearer Airbnb photos go with higher demand. Example: Nike ad, dark high-contrast background (low), product only (mid), 'high-performance tech' feel (high), with copy aligned to the visual. Limitation and so-what: extracting every feature wastes effort and invites spurious correlations; pick the level that matches the decision, control for low-level features like colour so you do not credit content for a colour effect, and validate AI scores against human labels, as the Chanel vs Dior exercise required.
shorts.minimum: Outcome → feature level → measure → validate. Low = colour/brightness; mid = objects/faces/logos; high = emotion/aesthetics. Match level to decision; validate against humans.
marking: Three levels correctly defined with examples
Why not extract everything: match to decision, control for colour

shorts.stem: How can a firm derive sentiment from free-text reviews, and what challenges did the Boost Juice exercise reveal?
shorts.model: Concept: text analytics extracts sentiment, topics and emotions from unstructured reviews so managers can compare outlets and find issues. Mechanism, from simple to advanced: lexicon or dictionary methods (VADER, LIWC) count positive and negative words; supervised machine learning trains a classifier on labelled reviews; pretrained transformers (BERT) are fine-tuned for sentiment; LLM prompting scores from −1 to +1 and can return topics and reasons zero-shot. Example: in the Boost exercise VADER scored the review 'Product's great but no system: 15 + 30 min waits' as +0.81 and 'Terrible experience, wrong juice three times' as +0.42, while a contextual LLM reading gave −0.4 and −0.9; both methods ranked Outlet 2 above Outlet 1, but the lexicon hid how bad Outlet 1 was (−0.06 vs −0.58). Topic analysis showed six of ten Outlet 1 reviews complained about waits and four about rude staff. Challenges: sarcasm, mixed reviews, negation ('not bad'), Singlish and typos, domain words ('ice' as a complaint), emojis and encoding, aspect-level sentiment, LLM consistency and cost, and the need to validate scores against human labels. Limitation: ten reviews per outlet over-represent extremes, so treat results as a descriptive signal to investigate, not proof of cause (Tadelis principles 2 and 3).
shorts.minimum: Methods: lexicon, supervised ML, transformers, LLM prompting. Boost: VADER misread mixed/negated reviews; LLM showed Outlet 1 far worse. Validate against humans; small sample is descriptive only.
marking: Names at least three methods in order of sophistication
Boost example with a mis-scored review
Lists several challenges (sarcasm, negation, Singlish, mixed reviews)

shorts.stem: 'We only use vendors' models; we didn't train them.' Are you responsible for bias, IP and privacy risks? Explain and give the controls.
shorts.model: Concept: yes; AI risk is both inherited (baked in by the vendor through training data, labels and objective) and added (introduced by you through prompts, pasted data, how much you edit and what you publish), and both land on the brand. Mechanism: you chose the vendor and chose to publish, and customers, regulators and media blame the deployer, not the model provider; NEDA was blamed for Tessa, not X2AI. Bias can enter through your own objective with perfect data (the STEM ad shown to more men because a cost-minimising algorithm bought cheaper male impressions). IP: publishing infringing output is fully your added risk, and purely AI output may not be copyrightable in the US. Privacy: pasting customer data into public tools (Samsung) and inferring sensitive traits (Target) are both yours. Example controls: vendor due diligence on licensed data, indemnities and retention; a data-classification policy for which data may enter which tool; subgroup testing of outputs; human review with prompt and edit logs; an Ethical Matrix by stakeholder and severity; the NIST Govern–Map–Measure–Manage loop. Limitation and so-what: inherited risk is largely a black box you cannot audit, so control what you can and keep evidence of oversight; 'not building the model does not remove your responsibility.'
shorts.minimum: Yes: inherited and added risk both land on you; you chose the vendor and chose to publish (NEDA). Controls: due diligence, data policy, subgroup tests, human review with logs, risk map.
marking: Defines inherited vs added and says both are yours
Gives the 'you chose vendor and publish / brand gets blamed' mechanism with a case
Covers bias, IP and privacy each with an example
Names at least four concrete controls

shorts.stem: A model has excellent overall accuracy. Can it still be biased? Explain using the three sources of bias and say how you would detect it.
shorts.model: Concept: yes, in all three cases, because aggregate accuracy hides patterned unfairness. Mechanism: with biased training data the model accurately predicts a biased label; the US health algorithm predicted cost, which is lower for Black patients at the same sickness level, so it under-flagged them even with race removed, because proxies carry the bias. With non-representative data the majority dominates the average; Gender Shades tools looked accurate overall but failed darker-skinned women. With the wrong metric the model hits its objective and the harm is a side effect; the gender-neutral STEM ad went to more men because women cost more per impression. Detection: disaggregate performance and delivery by subgroup (race, gender, age, geography); apply MIT SMR's Explainable Fairness by comparing outcomes after controlling for legitimate factors and setting thresholds such as the four-fifths rule; red-team the system against every red cell of the Ethical Matrix; benchmark, mindful of Goodhart's law. Limitation and so-what: deciding which factors count as legitimate is an ethics and policy question, not a maths problem (FICO scores look neutral but carry redlining history), so fairness needs owners and policy, not only tests.
shorts.minimum: Yes: biased label (health cost), under-represented groups (Gender Shades), wrong objective (STEM ads). Detect by disaggregating by subgroup, fairness thresholds, red teaming.
marking: Says yes and explains why accuracy hides bias
All three sources with the matching case
Removing race fails because of proxies
Detection: disaggregate by subgroup plus one more method
Legitimacy is a policy question caveat

shorts.stem: Given the lawsuits, should a marketing team use generative AI images at all? Give a reasoned recommendation with guardrails.
shorts.model: Concept: yes, with guardrails; a blanket ban gives up real efficiency while uncontrolled use creates legal and reputational exposure. Mechanism: IP risk is inherited (did the vendor have rights to its training data?) and added (does the output you publish infringe?). The legal landscape is unsettled: Bartz v. Anthropic found training on legally acquired books to be fair use but pirated copies not, driving a US$1.5bn settlement; Getty v. Stability (UK) found no copyright liability but trademark infringement from reproduced watermarks; NYT v. OpenAI and Andersen v. Stability are ongoing; and purely AI-generated output may not be copyrightable in the US, so competitors could reuse it. Recommendation: use enterprise tools with licensed training data and IP indemnity (e.g., Microsoft's Copilot Copyright Commitment); ban prompts naming living artists, brands, celebrities or 'in the style of'; run similarity and reverse-image checks plus legal review for hero assets; add meaningful human creative input and log prompts and edits to support authorship and show no wilful copying; track key cases. Limitation and so-what: 'fair use is not a get-out-of-jail-free card', wilful infringement can cost up to US$150,000 per work, and the IAB found 70% of marketers have already had an AI incident, so the guardrails are the price of the efficiency.
shorts.minimum: Yes with guardrails: indemnified licensed tools, no 'in the style of' prompts, similarity checks, human input plus prompt logs, monitor cases. Pure AI output may not be copyrightable.
marking: At least two cases cited correctly
Ownership point: AI output may not be copyrightable
shorts.source: S9 slides 19–24; Q6; HBR IP article

shorts.stem: Target predicted a customer's pregnancy from shopping data without any data leak. Is this a privacy breach? What controls should a marketer adopt?
shorts.model: Concept: yes, it is a privacy harm through inference, the second kind of added privacy risk alongside input leakage. Mechanism: AI personalisation can infer sensitive attributes people never disclosed (pregnancy, health, financial distress, sexual orientation); the firm created sensitive data and acted on it, revealing it to the family. Legality may be grey because the purchase data was collected lawfully, but it fails the reasonable-expectations or 'creepiness' test and destroys trust, which matters because the CMR reading shows 70% of consumers are uneasy about data collection even though 64% engage more with personalised brands. Example: Target reportedly hid baby ads among unrelated products so they looked random, which disguises rather than solves the problem; Samsung's ban after engineers leaked code is the contrasting leakage case. Controls: flag sensitive inferred categories and require opt-in before using them; do not build or sell such profiles; collect and keep only what is needed; transparent data use with real opt-outs; privacy by design, anonymisation and federated learning (Apple ATT, Google Gboard); monitor and restrict sensitive profiling, with a privacy impact assessment for new targeting. Limitation and so-what: the paradox is real, consumers want relevance and fear misuse, so the goal is 'personalisation with protection' balanced on trust and transparency.
shorts.minimum: Yes: inference harm; the firm created sensitive data and acted on it, failing reasonable expectations. Controls: flag inferred sensitive categories, opt-in, minimisation, transparency, no sensitive profiles.
marking: Identifies inference (not leakage) as the mechanism
At least four controls from slide 30 / CMR

shorts.stem: Explain how AI governance should classify and control risks, and how the Ethical Matrix and NIST framework fit together.
shorts.model: Concept: AI governance is systematic monitoring of the whole AI workflow, not a one-off approval. Mechanism: first assess inherited and added risk; then classify each risk as deliberate (someone chose it or accepted a known trade-off) or accidental (it emerged unintended). Deliberate risks need policy, incentive and accountability controls, for example a written fairness requirement, a named owner and KPIs that include reach parity when management accepts a cost-vs-reach trade-off; accidental risks need detection, monitoring and review controls such as red teaming, subgroup audits and four-eye sign-off when an image generator stereotypes a group.
