Then map each risk by stakeholder and severity (likelihood × impact) in an Ethical Matrix: rows are stakeholders with vulnerable subgroups split out, columns are concerns, cells coloured red, yellow or green, with harm to vulnerable groups or a legal hard constraint automatically red; it is a living document. Example: the class exercise on a government financial-literacy campaign put cost-driven exclusion and scam cloning at severity 9. NIST's Govern–Map–Measure–Manage ties it into a repeatable loop: Govern sets culture and owners, Map is the matrix, Measure is red teaming, benchmarking and subgroup metrics, Manage is prioritising and responding. Limitation: if risk cannot be reliably measured, perhaps AI should not be used in that context; the auditor finds problems, leadership decides.
shorts.minimum: Assess inherited/added; classify deliberate (policy, accountability) vs accidental (detection, review); map stakeholder × severity in an Ethical Matrix; run the NIST Govern–Map–Measure–Manage loop.
marking: Deliberate → policy; accidental → detection, with an example of each
NIST four steps mapped to the tools
Living document / may decide not to use AI

shorts.stem: Where do typical marketing AI uses fall in the EU AI Act's risk tiers, and what is the key insight about how tiers are assigned?
shorts.model: Concept: the EU AI Act is binding law that sorts AI systems into four tiers, unacceptable, high, limited and minimal, based on how and where a system is used, not on the underlying technology. Mechanism: unacceptable (banned) covers manipulative techniques and systems that exploit vulnerabilities due to age, disability or social or economic situation in ways that distort behaviour and cause significant harm; high-risk covers areas such as credit scoring and access to essential services, close to marketing for financial products; limited risk carries transparency duties, so chatbots must disclose they are AI and deepfakes and AI-generated content must be labelled (Article 50 duties applying from August 2026); minimal covers most copywriting help, recommendation engines and spam filters. Example: a financial-literacy ad for lower-income citizens is not banned because it aims to help, but its AI content would need labelling in the EU, and the vulnerability clause warns against dark patterns on that audience. Limitation and so-what: the same model can sit in different tiers depending on use, so governance must assess each use case, which matches MIT SMR's advice to audit one use case at a time; by contrast NIST is voluntary and process-based, and Singapore's IMDA framework is guidance, not EU-style law.
shorts.minimum: Tiers: unacceptable, high, limited, minimal, by use not technology. Chatbots/deepfakes = limited (disclose/label). Most marketing = minimal; financial products near high.
marking: Assigned by use and context, not technology
Same model, different tiers insight; contrast with NIST

shorts.stem: Why is changing a colour or a model's face between segments not personalisation? What would make it personalisation?
shorts.model: Concept: the project brief states that randomly changing a colour or a face is not personalisation. Personalisation requires a genuine link between a segment's underlying motivation (Maslow need, usage occasion, experience level, aesthetic preference) and the specific creative choices (composition, palette, copy, tone, imagery, CTA). Mechanism: two conditions make the link real. The segments must be identifiable on the ad platform, otherwise the variant cannot be delivered; and every creative lever must trace back to segment evidence, ideally a verbatim quote or a metric from the research. Brand elements are held constant so that differences are visibly segment logic. Example: Nespresso sold one machine as an iced café treat to Gen-Z (belonging/esteem; pastel Vertuo Pop, two friends, 'Café at home, minus the queue'), as ten quiet minutes to time-poor parents (self-care; warm morning light, subscription CTA) and as a fair-price upgrade to switchers (value; price badge, trade-in). A contrast check explains why each other segment would scroll past. Limitation: with simulated research the links are hypotheses, so the team planned a synthetic ad test and then a real A/B test on CTR and incremental sales.
shorts.minimum: Cosmetic change has no link to motivation. Personalisation = identifiable segment + each creative lever traced to the segment's need/evidence, with brand held constant. Nespresso: one machine, three needs.
marking: Nespresso example with at least two levers
shorts.source: Group project brief; Nespresso Prompt Pack v2, Prompt C

shorts.stem: What makes a segment 'usable' for personalised advertising, and why did the Nespresso team drop some segments?
shorts.model: Concept: Session 1 targeting evaluates segments on size, growth, alignment and competition for ROI; the project adds a hard requirement from the brief, identifiability on a real ad platform. The prompt pack scores each candidate on size, value, distinctiveness of response (would a different message change behaviour?) and identifiability (exact Meta routes: core demographics, detailed interests, life events, custom audiences from pixel or CRM, lookalikes, Advantage+ self-selection). Mechanism: a segment that fails any one is dropped; a psychologically interesting but untargetable segment is explicitly unusable. Example: Nespresso's six synthetic segments were cut to three with clear funnel roles (acquire Gen-Z aspirants via interests and café-hopping signals; retain time-poor owners via CRM lists; convert value switchers via Dolce Gusto owners and 11.11 timing). Rejected segments were too small, too similar in response or not reachable. Limitation: segment sizes from synthetic data are guesses; Meta Audience Insights and a few real interviews per segment are needed to confirm size and difference before spending.
shorts.minimum: Usable = sizeable, valuable, different in response, identifiable on the platform. Drop segments that are too small, too similar or unreachable, even if psychologically interesting.
shorts.source: Group Project Master Prompt Pack, Phase 2; Nespresso pack Part 1

shorts.stem: How should synthetic market research results be treated in the project report, and what must the methods section contain?
shorts.model: Concept: results from LLM personas are simulated, so the brief and Session 2 require them to be presented as hypotheses, not findings. Mechanism: the methods section must make the work reproducible: the exact questions (summarised by block, full wording in the appendix), the number of participants and how they were generated (Nespresso: 150 respondents, 14 questions, six independent chats of 25), the independence and steering instructions used, and the analysis method (an analyst prompt, two independent analyst runs with an 88% agreement check, counts cross-checked against raw data, one miscount corrected). It must then discuss validity honestly against the four cons: hallucination, bias amplification (the 85% female skew and halal-only-among-Malay pattern led the team to avoid demographic targeting), regression to the mean (template repetition) and trained positivity (polite answers). Example: each limitation should lead to a concrete decision in the report. Limitation: even with all this, the professor's stance is 'apply but remain cautious', so the conclusion should name the human validation step, interviews and a live A/B test.
shorts.minimum: Treat as hypotheses, say they are simulated. Report questions, N and generation method, analysis and cross-checks, and the four validity concerns with the decisions they drove.
marking: Reproducible methods: questions, N, generation, analysis
shorts.source: Nespresso Prompt Pack v2, Prompts D and G; S2 slides 25, 33

shorts.stem: What risks does a personalised, AI-generated ad campaign like the Nespresso project create, and how should the report address them?
shorts.model: Concept: Session 9 says risk is inherited from the vendor and added by what you prompt, paste and publish; the project adds AI-generated images and segment profiling, so it carries bias, IP and privacy risk. Mechanism: bias – image generators may stereotype a segment (the team saw an 85% female skew), so prompts should specify diversity and outputs be reviewed before publishing; IP – generated visuals may resemble protected work and purely AI output may not be copyrightable, and the real Nespresso logo is used, so the appendix states academic use and logs prompts, iterations and human edits; privacy and creepiness – targeting by life events or inferred traits can feel like surveillance, so the team used behaviour and interest signals, not inferred sensitive attributes, and avoided gender or ethnic targeting; disclosure – IAB data show Gen Z is sceptical of AI ads but 73% accept them when disclosed. Example: the AI tool disclosure table (tool, use, human check, who) and the note that offers are illustrative. Limitation: a single risk slide with an Ethical Matrix (stakeholder × severity) would make the governance explicit, which is what the Session 9 exercise trains.
shorts.minimum: Bias in generated imagery, IP on visuals and logo, privacy/creepiness in targeting, disclosure. Address with prompt rules, human review, logged prompts, academic-use note, behaviour-based targeting, AI disclosure.
shorts.source: S9 slides 8, 24, 30; Nespresso Prompt Pack v2, Prompt F; S4 slide 34

cases.scenario: Kopi Kaki, a Singapore ready-to-drink coffee brand, wants to launch a low-sugar oat-milk latte in cans. Budget for research is small and the launch date is eight weeks away. The brand manager proposes using an LLM to simulate 200 consumers aged 25–40 in Singapore, asking whether they would consider the product, which brands they would compare it with, whether a S$3.50 price is fair, and the product's strengths and weaknesses. The first run shows 92% would consider it, every respondent names the same three competitors, and almost no one calls the price too high. The manager is delighted and wants to take the results to the board as evidence of demand.

questions.q: Which Session 2 validity concerns are visible in these first results, and what in the output points to each?
questions.model: Trained behaviour: 92% consideration and few price complaints suggest polite, agreeable responses from harmlessness tuning rather than real demand. Regression to the mean: every respondent naming the same three competitors shows answers collapsing to the average internet view with too little spread. Possible hallucination in prompt interpretation: the model may infer that a 25–40 Singapore consumer is health-conscious and premium-minded. Bias amplification is also plausible if the persona set leans toward one profile. The 'suspiciously uniform' pattern is the signal; real consumers disagree more.

questions.q: How should the manager redesign the prompts and process before trusting any numbers?
questions.model: Run several independent chats with smaller batches rather than one chat of 200, and instruct the model to treat each consumer as independent and randomly varied, allowing some to reject oat milk, prefer sweet drinks or ignore new brands. Separate facts given in the prompt from assumptions the model adds, and ask for honest negatives. Vary persona detail (PyMC Labs style) and compare runs for stability. Use a second analyst pass to count answers and cross-check the tallies against the raw text. Then write a limitations section stating the results are simulated, not findings, exactly as the Nespresso project did.

questions.q: Should the results go to the board as evidence of demand? Give the professor's stance and a practical recommendation.
questions.model: No. The professor's conclusion is 'apply but remain cautious': synthetic research is valuable for speed, scale and cost, but has severe validity concerns. Present it as exploratory hypotheses that shaped the concept and questionnaire, not as demand evidence. Recommend a quick human check within budget: a small quota sample of 30–50 real consumers in the segment, or an in-market test such as a pre-order page or a two-week pilot in a few outlets, and compare the human answers with the synthetic ones to calibrate how far to trust the LLM for this category in future.

cases.scenario: Kaya Kopi is a 40-year-old family coffee roaster in Singapore with three outlets and a small online shop (6% of revenue). The second-generation owner wants to grow online sales among 25–40-year-olds. A boutique agency quotes S$4,000 per month for social content. Her niece, a marketing graduate, proposes making all content in-house with Canva, ChatGPT and an AI video tool, and running a two-week Instagram test: AI-only versus agency-made, each in two formats (static post and 30-second reel) and two objectives (recipes versus heritage story), with equal S$60 budgets per ad. The owner worries the brand's heritage will feel fake, and that customers will notice AI imagery of the roastery and its signature tins.

questions.q: Design the test properly. What should be held constant, what should be measured, and which metric should decide the budget split?
questions.model: Hold constant the media budget per ad, the run dates, the audience definition and the brand elements (logo, colours, tin design), and run the cells in parallel on Meta's experimentation tool, as Timperio did with 12 ads and equal budgets. Measure not just interactions, which reels inflate with cheap views, but likes, saves, link clicks and ideally website visits and sales, since the business goal is online revenue. Include the agency fee in cost per result, otherwise the comparison understates the agency's true cost by several times. Decide on cost per meaningful interaction and, best of all, incremental conversions using a holdout audience, because Meta's delivery algorithm chooses who sees each ad and can create audience differences that are not creative effects. Treat a two-week test as directional and repeat it.

questions.q: What prompting and brand-fidelity problems should the niece expect, and how should she handle them?
questions.model: She should expect the Timperio problems: AI image tools will not reproduce the real signature tins and roastery accurately, text inside images will render badly, hands and details will look wrong, and vague prompts will produce generic 'coffee stock photo' scenes that drift to the average. The fixes are to composite real product photography over AI backgrounds, keep captions and text as overlays, write prompts that specify objective, audience, brand voice, palette, composition and what to avoid, and document every prompt and parameter so the twelve pieces share one look and voice. Every piece needs a human check for hallucinated claims such as invented health benefits or false origin stories, and for IP or likeness issues. Prompting here is a strategic skill, not a shortcut.

questions.q: Should Kaya Kopi disclose AI use, and what overall model (agency, in-house, hybrid) would you recommend? Justify with course evidence.
questions.model: Yes, disclose where AI is material, especially AI video and images. The IAB finds Gen Z are the most sceptical (39% negative) and call AI brands inauthentic, yet 73% say disclosure would not reduce purchase likelihood and clear disclosure is a top attention driver. For a heritage brand, being found out would cost more trust than being open. Recommend a hybrid: an AI-first in-house co-pilot for high-volume reels, recipes and seasonal posts, where Timperio's AI-only ads won on cost and likes; agency or professional photography for flagship heritage pieces and product-accurate informative visuals, where the agency won; human review and brand checklists before publishing, since 70% of marketers have had an AI incident; and monthly tests with like-rate and click-through as decision metrics. Invest in the niece's prompting skills rather than paying per asset.

cases.scenario: Lotus Lane is a chain of 12 bubble-tea kiosks in Singapore MRT stations. Each kiosk receives a fixed batch of fresh tapioca pearls every morning; unsold pearls are discarded at closing. A vendor pitches an AI pricing system with two modules. Module A changes drink prices through the day using weather, station footfall, time and remaining pearl stock, and recommends a daily price schedule learned from past sales. Module B pushes personalised app offers using each customer's purchase history, phone model and location, and proposes showing higher base prices to customers it predicts are less price-sensitive. The founder likes the projected 12% margin gain but has seen the Delta story and worries about backlash in a market where many customers are students.

questions.q: Classify Modules A and B using Kopalle's four Ps and the course's distinction between dynamic and surveillance pricing. Which raises more trust and legal risk, and why?
questions.model: Module A prices on Periods (time, footfall), Places (station) and Products (freshness and remaining stock), using non-personal market data. That is classic dynamic pricing in the accepted family, like surge or expiry markdowns. Module B prices on People using personal data (history, device, location) to estimate willingness to pay and shows higher base prices, which is surveillance pricing. It carries the trust and legal risk: Delta had to back down on perception alone, New York requires a notice when an algorithm uses personal data and Connecticut when it raises a price, and FPF warns that device type and inferred traits sit on the 'sometimes or never permitted' side. With a student customer base, hidden mark-ups would read as exploiting ability rather than willingness to pay, the American Prospect critique.

questions.q: Module A learns a daily schedule from past sales. Using the ML versus RL distinction and the Roast & Reward logic, what weakness should the founder look for, and how should the system learn prices?
questions.model: A schedule predicted from past sales is one-off machine learning: it forecasts demand at each hour but does not treat the day as a chain of decisions. Like the ML adviser in Roast & Reward, it can ignore remaining pearl stock and the end-of-day waste, selling out before the evening rush or leaving pearls to be discarded. The system should behave like an RL agent: observe the state (weather, footfall, hour, stock), set a price, record the reward (profit minus waste), and learn a policy that paces stock, marking down late if behind pace and holding price if ahead. It should explore early with a spread of prices across kiosks, then exploit, keeping a small share of ongoing tests as A/B cells or bandits, since station patterns shift with school terms. Humans should set floors, ceilings and the markdown rule.

questions.q: Recommend how Lotus Lane should implement pricing, including framing, disclosure and governance. Justify with course evidence.
questions.model: Do the safe step first: get the uniform menu price right across kiosks, since ZipRecruiter's biggest gain (+55%) came from fixing the base price and personalisation added only 19% with far more risk. Deploy Module A with human-approved guardrails, including a daily waste report. For Module B, personalise discounts, not prices: keep one public base price and send earned offers (first-visit, lapsed-customer, student-hour deals) from a real baseline, because '$1 off for you' respects the reference price while 'your price is higher' breaks it, and fake 'was' prices are deceptive. Use behaviour the customer knowingly shared (app purchases), not inferred traits like phone model. Disclose in plain language in the app and explain why an offer appears, as FPF recommends. Follow FPF's seven steps: map data, test for bias across customer groups, set allowed and never-allowed data rules, protect vulnerable groups, and align the vendor by contract, keeping final pricing decisions in-house. Measure incremental margin with holdout kiosks and watch churn and social sentiment, since backlash is the cost the models leave out.

cases.scenario: KopiKart, a Singapore online grocer, launched a customer-service chatbot built on an off-the-shelf LLM with a short system prompt. Within a month, complaints rose. Customers say the bot gives confident but wrong delivery slots, repeats 'please rephrase' when they ask about refunds and substitutions in one message, and never offers a human; one customer typed 'agent' eleven times. Internal data show the bot cut cost per contact by 40%, but the share of issues fully resolved in self-service is 18% and repeat-purchase rates among customers who used the bot fell 6 percentage points. The CEO wants to add a voice line next quarter and asks whether to fine-tune a private model instead. The product team has two engineers and no ML specialists; delivery policies and promotions change weekly.

questions.q: Diagnose KopiKart's chatbot problems using the session's frameworks. Which are technology problems and which are design or psychology problems?
questions.model: Wrong delivery slots are a grounding problem: an off-the-shelf model is answering operational facts from memory (hallucination) instead of from systems of record. Failing on 'refunds and substitutions in one message' is a multi-intent understanding failure, surprising for Gen-AI and probably caused by a thin system prompt. No path to a human is CMR's number one irritant and a design choice: the bot was deployed to contain customers and cut cost (40% saving, the visible benefit) while resolution is only 18% and repeat purchase fell, the hidden cost. Expectations and the bias against bots (HBR, −8.5%) amplify every failure. So one technology fix (grounding) and mostly design and psychology fixes (expectations, handover, tone).

questions.q: Should KopiKart fine-tune a private model as the CEO suggests? Recommend an architecture and justify it.
questions.model: No. Fine-tuning suits a large enterprise with stable, specialised knowledge and ML talent; KopiKart has two engineers, no ML specialists, and weekly-changing policies, so a fine-tuned model would be expensive and stale within a week. Recommend off-the-shelf plus RAG: ingest delivery policies, substitution rules, promo pages and FAQs as chunked embeddings, and connect delivery slots and order status to the order system via API so operational facts come from systems of record, never guesses (Microsoft pass 4). Update a document, not the model. Add a system prompt that sets expectations, repeats back multi-part requests (active listening), and defines escalation triggers with a context summary. Measure resolution, repeat purchase and NPS, not only cost per contact.

questions.q: Advise on the planned voice line: what should KopiKart do first, and which tier should it choose?
questions.model: Fix the text bot first; voice amplifies every weakness because customers expect split-second answers, interrupt, cannot scroll back and carry emotion in their voice. Then start with one high-volume scenario, such as 'where is my delivery', with a clear task, grounded data and an escalation trigger (Microsoft: one rock-solid scenario beats five shaky ones). Choose Tier 2, generative AI voice grounded in order data, the mainstream sweet spot for order tracking and billing; Tier 1 IVR is too rigid for substitutions, and Tier 3 real-time speech-to-speech is costly and only worth it where conversation is the brand. Design receipts (repeat the slot and order before changing anything), latency messages, keypad fallback, and hand-off with context. Test a dozen messy calls and rerun after each change before scaling.

cases.scenario: Lumi Skincare, a Singapore DTC brand, hired its first data analyst and gave every marketer access to an AI assistant connected to the sales database. Within weeks the brand team reported three 'insights': (1) customers who received the loyalty-app push notification bought 2.4 times more often than those who did not, so push should be sent to everyone; (2) a churn model flags 12,000 'at-risk' customers, so all should get a 20% voucher; (3) Instagram posts featuring a model's face get 60% more likes than product-only posts, so all future posts should show faces. The regional team defines 'active customer' as a purchase in 90 days; the e-commerce team uses 180 days. The CMO is pleased that analysis now takes minutes rather than weeks and wants to double down.

questions.q: Apply Tadelis's principles to the three 'insights'. Which question type is each, and what is wrong with the conclusion drawn?
questions.model: Insight 1 is a descriptive association presented as causal: customers who opted into push are more engaged to begin with (selection bias), so 2.4× does not mean push caused purchases; it fails the no-competing-explanation condition, like eBay's branded search. Insight 2 confuses predictive with causal: 'who is at risk' is predictive, 'whose behaviour will change if we give a voucher' is causal; blanket vouchers waste margin on customers who would churn anyway or who would stay anyway. Insight 3 is descriptive and context-dependent: Li & Xie show faces lift social engagement but product images drive purchase intent, and likes are not the decision metric. Underlying all three: AI answered before the question was labelled, polished output raised confidence not truth, and the two 'active customer' definitions mean the metrics are not governed.

questions.q: Design the analyses Lumi should run instead for insights 1 and 2.
questions.model: Insight 1: run a randomised holdout, send the push to a random treatment group and withhold it from a comparable control group, then compare purchase rates; incremental lift is treatment minus control, as in the prospecting vs retargeting table where a 10% rate turned out to be only +0.5 pp incremental. Report cost per incremental purchase. Insight 2: use the churn model to identify the at-risk pool, then run an uplift experiment, randomly giving the voucher to half the pool and none to the other half, to measure whose behaviour actually changes; target vouchers only at segments with positive incremental retention, and validate that the model's scores are stable. Before either, govern the metric: one definition of 'active customer' agreed across teams (Airbnb Minerva), so both experiments measure the same outcome.

questions.q: The CMO wants to 'double down' on fast AI analysis. What governance and organisational advice would you give, drawing on P&G, DBS and Davenport & Bean?
questions.model: Speed is efficiency, not decision quality; double down on the guardrails, not just the access. Set up a small hub (the analyst plus a metric owner) that governs definitions, maintains a single source of truth and validates any analysis that moves budget or pricing, with triage so low-stakes questions move fast and high-stakes ones get review of question, method and counterfactual. Keep marketers as embedded 'spokes' who share KPIs with the analyst (DBS 2-in-a-box) so analysis stays decision-first. Build a light 'AI factory' habit: reusable, documented queries and metric definitions (P&G's shared platform). Invest in culture and training on how models go wrong, since 92% of leaders say culture, not technology, is the barrier; reward truth-seeking, so the brand team is praised for discovering that push was not incremental rather than for a flattering number. Measure GenAI gains with controlled experiments rather than claims.

cases.scenario: SiloBank, a Singapore digital bank, plans a 'Save Smart' campaign to get young gig workers to open savings accounts. Marketing will use a gen-AI tool to produce ad copy and images of 'typical gig workers', and a vendor's targeting algorithm will optimise sign-ups per dollar across Meta and TikTok using the bank's transaction data plus a data broker's income estimates. A chatbot built on an off-the-shelf LLM will answer product questions. A junior marketer has already pasted a sample of 2,000 customer transaction records into a public AI tool to 'get persona ideas'. The campaign lead argues the vendor is responsible for any algorithm issues since SiloBank did not build it.

questions.q: Identify the main risks across the create, target and live stages, tagging each as inherited or added and deliberate or accidental.
questions.model: Create: stereotyped or stigmatising images of gig workers (bias sources 1 and 2; inherited plus added; accidental); hallucinated financial facts in copy or chatbot answers about interest rates or terms (HBR misapply; added; accidental); IP exposure from generated images and possible lack of copyright in pure AI output (inherited plus added); input leakage from the 2,000 records pasted into a public tool (privacy; added; accidental). Target: optimising sign-ups per dollar may under-deliver to costlier or harder-to-reach subgroups such as older or non-English-speaking gig workers (bias source 3, the STEM-ads effect; added; deliberate trade-off); inferring income from broker data is sensitive profiling and mis-targeting via proxies (privacy inference and bias; inherited plus added). Live: an official-looking savings offer aimed at a financially stressed group is a template for scam cloning (misuse by third parties, victims' misadventure); undisclosed AI use discovered later (deliberate; trust). The lead's claim is wrong: not building the model does not remove responsibility.

questions.q: Score the three most severe risks (likelihood × impact, 1–3 each) and build a mini stakeholder × risk map.
questions.model: Cost-driven exclusion of costlier subgroups: likelihood 3, impact 3, severity 9, since the algorithm's objective guarantees it and it defeats the campaign's purpose. Scam cloning of an official-looking financial offer to a vulnerable group: 3 × 3 = 9. Income inference and profiling plus the leaked records: 2 × 3 = 6, with the leak already realised. Stereotyped imagery: 3 × 2 = 6. Hallucinated rates in chatbot copy: 2 × 3 = 6. Mini matrix: rows are targeted gig workers (red on exclusion, scams, profiling), vulnerable subgroups such as older or non-English speakers (red on exclusion and scams), excluded or mislabelled workers (red on proxy mis-targeting), SiloBank and staff (red on leak, hallucinated facts, backlash), regulators and society (amber on trust and fair access), the data broker and ad platforms (amber on sensitive-category policy). The red cells cluster on the very people the campaign is meant to help, plus the bank's licence to operate.

questions.q: Propose controls for the top risks, labelled by control type, and frame them with NIST.
questions.model: Deliberate risks need policy and accountability: change the targeting KPI from sign-ups per dollar to sign-ups with minimum reach quotas by age, language and platform, report delivery by subgroup weekly, name an owner, and target by context and consented first-party behaviour rather than broker income estimates, with a privacy impact assessment (policy). Accidental risks need detection and review: red-team the image prompts and run a community panel of gig workers for dignity and diversity; four-eye review of all copy and chatbot answers by product and compliance experts, and ground the chatbot in approved product documents via RAG so rates come from systems of record, not guesses; immediately report and contain the leaked records, adopt a data-classification policy for which data may enter which tool, and move staff to an enterprise tool with no-training settings. Scam cloning: one official domain and channel in every ad, never ask for transfers or details, label AI content, monitor and take down clones, align with anti-scam messaging. NIST: Govern (owner, AI-use and disclosure policy), Map (this matrix), Measure (subgroup delivery, red-team results, chatbot accuracy), Manage (incident and takedown plan, matrix reviewed monthly).

cases.scenario: Lumi Cycles sells one mid-priced electric bicycle in Singapore and Kuala Lumpur. Sales come mostly from a single Instagram ad showing the bike against a skyline with the line 'Ride the future'. A new marketing lead runs LLM-based synthetic research with 120 personas and finds four candidate groups: commuters who hate MRT crowds, parents doing school runs, weekend café riders who care about looks, and 'eco-idealists' who want to cut carbon but are spread across all ages and interests. The lead wants three segment-specific static ads within two weeks and asks whether to simply recolour the current ad in three palettes and change the model's age in each version.

questions.q: Evaluate the four candidate segments using the project's usability criteria and recommend which three to keep.
questions.model: Score each on size, value, distinctiveness and identifiability. Commuters: large, high value, distinct need (reliability, time saved), identifiable through location, interests in public transport apps and commuting behaviour – keep. Parents: moderate size, high lifetime value with accessories, distinct need (safety, cargo), identifiable via life events and parenting interests – keep. Café riders: smaller but high-margin for colour variants, distinct need (esteem, aesthetics), identifiable through café, design and fashion interests – keep. Eco-idealists: psychologically appealing but spread across all demographics and interests, so not identifiable on Meta; the brief calls such a segment unusable. Drop it, or fold eco messaging into the other three as a secondary cue.

questions.q: Is recolouring the ad and changing the model's age personalisation? What should the three ads vary instead, and what stays fixed?
questions.model: No. Randomly changing a colour or a face is explicitly not personalisation. Each ad must link the segment's motivation to creative choices. Commuters: safety and time – a rush-hour street scene, headline about beating the crowd, bullet on range and charging, CTA 'Book a test ride'. Parents: safety and care – school-gate scene with child seat, calm palette, headline on safe, easy mornings, CTA on family bundle. Café riders: esteem and looks – stylised café setting, colour variants hero, headline on style, CTA for a limited colour edition. Fixed: logo, bike shown, format, claim rules. Add a contrast check explaining why each other segment would scroll past.

questions.q: Before spending the media budget, how should Lumi validate the segments and the ads, and what caveats belong in the report?
questions.model: Treat the synthetic results as hypotheses and state that they are simulated. First run a synthetic ad test with each segment's personas choosing among the three ads, looking for about 60% of each segment choosing 'its' ad, and iterate honestly if not. Then validate with humans: 10–15 interviews per segment, Meta Audience Insights for size, and a live A/B test with each ad in its audience plus a control 'average' ad, measured on CTR, cost per add-to-cart and incremental test-ride bookings rather than likes. Caveats: the four Session 2 validity concerns, any stereotyped imagery from the image generator, IP on generated visuals, and AI disclosure in the ads.

S1: Session 1 is the frame for everything else. If you can draw STP → 4Ps → funnel from memory, every later topic has a place to live.
Watch the two four-item lists: marketing-mix 4Ps versus Kopalle's dynamic-pricing 4 Ps. The exam will put both in one question.
A 'friend or foe' answer earns marks for structure, not for your opinion. Four headings, two sides each, then a conditional verdict. You have this.
S2: Four cons, in order: hallucination, bias amplification, regression to the mean, trained behaviour. Say them twice and the S2 MCQs are yours.
Participant versus twin is the single most likely S2 distinction question. Twin = calibrated on a real person's past answers. Everything else follows.
Whenever an S2 question looks like it wants a yes or no, the A+ answer is 'apply but remain cautious' plus one concrete check. That is the professor's own line.
S3: GEO in one breath: not rank but inclusion; not links but being discussed; not keywords but quotes, statistics and citations. Say it and you have the core.
The 41% figure and 'bigger gains for lower-ranked sites' are the two numbers he put on the slide. Numbers on slides become MCQs.
If a question mentions State Property, the honest timeline lesson is the A+ touch: copy cannot fix a product gap, and false claims are off limits. You know this story well.
S4: If you can say '82% vs 45%, Gen Z 39% vs 20%, 73% fine if disclosed', the IAB questions are already yours. Numbers win MCQs; feelings don't.
Timperio is a story with one twist: AI won on cost and likes, the agency won informative images, and reels beat everything. Tell the twist and add the caveats. That is the A+ answer.
Static versus DCO, mass customisation versus hyperpersonalisation: ask yourself 'when is the decision made?' and 'is it tied to a named person?' Two questions, four concepts sorted.
S5: Two numbers carry this session: +13.3% versus –2.1%, and 52% already follow one. Say the signs out loud once and they will stay put.
Every ethics or authenticity question wants the triad: credibility, transparency, reputation. Name all three, then add 'multiplicative, not additive'. That phrase is worth a mark.
Independent versus brand-owned: Miquela (Brud) versus Lu (Magazine Luiza). If a question mentions Brazil, it is Lu and it is brand-owned. You have this.
S6: Three numbers unlock most of S6: +55% (uniform), +19% (personalised), over 60% (customers better off). Say them in that order and the ZipRecruiter questions answer themselves.
When a stem says '4 Ps', pause. If pricing or Kopalle is anywhere nearby, the answer starts with People, not Product. That single pause is worth a mark or two.
RL in one breath: state, action, reward, policy, sequential, explore then exploit. If you can say that, the Roast & Reward questions are a gift, not a trap.
S7: If you can draw the three-column architecture table from memory, you already own a third of the S7 marks. RAG = open-book exam, say it out loud.
Every S7 short answer ends the same way: the problem moved from technology to psychology and design. Write that sentence and you have the conclusion mark.
Numbers to carry in: $0.70, 8.5%, 37%, 77%, 88%. Five numbers, one session, done. Breathe.
